sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
Studying Photography and Painting, Then Turning to How Images Work

Born in Mainz in 1970, Gütschow studied at the University of Fine Arts Hamburg from 1993 to 2000 and spent 1997 at the Oslo National Academy of the Arts. Her teachers included Bernhard Blume and Wolfgang Tillmans*12. Studying photography and painting together gave her a basis for asking what makes an image appear real, without treating one medium as superior to the other.

Gütschow has said that “every image has a reference outside itself”*13. A photographed tree or building retains a place, a light, and a moment. When such fragments are arranged within a historical composition, the specificity of photography and the deliberate construction of the whole can operate together. After graduation, she continued to examine how pictorial forms produce ideas of idyll and utopia*5. An interview introduced by the Academy of Media Arts Cologne describes an artist who designs images through drawing, photographic fragments, and montage*21.

The Düsseldorf School and Digital Compositing in the 1990s

When Gütschow began the LS works in the late 1990s, the precise architectural and industrial photographs of Bernd and Hilla Becher and the Düsseldorf School remained a major reference for photographic description in Germany. At the same time, digital processing was changing from a means of retouching photographs into an environment for designing entire images. In another conversation, Gütschow argued that understanding the world requires an understanding of the technologies that support its images*22.

She placed fragments made with an analog camera onto an empty digital canvas. An official text describes this “pre-photographic method,” in which the composition is determined in advance, while also referring to the documentary formats of Thomas Ruff, Thomas Struth, and Candida Höfer*17. Leaves, clouds, roads, and buildings remain tied to real sites and moments, but montage changes their distance, geography, and perspective. The Hamburger Kunsthalle presents the results as images that recall known cities and landscapes yet lead back to no actual place*6. Documentary precision and digital construction allow trust in individual details to support a nonexistent whole.

sections.title: Core Ideas
sections.body_html:
LS—Constructing Photographs Through Seventeenth- and Eighteenth-Century Landscape Painting

The LS series digitizes trees, clouds, fields, water, and buildings photographed in different places with a medium-format camera and assembles them into single landscapes. According to the official description, the process begins with a collection of analog photographs and continues in Photoshop, where Gütschow adopts the expansive perspective and theatrical arrangement of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century painting*16. Cut trees, weeds, corrugated metal, and trampled ground enter orders reminiscent of Claude Lorrain, Nicolas Poussin, and Jacob van Ruisdael.

The central issue is the compositional rule that allows foreground, middle ground, and distance to make a contemporary photograph read as “landscape.” The Museum of Contemporary Photography in Chicago exhibited LS and S as two series concerned with historical genres and photographic reference*1. The Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation likewise explains how a limited set of compositional conventions can make a photograph recognizable as a painterly landscape*11.

Why Photographed Details Make the Fictional Whole Convincing

The Metropolitan Museum of Art describes LS #3 as an image whose individual parts are photographically specific while the whole remains a calculated fabrication*2. The contours of leaves, wetness of soil, and density of clouds derive from things that stood before the camera. Fully computer-generated imagery would lack that relation from the outset. Straight photography, by contrast, cannot easily gather foreground, middle ground, and distance from separate sites and exchange their geography. Montage lets photographed fact and constructed place coexist. Once the viewer trusts the whole through the certainty of its details, the process by which a photograph is accepted as a place becomes perceptible.

S—Turning Postwar Modernist Architecture into a Nonexistent City

The S series constructs monochrome cities from buildings, roads, rubble, and people photographed in different countries. The official text connects the work to modernist faith in planning and technology, and to the expansionist thinking that continued into the 1970s. It also identifies the black-and-white format as a reference to American documentary photography of the 1960s and 1970s*17. Linear façades, pedestrian bridges, vacant lots, and damaged concrete create a fictional stage where ideals of rationality and equality have decayed. The work condenses an architectural ideology shared across nations into one nonexistent city. A Prix Pictet artist text likewise presents architecture as an expression of social ideals and explains the gathering of similar urban spaces into a single imagined metropolis*3.

Sparse Figures, Architecture, and Power

Figures appear sparsely in S, less as protagonists than as small measures of architecture and open space. The Berlinische Galerie notes that the works refer simultaneously to modern and postmodern buildings and to the accumulated conventions of architectural photography*4. The near-absence of people lends the images the appearance of neutral architectural records, yet streets, walls, plazas, and open sightlines organize movement in advance. A 2025 book talk connects Gütschow’s long-term urban research to structures of power and social control*14. The gaze that appreciates architecture as form overlaps with the system through which architecture distributes bodies.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
LS #3—Contemporary Time Inside an Ideal Landscape

LS #3 brings the stable depth of classical landscape painting into contact with the high-resolution surface of photography. The Met explains that the work was assembled from numerous photographs and consciously follows seventeenth- and eighteenth-century composition*2. Every natural element was photographed, yet the fragments do not belong to one weather system, season, or site. The image achieves the order of an ideal landscape while contemporary details interrupt its claim to timelessness, showing how landscape is repeatedly seen through earlier pictures.

LS#17 and Shifting Viewing Distance in the Large-Scale Print

From a distance, the Guggenheim’s LS#17 reads as a continuous landscape; at close range, inconsistencies in vegetation and terrain emerge*9. The museum’s artist page allows the LS works in its collection to be viewed in relation to one another*8. The large print joins the total composition associated with painting to the minute information of photography. The viewer moves back to receive the ideal scene and forward to examine origins and seams. This movement repeats the act of believing the image before testing it.

Untitled, 2001—Numbering That Withholds Geographic Identification

SFMOMA’s Untitled, 2001 withholds the location promised by the image through a title without a place name*10. Series labels and numbers reduce geographic explanation and present the works as comparable images. The cool organization recalls Düsseldorf typology, while each picture has left the record of a single subject behind and operates as a self-contained fiction assembled from memory and rules. The appearance of classification is applied to an image with no stable referent.

HC—Using Photogrammetry to Remove Central Perspective

HC photographs an urban park in as many as 150 exposures, then uses photogrammetry to generate a polygon mesh from corresponding points. According to the official account, Gütschow projects the photographic surfaces onto this three-dimensional data and converts the scene in 3D software into oblique or parallel projection, where depth lines no longer converge on a single point*18. The title derives from hortus conclusus, the enclosed garden, and refers to medieval manuscript images made before central perspective was codified. Removing the monocular perspective built into the camera gives walls, benches, plantings, and ground comparable visual weight. Photographic detail and nonphotographic space coexist within one image.

sections.title: Criticism and Reception
sections.body_html:
The 2007 LS/S Exhibition and the Early Reception of Composite Photography

In 2007, the Museum of Contemporary Photography in Chicago exhibited LS and S together. It connected the former to the pastoral order of seventeenth-century landscape painting and the latter to the ruined city of 1950s and 1960s architectural and documentary photography*1. A Newcity review that year described the color landscapes and large monochrome cityscapes as two series moving between photographic modernism and postmodernism*20. Early reception focused on the technical fluency of the composites and on the pairing of ideal nature with urban debris. The exhibition made it possible to compare how images from different eras organized social visions of the future.

Idyll, Failed Utopia, and the Contemporary City

Deichtorhallen’s exhibition IDYLLE treated the idyll as a form where dream and deception meet and placed Gütschow’s artificial landscapes within that critical lineage*7. An interview program at the Museum Angewandte Kunst framed constructed images as a way to think about “imagined reality,” rather than simply as examples of deception*13. The beauty of landscape and the deterioration of the city become different historical moments in the design of desirable societies through images.

Using the Düsseldorf School’s Documentary Clarity for a Fictional Whole

Gütschow addressed documentary reference and image construction at roughly the same time as Thomas Ruff, Andreas Gursky, and Thomas Demand. The official text for S refers to the authenticating documentary forms used by Thomas Ruff, Thomas Struth, and Candida Höfer*17. In the lineage of the Bechers, standardized conditions made architectural comparison possible. Gütschow uses comparable clarity to gather fragments from Berlin, Chicago, Kyoto, Los Angeles, New York, and Sarajevo into one city*1.

The detail of each building makes its former existence credible, but nothing proves that the buildings ever stood in one city. Gütschow’s decisive move was to direct the Düsseldorf School’s visual authority toward a fictional whole. The appearance of documentary photography shifts from a guarantee of reality into material for examining how an urban image becomes believable.

Exchanging the Rules of Landscape, City, and Perspective Through Photographic Fragments

LS borrows the foreground–middle ground–distance structure of painters such as Claude Lorrain. S combines modernist buildings from around the world with corroded walls, rubble, and vacant land in one city. Gütschow has described S as treating architecture as a representation of ideology and photographing the deterioration of structures built on faith in progress*3. HC converts photogrammetric data into parallel projection and creates a space unlike the central perspective built into a camera*19. Because all three series begin with photographic fragments, their differences can be traced to changing compositional systems. Painting, architectural ideology, optics, and software can be compared without confusing them with changes in subject matter. SFMOMA’s The More Things Change included Gütschow in a broader reexamination of the boundary between record and construction in contemporary photography*15. Across the three series, she retains photographed fragments while changing composition, geography, and perspective to test which elements make a place feel real.

beato.html.lead_html: Beato, Venice-born and naturalized British, followed British and French imperial campaigns from Crimea through India, China, and Japan. Based in Yokohama from 1863, he sold hand-colored photographic albums of Japanese landscapes and people to foreign visitors. His relationship to imperial power and the commodification of his subjects remains a subject of critical examination.
beato.html.thesis_html: Moving through the Crimea, India, China and Japan in the wake of the Anglo-French military, Beato photographed both the “aftermath” of the battlefield and the landscapes and people of the East with the same commercial eye. Based in Yokohama, he marketed hand-coloured photographic albums to foreign travellers, and his style — binding the wet-plate technique to colouring by Japanese painters — became the template for early-Meiji Yokohama photography. At the same time, his battlefield views with their arranged skeletons and his studio portraits staging the “exoticism of the East” for souvenirs embody a tension between record and commodification — and the imperial gaze — that colonial-photography scholarship continues to re-read critically today.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Felice Beato was born around 1832 in Venice and was later naturalized as a British subject. The earliest documented record of his activity is the Crimean War (1855), where he photographed alongside James Robertson. From that point he consistently followed British and French imperial campaigns*1.

After the Indian Rebellion (1857–58), he photographed the "aftermath" at Lucknow, including the Secunderbagh — a site where British forces had fought — showing scattered skeletal remains. The photographs are understood as a return visit months after the battle, and the arrangement of human remains has been questioned*2. During the Second Opium War (1860) he followed the Anglo-French forces through Beijing, Tianjin, and the Dagu Forts.

In 1863 he moved to Yokohama with the British illustrator Charles Wirgman, opening the Beato & Wirgman studio. He worked there until around 1877, selling hand-colored photographic albums of Japanese landscapes, people, and customs to foreign visitors, travelers, and diplomats*3. After leaving Yokohama he is documented in Burma (1885), Sudan (1885–86), and Korea (around 1904). He is thought to have died around 1909*4.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Beato's Japan photographs fall into two broad categories: landscapes and architecture (Mount Fuji, temples, post towns) and studio portraits of "typical Japanese" figures — geisha, samurai, craftsmen, farmers. Both were made for photographic albums sold to foreign visitors as souvenirs, based on a precise understanding of what Western consumers wanted from images of Japan*5.

Beato popularized hand-coloring of photographs in Yokohama, with the coloring usually carried out by Japanese painters. This created a distinctive hybrid production that fused Western photographic technology with Japanese pictorial tradition. The hand-colored album format became the standard for Yokohama photography in the Meiji period and was adopted by multiple Japanese photographers*6.

The staging questions around his "aftermath" photographs in India and China — rearranged bones, moved bodies — continue to be cited in discussions of documentary ethics. Beato's work embodies the tension between recording military violence and performing "Oriental otherness" for a Western commercial audience*7.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
Beato's work long occupied a marginal position in photographic history, but has undergone substantial reassessment from the late twentieth century through the development of postcolonial criticism, colonial photography studies, and Asian photographic history. MIT's Visualizing Cultures project has produced detailed analysis of his Japan photographs in the framework of "imperial gaze," advancing the critical reading of their commercial and political context*8.

The Metropolitan Museum, the Getty Museum, and the Yokohama Archives of History hold Beato's work. In Japanese photographic history, continuing research examines the influence of the wet-collodion techniques and hand-colored album format Beato brought to Yokohama on the development of early Meiji photography*9.

As visual documentation of Japan in the late Tokugawa and early Meiji periods, Beato's albums have significant historical and ethnographic value. At the same time, contemporary photographic history requires critical examination of the imperial power relations embedded in that gaze*10.

becher.html.lead_html: Bernd and Hilla Becher worked as an artistic partnership, using large-format cameras and standardized shooting conditions to document water towers, blast furnaces, winding towers, and cooling towers disappearing with the decline of coal and steel. Their book Anonyme Skulpturen and their gridded typologies transformed records of industrial architecture into works that allow viewers to compare buildings with the same function and read historical and regional variation. This page examines how their method connected postwar German photography, New Objectivity, Minimal and Conceptual art, New Topographics, and the Düsseldorf School, and considers the critical implications of that connection.
becher.html.thesis_html: The Bechers photographed vanishing industrial structures under consistent conditions and built an archive spanning several decades. Their grids and photobooks shifted the center of the work from the finish of a single print to a system that places buildings of the same type side by side so that similarities and differences can be read. Each photograph records an existing structure, while the series makes visible a plan: what to collect, under which conditions, and how to classify it. The photograph’s evidentiary force, the sculptural appearance of the subject, Minimalism’s repetition, and Conceptual art’s rules converge, bringing photography into contemporary art’s debates about space, classification, and institutions.

sections.title: The Vanishing Industrial Region and the Turn to Photography
sections.body_html:
Siegen’s Industrial Landscape—Demolition Made Photography Necessary

Bernd Becher grew up in the Siegen region, where his grandfather and uncles worked in iron mines and blast-furnace plants. Industrial facilities shaped both his family history and the everyday landscape. Hilla explained that the project also allowed Bernd to “preserve his childhood.” As industry contracted during the 1950s and 1960s, the mines and factories he had been drawing closed and were demolished faster than he could complete sketches or prints. He began taking small-camera photographs as aids to memory, then recognized that photography could respond to the speed at which the structures were disappearing.*1

Their early collaborations included timber-frame workers’ houses in the Siegen region. Repeated frontal views of the dark structural grids crossing white walls joined a record of local social history with a comparison of variations within one building type. Hilla Wobeser had formal photographic training and experience in commercial photography. She brought precise technical description of materials and structures to Bernd’s developing interest in industrial landscapes. They began working together in 1959.*25

The Met’s 2022 retrospective returned Bernd’s mining drawings and photographic collages, along with Hilla’s pre-collaboration photographs of steel wire, metal components, botanical specimens, transmission towers, and industrial-exhibition architecture, to a shared account of their development. It examined their working process through materials extending beyond finished photographs.*19 The evidence resists a simple division in which one partner supplied nostalgia and the other technical assistance. Memory of the industrial region converged with a way of isolating and clearly describing objects, and the combination developed into a long-term collaborative undertaking.

Subjective Photography and New Objectivity—Reframing Objectivity in Postwar Germany

When the Bechers began collaborating in the late 1950s, Otto Steinert’s Subjective Photography was an influential force in the reconstruction of West German photography. Steinert used photograms, stark tonal reduction, severe cropping, long exposures, negative reversal, and multiple exposure. He emphasized the creation of an image autonomous from straightforward description. His approach sought to restart avant-garde photography, interrupted by the Nazi regime and the war, through the individual artist’s formal imagination.*27

The Bechers chose fixed viewpoints, even light, and repeated shooting procedures. Authorship moved away from dramatic effects within a single image and into the rules of photography and the design of a series. The Met places their method between Steinert’s expressive direction and the lucid description associated with New Objectivity in the work of August Sander, Karl Blossfeldt, and Albert Renger-Patzsch.*3 SK Stiftung Kultur, which maintains the Becher Archive, likewise identifies early photography, nineteenth-century painting, New Objectivity, and a systematic commitment to empirical verification among the lineages that informed their work.*18 The Bechers did not simply revive New Objectivity. They used comparisons among multiple images to show how structures serving the same function assumed different forms across periods, regions, and technologies.

The method is described as Conceptual because the organizing principle lies in the plan, not because the photographs detach themselves from reality and become “concepts.” Each image remains a specific record of an existing building. The work as a whole is governed by a plan: photograph structures with the same function under the same conditions, collect them over long periods, classify them, and arrange them. Authorial decisions are distributed across the choice of subject, shooting conditions, duration of collection, taxonomy, and sequence. The plan becomes visible as the work. The Met distinguishes this rule-based method from Steinert’s Subjective Photography while placing it in relation to Minimal and Conceptual art.*3 MoMA’s history of its photography department similarly describes Information (1970) as an exhibition in which photography was deeply integrated into Conceptual work, including that of the Bechers.*21

The Decline of Coal and Steel—Industrial Architecture as Social Infrastructure

When the Bechers began photographing, the coal- and steel-based industrial infrastructure of West Germany was entering a period of closure and demolition driven by technological change and shifting markets. MoMA describes Winding Towers as part of a project that recorded, for more than forty years, industrial structures in Europe and the United States that were disappearing during the transition from an industrial to an information society.*24 SK Stiftung Kultur likewise notes that many facilities lost their overall form soon after the photographs were made, through shutdown and demolition—a condition that shaped the archive from the outset.*18 Water towers and winding towers belonged to production systems that linked extraction, transport, smelting, and storage while organizing regional employment, housing, movement, and daily schedules.

The Zollverein Coal Mine Industrial Complex in the Ruhr encompassed mine shafts, a coking plant, railways, waste heaps, miners’ housing, and welfare facilities.*23 The Bechers’ frontal photographs extract one structure from such a network and make its function and form comparable with others. MoMA’s educational material explains that they waited for overcast skies to obtain neutral light and deliberately excluded workers, whose labor would ordinarily animate the scene.*20 The buildings consequently appear with exceptional clarity, while ownership, labor conditions, accident risk, noise, smoke, and environmental damage remain difficult to read directly from the photographs. As The Met’s Zeche Hannover demonstrates, older equipment vanished rapidly during technological modernization.*30 Isolating a structure from its social setting enables comparison, while also registering the process of deindustrialization through which equipment moved from productive tool to “heritage” or “sculpture.”

sections.title: What Does Typology Make Visible?
sections.body_html:
Overcast Skies, Frontal Views, and Large-Format Cameras—Rules for Comparison

The Bechers photographed water towers, winding towers, blast furnaces, cooling towers, gas tanks, grain elevators, and other structures with large-format view cameras, usually from the front or side. They waited for softly diffused overcast light, avoided people, vehicles, strong shadows, and dramatic clouds, and kept the subject’s scale and proportion within the frame consistent. Hilla explained that they excluded the “moods” created by sunshine, snow, or moonlight so that photographs could remain comparable and the sky would not become a second subject.*1 The Canadian Centre for Architecture’s catalog record for Water Towers describes a project comprising 224 towers photographed over roughly twenty-five years, in some cases from as many as eight directions. Waiting for cloud cover, adjusting the viewpoint with ladders or scaffolding, and securing cooperation from facility managers to clear people from the frame show that the apparently uniform surface was produced through sustained decisions in the field.*33

Rules did not eliminate judgment. The photographers still had to locate a front, back, and side within the dense pipework of a blast furnace, find a position from which a smokestack carried sufficient visual weight, and adjust verticals and margins. Hilla said that large-format photography demanded decision and experience, and that each subject required them to “invent our way of seeing it.” Their objectivity was designed to bring buildings from different places and periods into a common visual field where comparison could occur.*1

What Is a Typology? From the Single Photograph to a Field of Comparison

A typology arranges several buildings with the same function in grids of four, nine, sixteen, thirty, or another number of prints. A single water tower can be read as a record or portrait of a building. In a group, the contours of tanks, supporting legs, materials, braces, and regional variations become measures against one another. Numerous variants emerge within the general category “water tower.”*3

Typology did not appear suddenly as a format into which photographs were fitted after the concept had been completed. In a 2025 art-historical study, Andrew Moisey treats the grid as an outcome of close research into industrial architecture. It preserves the specificity of each building while making human design choices for a shared function available for comparison. The photographs remain documents; standardized presentation turns those documents into a visual classification distinct from a numerical table.*36 Issues in Science and Technology similarly notes that the Bechers understood typology as a “grammar” for comprehending and comparing different structures. Classification did not erase individuality through abstraction. It revealed differences of region, material, and period within a common function.*37

MoMA likewise explains that the unified format reveals a shared basic form while preserving details specific to each structure.*29

The format took shape through experiments of the late 1960s and early 1970s. The Met’s Framework Houses, Germany combines one overall view with nine details in a “one-plus-nine” arrangement. The museum explains that an archive standardized in formal and compositional terms made comparison possible, and that an “ideal type” or prototype forms in the viewer’s mind only when multiple variants are placed together.*28

According to Hilla, the grouping began when three photographs of cooling towers were placed on a white floor and the images “started to dance.” In books, they adjusted the rhythm through page sequence; on walls, they used horizontal rows, nine-part grids, and diagonals. Typology brought the taxonomic chart and formal composition onto the same surface, turning the ordering of information into a perceptual experience.*1

This shift meant that photographic meaning no longer ended within a single frame. It emerged through comparison among images. MoMA explains that the grid allows individual towers to be compared with ease, each retaining its specificity while appearing as a variation on an ideal form.*29 Photography expanded from a single act of discovery into collection sustained over decades, and the work expanded from one print into a system encompassing selection, sequence, and spacing. An exhibition text from the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin also shows how horizontal, vertical, and diagonal reading paths generate the grid’s formal meaning.*22 Typology’s critical force lies in establishing a structure through which buildings with the same use can be read for differences of region, material, date, and alteration.

“Anonymous Sculptures” and the Readymade—From Selection to a Long-Term Archive

The term “anonymous sculptures” describes industrial structures whose forms were shaped less by a named designer than by function, technology, and accumulated modification. Blast furnaces and coal-preparation plants were built by teams of engineers and workers, then altered as machinery and pipes were added. Hilla explained that they did not emerge all at once from a single design; they changed over time. Once isolated from their surroundings and grouped together, everyday equipment appears as an autonomous system of forms.*1

The Met reads Anonyme Skulpturen as an implicit response to Marcel Duchamp’s readymade because the Bechers also selected existing objects, isolated them photographically from their functional environment, and gave them a new name and exhibition setting. In both cases, value shifts from manual fabrication alone toward decisions about what to choose, where to place it, and how to name it.*3

The Bechers’ project, however, began with the need to preserve buildings facing demolition. Hilla described field research, large-format photography, repeated standardized procedures, classification, and arrangement as developments arising from that initial need.*1 A readymade can be established through the selection of a single manufactured object and a change of exhibition setting. The Bechers’ acts of selection extended across a decades-long archive, and the photograph served both as a recontextualized work of art and as evidence of lost architecture. The present archive maintains cross-references among negatives, prints, classifications, and arrangements used in exhibitions and publications.*18

Its Conceptual character therefore lies in making the criteria of collection and the procedures of classification into part of the work. It does not replace each building with an abstract idea. Every print conveys a specific structure; the grid displays the rules through which the structures can be compared. MoMA’s departmental history places the Bechers’ exhibitions within a sequence in which Information (1970) brought photographically based Conceptual work into the museum and Projects (1975) unsettled the distinction between photographers and artists who used photography.*21 A project that began as preservation entered the institutional space shared by photography and contemporary art through procedures of selection, repetition, and classification.

Typology and Industrial Landscape—Comparing Form, Recording Place

The best-known grids suppress much local information, allowing buildings from distant countries to carry equal visual weight. At each factory or mine, however, the Bechers also photographed industrial landscapes that included relationships among structures, rail lines, roads, housing, and terrain. MoMA presented the frontal typologies as images with the clarity of an engineer’s drawing and the industrial landscapes as a form directed toward the experience of a particular place, describing them as two poles of photographic description. Images that isolate the object and images that return it to place move between formal comparison and an understanding of the industrial system.*4

This range is also visible in retrospectives and collections. Centre Pompidou’s 2004 retrospective included about forty industrial landscapes and a documentary study of the Zollern II mine made in the early 1970s, extending the account of their work from comparison among individual buildings to the record of an entire mine.*32 In Dia Art Foundation’s two-part Mines of Giraumont, Lorraine, France, attention shifts from isolated exterior views to the beams and trusses that form an underground interior structure.*34 Frontal views, industrial landscapes, and photographs of interiors or details functioned as different descriptive units through which the form and location of a facility could later be cross-checked.

Collaboration and Hilla Becher’s Printing

In the field, they used two cameras and divided limited periods of access, each returning with selected viewpoints. Hilla made most of the prints in the darkroom, while both examined negatives, camera positions, tonal density, and arrangement. From locating subjects through editing grids, each partner’s decisions revised the other’s, producing a collaborative vision that is difficult to separate into individual authorship. The professorship established in 1976 was formally held by Bernd, although institutional rules prevented their simultaneous appointment.*3

sections.title: Major Works, Photobooks, and Exhibitions
sections.body_html:
Water Towers, 1963–80—One Function Seen Across Sixteen Prints

Water Towers is a representative typology that combines towers from different places and periods in equal-sized prints, allowing the tank and its supporting structure to be compared. The Met’s work consists of sixteen photographs made between 1963 and 1980, compressing geographic distance and more than a decade into one wall-based arrangement. Buildings that fulfill the same function take on different contours in response to regional technology, materials, capacity, and connections to existing equipment. The variation becomes visually legible before it is explained in words.*6

Cooling Towers/Steel-Wood, 1972—Measuring Material Difference in Two Prints

Cooling Towers/Steel-Wood is a two-part work from 1972 that places a steel cooling tower beside a wooden one. In the National Gallery of Art’s work, the consistent framing of the two large structures makes differences in cladding, framework, and visual weight legible as effects of material.*7 The two-part Winding Towers from the same year compares the frameworks of the towers and the configuration of their machine houses, showing that even two images can reveal both the shared traits of a type and the individuality of each example.*8 The National Museum of Art, Osaka, also holds an eight-part Cooling Towers from 1986, making a typological arrangement available in a Japanese public collection.*16 The number of prints was not a fixed stylistic formula; it was chosen in relation to the material being compared and the exhibition space.

Anonyme Skulpturen, 1970—From Photobook to Contemporary Art Exhibition

The photobook Anonyme Skulpturen: Eine Typologie technischer Bauten was published in 1970, joining function-based sequences with the designation “anonymous sculptures.” In the same year, a series of cooling towers appeared in MoMA’s Information, placing the Bechers’ photographs in the same exhibition space as Conceptual art organized around information, rules, and classification.*21 MoMA presented a solo Projects exhibition in 1975.*10 That year, they also participated in New Topographics with Robert Adams, Lewis Baltz, Stephen Shore, and others, becoming part of a new photographic approach to human-altered landscapes characterized by visual restraint.*26 Together, these events show their work being received through three distinct channels: the photobook, the contemporary art exhibition, and the landscape photography exhibition.

At the 44th Venice Biennale in 1990, their photographs of industrial structures received the Golden Lion for sculpture.*11 The Met argues that their standardized frontal views and grids resonated with the serial and programmatic structures of contemporary Minimal and Conceptual art, challenging the assumed separation between documentary photography and fine art.*19 The award in the sculpture category signaled recognition not simply of the subjects’ forms, but of a display structure built through repeated, uniformly scaled prints and a plan of classification—concerns that extended beyond conventional accounts of photography.

sections.title: Criticism and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
How Neutral Are Photographs That Appear “Objective”?

The Bechers’ photographs are often described as “objective” or “impassive.” In 1977, critic Hilton Kramer reportedly compared them to photographs made for a real-estate company, a comparison Hilla accepted.*2 Yet the images contain decisions about waiting for cloud cover, raising the camera on a ladder, locating the most revealing side of a structure, and determining how much surrounding land to include. Their uniform appearance results from choices that suppress emotional staging and intensify comparison. The Met argues that this apparent objectivity connected documentary photography with Minimal and Conceptual art and unsettled the boundary between documentary and fine-art photography.*5

What Remains of Labor When People Are Excluded?

The Bechers removed people as elements that would interfere with comparison, clarifying the buildings’ outlines and construction. MoMA’s material notes that workers would ordinarily animate these scenes through labor and that the Bechers deliberately excluded them from the compositions.*20 The rule allows the photographs to convey the forms of towers and furnaces in detail, while offering little direct information about ownership, working conditions, accidents, or industrial pollution. Objectivity determines what can be compared and what remains outside the frame. Art historian Blake Stimson argues that this separation temporarily withdraws the industrial equipment’s social, political, and economic values, allowing an aesthetic concentration on form to take their place. Neutrality here contains a tension: it does not deny social meaning, but opens another way of seeing without directly explaining that meaning.*35

Human work nevertheless remains on the structures’ surfaces. Writing on Water Towers, architectural critic Reyner Banham observed that human presence is excluded while human handiwork is visible everywhere. Welds, braces, added pipes, and repaired joints carry the collective labor of unnamed engineers and workers. The absence of people makes labor less visible, while preserving its material results at high density. That contradiction raises the question of how fully photography can carry the memory of industrial society.*6

The Record of the Entire Mine Behind the Grid

Later reception made typology the Bechers’ representative form and obscured bodies of photographs that recorded factories and mines from many directions. In his review of the 2022 retrospective, James Welling suggested that the easily recognizable format sought by contemporary art may have overshadowed broader documentary projects such as the Concordia mine.*9 Industrial landscapes, working notes, and records made from multiple viewpoints show a project extending beyond a collection of forms. It also served as a documentary undertaking from which an industrial facility could later be reconstructed.

From the Single Photograph to a Wall-Based System—Connecting Photography with Other Visual Arts

When The Met acquired the sixteen-part Water Towers in 1980, the Bechers’ repetitive and seemingly prosaic project puzzled conventional photography collectors and museums. The museum states that by the late 1980s they had become among the first photographers to bridge the divide between photography and the other visual arts.*6 In a display that treats the single print as a window onto the world, each photograph remains an independent unit. In a grid, each print becomes an equivalent module and the wall as a whole becomes the work. The Met’s retrospective connects their serial arrangements with Minimal and Conceptual art because repetition, spacing, and overall scale organize the act of viewing alongside the content of the images.*19 Looking extends laterally and diagonally instead of remaining fixed before one image. Städel Museum explains that reality in the Bechers’ typologies is not represented by a single photograph but perceived through the simultaneous arrangement of multiple images. It relates their strict repetition, industrial forms, and work assembled in stages to Minimal and Conceptual art. Photography approached the other visual arts through a form that designed the entire wall as a work, as well as through sculptural subjects.*31

Each photograph conveys details of an existing tower, while the complete grid is perceived as a type. The photograph’s evidentiary relation to the world, the objecthood of the subject, Minimalism’s repetition, and Conceptual art’s rules operate on the same wall. Photography thereby entered discussions of space, repetition, institutions, and classification that had long been associated with painting and sculpture. The Met’s claim that the Bechers challenged the boundary between documentary photography and fine art refers to this double character.*19 The Golden Lion in the sculpture category in 1990 marked the art institution’s recognition of that shift.

The Düsseldorf School—Inheriting Rules of Production, Not a Visual Formula

Bernd taught at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf from 1976, and his class included Thomas Struth, Thomas Ruff, Candida Höfer, Andreas Gursky, and others. They inherited a method of repeating subjects and making shooting conditions and series structure integral to the work’s logic. Industrial architecture and black-and-white photography were not the defining legacy. A 1997 exhibition at the National Museum of Modern Art, Kyoto, presented the Bechers alongside their students and described the movement between distant observation and close attention to detail as a lineage within postwar German photography.*15 Städel Museum’s Photographs Become Pictures argues that this teaching established photography as an expressive medium equal to other arts, while students further unsettled boundaries among photography, painting, and sculpture through scale, color, display, and digital processing.*31

Gursky’s vast social spaces, Ruff’s portraits and reproduced images, Struth’s streets and museums, and Höfer’s public interiors do not share one visual appearance. They nevertheless extend an approach built on repetition, distance, rules, and comparison into different subjects, color, large prints, and digital processing. The Düsseldorf School’s influence lies less in a style of “deadpan photography” than in the idea that photographers design rules through which to examine the world.*3

The Industrial-Heritage Archive—Reading History Through Comparative Form

The Bechers’ work altered the institutional position of photography and art while also creating a body of material through which vanished industrial architecture can be studied. Since 1996, SK Stiftung Kultur has continuously developed the Becher Archive, preserving works, negatives, classifications, and arrangements used in exhibitions and publications according to the order established by the artists.*18 The Erasmus Prize recognized that their systematic series, made under consistent conditions, unsettled the distinction between documentation and art and became a source for industrial-heritage research.*13 The Bechers stated that they would use the award money to preserve and organize the work, opening unprinted negatives, maps, plans, and travel records to future researchers as a cross-referenced archive.*14

On-site preservation and a photographic archive retain different kinds of knowledge. Industrial heritage sites such as Zollverein physically convey the relations among shafts, transport networks, housing, and equipment.*23 The Bechers’ photographs place forms from different countries and periods—including facilities that have been demolished—on the same surface for comparison. A preserved site presents the spatial whole of one industrial system. The photographic archive crosses distance and time to test the many solutions modern industry devised for the same function.

International recognition has addressed the project’s formal character, long-term documentary plan, and influence. The Hasselblad Award in 2004 honored the rigor of their method and its impact on subsequent generations.*12 Through roughly two hundred works, SFMOMA’s 2022–23 retrospective reconsidered the documentation of disappearing industrial architecture, typology, and industrial landscape within a single body of work.*17 The Met exhibition from which it developed drew on extensive access to the archive and working materials, presenting early drawings and collages through mature grids as the development of one method.*19 Recent reassessment has treated the Bechers’ work as a long-term project spanning photography, research, preservation, classification, and exhibition, rather than extracting only the finished typologies.

Recent scholarship has focused on the difficulty of reducing their method to either art or research. Moisey argues that the grid became an instrument for qualitative observation of variations among buildings with a shared function while preserving the architectural precision of each photograph.*36 Issues in Science and Technology describes the Bechers as “natural historians” of the industrial landscape, connecting New Objectivity, visual classification, and the end of the industrial era within a single method.*37 Their contribution to photographic history extends beyond presenting industrial architecture as art. They preserved each photograph as evidence of an existing structure, used the grid to make multiple pieces of evidence comparable, and employed industrial landscapes to return structures to sites of production and everyday life. SK Stiftung Kultur places the work at the intersection of photography, art, industrial history, and scientific classification because the method exceeds any single medium or discipline.*18 The Bechers turned a question into photographic rules, an archive, and a wall-based form: how can multiple images be made, gathered, and arranged so that standardization and regional variation, technological renewal and obsolescence, and the history of function and form become visible? That is their central legacy in photographic history.

ben-shahn.html.lead_html: Shahn participated in the FSA photographic unit while developing a visual language of social realism that crossed painting, murals, and posters. Though celebrated as a painter, his photographs directly engaged the visual politics and labor representation of the 1930s.
ben-shahn.html.thesis_html: Through participation in the FSA photography unit, he refused to confine social criticism to a single medium, developing social realism as a practice that crossed murals, posters, prints, and photography. Though celebrated as a painter, his photographs directly engaged the visual politics and labor representation of their time, and his cross-media methodology occupies a distinctive position in photographic history.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Ben Shahn was born in Kaunas, Lithuania, in 1898 and emigrated to New York City with his family as a child. Working as a lithographer while studying art, he travelled in Europe in the 1920s and came into contact with modernist currents. In the early 1930s, his series on the Sacco and Vanzetti trial established him as a socially committed artist, and he assisted Diego Rivera on the ill-fated Rockefeller Center mural. From around 1935, he worked with the FSA photographic unit at Stryker's invitation, photographing urban neighborhoods in New York and New Jersey as well as rural Appalachia. For Shahn, photography was one instrument within a broader social-critical practice that also encompassed murals, posters, and paintings addressing labor, immigration, and political injustice. In the 1940s he produced government murals and propaganda posters. MoMA's 1947 retrospective confirmed his canonical status in American social realism. He died in 1969.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
The Leica and street observation: the candid method

From the early 1930s, Shahn used a Leica concealed in his coat to take unposed street photographs in New York without looking directly at his subjects — a method also used by Walker Evans. Where Evans used this approach to produce finished typological photographs, Shahn's street photography was oriented more toward feeding the observation process underlying his paintings and murals. The Harvard Magazine article "In the Streets and in the Studio" and the Smart Museum's exhibition Ben Shahn's New York: The Photography of Modern Times both documented this relationship between his street photography and his studio practice.

FSA photography: urban workers and immigrant neighborhoods

His FSA photographs concentrated on urban environments — immigrant neighborhoods in Lower Manhattan and New Jersey — rather than on the rural South, and brought the visual density of working-class urban space into the FSA archive alongside the better-known rural documentation.

Social realism across media

His cross-media practice — murals, prints, posters, and photographs all addressing the same social subjects — means that his photography cannot be understood in isolation from the other forms. The Harvard Library's Ben Shahn Archive and the Rutgers University Ben Shahn Estate archive preserve the full range of this practice. The Reina Sofía's Ben Shahn On Nonconformity documents his position as an artist who maintained a self-consciously non-conformist stance toward both aesthetic convention and political authority.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: Shahn has been evaluated primarily as a painter in twentieth-century American art, though recent scholarship has increasingly read his photography alongside his other work. The Tate Research essay "Realism Reconsidered: Ben Shahn in London, 1956" examined his reception in Cold War Britain, documenting the unexpected context of a major London exhibition as an opportunity to understand his international standing during a period of heightened ideological tension. The NGA and SFMOMA hold his work in their permanent collections. The Smart Museum's exhibition remains the most focused critical assessment of his photography specifically. The Archives of American Art oral history and Ben Shahn Papers provide primary source access to his own account of his practice.

bill-brandt.html.lead_html: Brandt's shift from recording British class society to making radically distorted nudes with a wide-angle lens can be read not as a stylistic rupture but as a consistent interest in the strangeness of the real. His deep shadows and high contrast visualize social distance and psychological tension.
bill-brandt.html.thesis_html: He established a method of organizing the class divisions of Britain through photographs of interior spaces, visualizing social and psychological distance through deep shadows and high contrast. With his postwar ultra-wide-angle nudes, he demonstrated that the impulse to elicit the strangeness of reality by distorting the body is continuous with social documentation rather than a departure from it. His work, anchored in both documentary and art photography, occupies the most internationally recognized position in the history of British photography.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Bill Brandt was born in Hamburg in 1904 (details of birth date and place are disputed). In the late 1920s he went to Paris and worked as an assistant to Man Ray, absorbing Surrealist influences. Moving to London in the early 1930s, he began photographing British class society. His 1936 photobook The English at Home juxtaposed upper-class interiors with working-class domestic spaces; A Night in London (1938) recorded the city at night. During the Second World War he published in Picture Post and Lilliput, documenting Londoners sheltering in the Underground and the blacked-out streets. After the war he turned to radically distorted nudes made with an ultra-wide-angle lens, a shift that attracted sustained critical attention. He died in 1983. The V&A and Tate are the principal archive and collection institutions; the Bill Brandt Archive maintains the authoritative career overview.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Class and interior space: 1930s social documentation

Brandt's 1930s work operates by using interior space to show class division: photographing butlered mansions and miners' cottages with the same camera makes economic distance visible. The V&A's introductory essay notes that his social documentation draws on a method of extracting distance from the spatial relationship between figures and their environments. The V&A's "setting the scene" article documents how Brandt arranged spaces and lighting at shoots, confirming that his high-contrast printing was a deliberate technical choice rather than an incidental quality.

Night, shadow, and the function of contrast

His high-contrast printing and handling of darkness — deep shadows, night streets, interior gloom — materialize social and psychological distance as a visual property, making the image feel more isolated than documentary proximity alone would allow.

Wide-angle nudes and the dialogue with Henry Moore

The post-war nude series, made with an extreme wide-angle lens against coastal rock and sand, has been read as a continuation of his interest in the strangeness of physical reality rather than a stylistic break. The Bill Brandt / Henry Moore exhibition, shown at the Hepworth Wakefield, Sainsbury Centre, Yale Center for British Art, and Henry Moore Foundation, documented the connection between Brandt's distorted nudes and Moore's sculptural treatment of the body, placing Brandt's photography within a broader context of twentieth-century British art.

Publishing platforms: Picture Post and Lilliput

His sustained relationship with Lilliput, Picture Post, and Harper's Bazaar embedded his visual language in the institutional structure of British illustrated magazine culture; the National Galleries of Scotland artist page confirms this breadth of media involvement.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: Brandt is the most internationally recognized British photographer of the twentieth century. A 1969 MoMA retrospective gave him one of the earliest large-scale institutional validations of a British photographer in America; the exhibition catalogue PDF documents the critical framing. The Tate Britain retrospective (2004–05) brought together his social documentation, portraiture, and nudes in a major survey. The Art Institute of Chicago and the National Galleries of Scotland hold his work in their permanent collections. A 2002 retrospective at the National Portrait Gallery, Australia, with 155 vintage prints, confirmed his sustained international reception. The ICP constituent page provides a synthetic overview of his career.

brady.html.lead_html: Brady was the leading American portrait photographer of the 1840s–50s, building his reputation on photographs of presidents and public figures. He invested his own fortune in organizing more than twenty photographers to document the Civil War — the largest such project in American history. The 1862 exhibition of Antietam dead photographs marked the first time American civilians confronted photographic images of battlefield corpses.
brady.html.thesis_html: Drawing on his fame as a portraitist and his own funds, Brady deployed more than twenty photographers in mobile darkroom wagons across the battlefields, shifting photography's mode of production from individual shooting toward the organized production of a visual archive. With his own eyesight failing he photographed little himself, functioning instead as an editor-producer who marshalled planning, finance, distribution and credit — a prototype of the modern photographic enterprise. By exhibiting the Antietam dead in New York in 1862 he created the first occasion on which the public saw the dead of the battlefield in photographs, demonstrating photography's power to mediate the reality of war to society. At the same time, his practice of gathering every image under the studio name obscured the authorship of Gardner and O'Sullivan, drawing later criticism and reaction.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Mathew Brady was born around 1822 in Warren County, New York. He opened his first daguerreotype studio on Broadway in New York around 1844 and built a reputation through portraits of presidents — including John Quincy Adams, Andrew Jackson, James Polk, and Millard Fillmore — and other prominent Americans. By the 1850s he operated major studios in New York and Washington, D.C., and was widely regarded as the leading portrait photographer in the United States*1.

He won a medal at the 1851 Great Exhibition in London and maintained his position through the transition to wet-collodion photography in the 1850s, building an archive of American leaders through the Gallery of Illustrious Americans series*2.

At the outbreak of the Civil War in 1861, with official access secured from the government, Brady invested his own fortune in the conviction that the war had to be photographed. He organized more than twenty photographers and sent them into the field with mobile darkroom wagons. He later said: "A spirit in my feet said 'Go,' and I went"*3. The team, which included Alexander Gardner and Timothy O'Sullivan, produced more than ten thousand photographs.

In October 1862, photographs of the dead at Antietam were exhibited in his New York gallery — giving American civilians their first visual encounter with battlefield corpses. The New York Times reported: "Mr. Brady has brought the terrible reality of war to our doors"*4.

After the war the government refused to purchase his negatives. Brady was ruined financially by his Civil War investment. Congress eventually paid $25,000 for the negatives in 1875 — a fraction of what he had spent. He died in poverty in 1896*5.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
The organizational character of Brady's Civil War project was its defining feature. He deployed multiple mobile darkroom wagons simultaneously to different theaters, assigned photographers by region, and had wet-collodion negatives shipped back to his Washington studio for processing and storage. This system represents the transition from the individual practitioner to the organized production of photographic archives*6.

Brady's own eyesight had deteriorated significantly by wartime, and most of the actual field photography was done by other photographers in his employ. His function was to plan, organize, finance, and control credit — bringing all work under the studio name, suppressing individual photographers' bylines. In this sense Brady operated more as editor and producer than as photographer*7.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
Brady's legacy is double-sided. On one hand, he is credited as the creator of the Civil War's visual archive and as a systematic collector of presidential portraiture. On the other, he is criticized for the suppression of the labor and authorship of his photographers, particularly Gardner and O'Sullivan*8.

The Library of Congress holds approximately 6,000 negatives in the Brady-Handy Collection, and the Civil War photographs are also available in the Library's Civil War Photographs collection*9. The Metropolitan Museum holds more than twenty Brady portraits, positioned as an archive of nineteenth-century American political and cultural figures*10.

Brady's life embodies both the heroic ambition and the tragic failure of a moment when photography was establishing itself as a social and cultural infrastructure. His bankruptcy after investing in the Civil War record is a paradox of the period: the social value of photography did not translate into the economic return he had counted on*11.

brassai.html.lead_html: Settling in Paris in the 1930s as a photographer from Hungary, Brassaï documented the city at night — its brothels, cafés, and street graffiti. His photobook Paris de Nuit is regarded as one of the earliest photobooks to construct the nocturnal city as both a poetic and a social structure.
brassai.html.thesis_html: By combining long-exposure night photography techniques with documentation of the marginal social spaces of Paris, he established one of the earliest photographic book forms that systematically constructs the nocturnal city as a poetic and social structure. His documentation encompassing brothels, spaces for sexual minorities, and graffiti — beyond mere night-scene photography — has been inherited as a practice of archiving the "hidden culture" of the city.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Born Gyula Halász in 1899 in Brassó (now Braşov, Romania) in Austria-Hungary, Brassaï studied art and journalism in Budapest and Berlin before moving to Paris in 1924 to work as a journalist. He began photographing around 1929, developing his night exposure technique with the advice of André Kertész. His 1932 photobook Paris de Nuit brought him international recognition; it was one of the earliest systematic photobooks of a city at night. In Paris he moved in the circles of Picasso, Matisse, Giacometti, and the Surrealists, and also documented the city's brothels, cafés, and underground social spaces. His decades-long graffiti documentation project was published as a book in 1960. He died in 1984.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Night exposure and Paris's social spaces

The most significant technical and conceptual choice in Brassaï's practice is night photography. Working in 1930s Paris with long exposures at night required technical mastery of tripod, exposure time, and street lighting; the resulting images have a characteristic sharpness and luminosity that distinguishes them from the atmospheric blurriness of many night photographs. Paris de Nuit records cafés, bridges, cobblestones, and foggy streetlights while also including the city's other face — men on the run, women in front of brothels, late-night drinkers.

Brothels, cafés, and the social margins

Beyond night Paris, his photographs of brothels, lesbian bars such as Le Monocle, and artists' cafés documented the sexual and social margins of interwar Paris. The Metropolitan Museum's Couple d'amoureux dans un petit café and Fat Claude and her Girlfriend at Le Monocle are canonical examples of this documentation, held in the permanent collection with full provenance.

Graffiti: archiving the urban unconscious

His decades-long graffiti project — collecting faces, figures, and marks scratched into walls — functions as an archival impulse connecting to the Surrealist concept of urban unconscious and to Atget's systematic documentation of Old Paris. The Pompidou Centre has mounted multiple exhibitions of the graffiti work; the AIC and Met hold examples in their permanent collections.

Picasso and Surrealism

His close friendship with Picasso and other Surrealist-associated artists placed his photography in dialogue with the visual culture of interwar Parisian modernism; the Musée Picasso Málaga and Staatliche Museen zu Berlin exhibitions document this relationship.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: Brassaï is known by the honorific "L'Œil de Paris," but recent assessments tend toward a more complex reading that includes his documentation of sexual margins, his immigrant position in colonial-era Paris, and the archival ambition of the graffiti project. The Getty's exhibition The Eye of Paris provides a synthetic view of this reception; the MoMA 1956 exhibition catalogue documents the critical framing at the moment of his North American institutional reception. The Heide Museum of Modern Art's exhibition text addresses the breadth of his practice across night Paris, Picasso, Surrealism, and graffiti simultaneously.

His work follows waiting, peripheral activity, and collective life outside the decisive moment, examining how access, speed, captions, exhibitions, and institutions shape political images.

bruno-serralongue.html.lead_html: Bruno Serralongue has photographed international conferences, summits, migrant-support networks, the sans-papiers movement, the Calais “Jungle,” and the ZAD at Notre-Dame-des-Landes without press credentials, using a 4×5-inch view camera from the same spaces available to ordinary participants. His series attend to people waiting, temporary structures, peripheral conversations, and the time in which assemblies disperse instead of the dramatic peak of an event. The conditions under which a photograph becomes news become part of the subject.
bruno-serralongue.html.thesis_html: Since the 1970s, critical documentary has questioned the photographer’s power to represent others and the mechanisms through which news institutions select events. Serralongue turned that critique into a repeatable working procedure: traveling independently to conferences and protests, maintaining distance from press accreditation, making a limited number of photographs with a 4×5-inch view camera, and returning them through exhibitions and photobooks to a temporality different from that of the news image. At international conferences he photographed outside accredited viewpoints; in Calais, daily life organized around waiting to move; in the sans-papiers movement, the repeated public appearance of a collective; and at the ZAD, the overlap between protest and communal living. He shifted the center of political photography from dramatic confrontation to the time and material support that sustain a movement, making shooting conditions and routes of circulation part of the political facts shown by the image.
