sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
Advertising and i-D—Learning How Media Changes a Photograph’s Meaning

Takashi Homma studied photography at Nihon University College of Art and began working as a photographer for a Tokyo advertising agency in 1984*2. In 1991–92 he moved to London and worked for i-D, a magazine devoted to youth culture, music, and fashion. Tokyo Opera City Art Gallery describes this period as one in which he encountered photographers presenting work through a wide range of methods*24. In a magazine, clothing, headlines, typography, adjacent images, and readership all shape a photograph’s function and meaning. Homma’s commercial experience showed him that the same image could operate as an advertisement, a record of the city, or an artist’s work.

Advertising often demands a recognizable authorial signature, yet Homma avoided inscribing the photographer’s emotion heavily into the frame. Using a 4×5 camera, he aligned horizontal and vertical lines, stepped back from his subjects, and treated people, roads, houses, and signs as equivalent elements in the picture. He has explained that this position allows viewers to imagine where they themselves might be standing*21. The controlled surface leaves room for viewers to assess the scene through their own experience.

The same thinking extends to his commercial work. Homma places models, clothing, roads, signs, and architecture within a shared setting, and describes fashion photography as a document of the city and body of its time*12. The construction of a desirable commodity image and the recording of a city coexist within a single photograph.

Tokyo Suburbia and the Suburb Boom—Selections and Contradictions Identified by 藤田紅於

When Tokyo Suburbia appeared in 1998, Japanese debate focused intensely on new towns, roadside development, convenience stores, and standardized residential districts. After the 1997 Kobe child murders, newspapers, magazines, and sociological writing increasingly associated suburbia with a weakened sense of reality, fictionality, and the erosion of family and local community. 藤田紅於 compared contemporary reviews with suburban theory centered on Shinji Miyadai and traced how Tokyo Suburbia was received as visual evidence for this “suburb boom”*4.

According to 藤田, the sixty-three photographs concentrate on newer suburbs developed after the 1980s and largely omit accumulated signs of daily life such as laundry, potted plants, supermarkets, and banks. Nostalgic images of childhood also recede. Instead, the book repeatedly shows game centers, family restaurants, convenience stores, children in American and European brands, and landscapes suggestive of American film. These choices visually reinforced contemporary accounts of diminished reality, dispersed family life, and Americanization*4.

At the same time, the location list at the back returns apparently anonymous landscapes to places such as Tama, Makuhari, and Yokohama, while one photograph of adults with an infant unsettles the impression of a community composed only of children. 藤田 notes that contemporary newspaper and magazine reviews largely overlooked these contradictions and praised Tokyo Suburbia for visualizing a standard image of the suburban boom*4. The essay also warns against treating Homma’s suburban upbringing as sufficient proof of an insider’s viewpoint. The book carefully constructs the conventions of suburban discourse, then inserts place names and exceptions into them. Its critical force lies in this double movement.

Eggleston, Robert Adams, and Nobuyoshi Araki—Three Predecessors Named by Homma

Homma identifies William Eggleston, Robert Adams, and Nobuyoshi Araki as important predecessors*13. Eggleston brought color associated with advertising and family snapshots into art photography, treating ordinary objects, cars, interiors, and roadsides as events of color and composition*27. Within New Topographics, Robert Adams photographed the meeting of housing developments, roads, and plains in the American West from a quiet distance*26. From them, Homma learned that color and human-altered landscapes could be photographed as everyday environments in their own right.

Nobuyoshi Araki transformed private life into photobooks while working at an advertising agency, closely linking the photographer’s biography, titles, and publication. Homma cites Araki as one reason he became a photographer, yet in Tokyo and My Daughter he used a first-person title to prompt an autobiographical reading while mixing photographs of a friend’s daughter with snapshots made by her parents and rephotographed images*13. Homma’s concern extended from private subject matter to the power of the photobook and author credit to produce an image of the artist.

Daido Moriyama and Takuma Nakahira rendered Tokyo in the 1960s and 1970s as an urgent field of perception through the walking body, blur, grain, and print. Homma’s 4×5 photographs approach the later city from a fixed position several steps back, giving people, houses, roads, and signs comparable weight. The distinction lies in whether the photographer’s body anchors the urban image or attention shifts toward the arrangements and consumer signs that structure suburbia. These histories reached Homma by different routes. Eggleston, Robert Adams, and Araki are predecessors he named himself; Moriyama and Nakahira serve as points of comparison within Japanese urban photography.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
The 4×5 Camera—Restraining the Photographer’s Gesture, Recording Suburban Arrangement

Homma chose the 4×5 camera for more than its descriptive precision. The camera requires a tripod, careful alignment of horizontal and vertical lines, and the placement of people and architecture within the same frame*10. By stepping back, he removes facial expression from the center of psychological drama, allowing roads, houses, sky, and signs to become equal conditions of the image. He has said that this position helps viewers imagine where they themselves might stand*21.

Through the 1980s, a major current in Japanese urban photography entered the street with a small camera and registered the photographer’s speed and reaction in the frame. The 1990s suburbs Homma photographed were planned spaces of recurring intersections, houses, convenience stores, and construction sites. Proximity and quick response could intensify an individual scene; a fixed distance made the repetition of planned space more legible. The 4×5 format showed where a person stood among roads, buildings, and commercial signs.

What Homma calls an “open photograph” withholds the photographer’s emotion as a final conclusion and allows viewers to compare the arrangement in the frame with their own memories*13. His ordered 4×5 pictures still involve decisions about place, distance, weather, and people. Directing those decisions toward suburban arrangement while keeping expressive gesture out of the foreground defines his measured distance.

Magazines, Photobooks, Museums—Changing the Use of the Same Image

A defining feature of Homma’s publishing work is the repeated movement of the same image through different media, making changes in use and evaluation part of the work’s structure. A photograph used to present clothing in i-D becomes a record of the post-bubble city in Tokyo Suburbia, then material for examining the institutional division between commercial and artistic photography in “New Documentary”*6. Existing images reappear with traces of their earlier uses, weakening the expectation that each book must close around an entirely new body of work.

Homma has produced more than sixty publications and has said that he prefers thin books made for particular exhibitions or moments*20. In Japanese photography, Daido Moriyama and Nobuyoshi Araki placed magazines and photobooks at the center of production and changed photographic meaning through print. Homma brought advertising, fashion magazines, family albums, and museums—each with different systems of ownership and evaluation—into that history.

What distinguishes Homma’s work from the ordinary integration of shooting, selection, and book design is the recirculation of identical images. As a photograph moves from one medium to another, it may be treated as commodity, urban record, family memory, or artwork. Making that shift a sustained subject separates his books and exhibitions from a conventional editorial process.

Tokyo and My Daughter—Separating Photographer, Custodian, and Author Credit

In Tokyo and My Daughter, the author’s name on the cover and the first-person title suggest an autobiography following the photographer’s own child. The girl is in fact a friend’s daughter, and the book mixes photographs by Homma with snapshots by her parents and rephotographed images*6. Before establishing each photograph’s provenance, viewers use the title and author credit to construct a single family story.

In a family album, the person pressing the shutter, the family represented, the household preserving the photographs, and the album’s owner often overlap. Tokyo and My Daughter separates these roles and gathers images by different photographers under Homma’s name. Photographer, custodian, selector, title-giver, and publisher each participate in the photograph’s meaning and sense of ownership.

The work therefore shifts from a single photographer’s private confession to the mechanism by which family photographs are recognized as someone’s memories. Its subject is the division of labor among shooting, preservation, selection, naming, and publication. Different people perform these tasks, yet their combined work establishes whose story the book appears to tell.

Camera Obscura—Examining Authorship Through an Optical Apparatus

Since the 2010s, Homma has darkened hotel rooms and houses, admitted daylight through a small aperture in a window, and projected an inverted city onto walls or photosensitive material. Because the entire room functions as a camera, its architecture, the direction of the window, the weather, and long exposure times directly shape the image. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum presented the camera obscura as a central element of his recent inquiry into photographic apparatuses and photographic history in Revolution 9: Homma Takashi*23.

In The Narcissistic City, rooms in Tokyo, New York, Milan, and other cities become camera obscuras, allowing the city to leave its own image on photosensitive material through architecture*8. Nonaka-Hill describes this as using the city as an apparatus to photograph itself, with inversion, chance, and repetition as constitutive elements*7. The early 4×5 photographs and the camera-obscura works differ greatly in technique and appearance. They share a distance from the idea that the author’s instantaneous perception alone grounds expression. In the 4×5 pictures, the photographer’s gesture recedes; in the camera obscura, architecture, aperture, daylight, and exposure time divide responsibility for the image.

The available sources show that Homma developed the camera-obscura work as research into photographic history and architecture; it also casts his earlier understanding of authorship in a different light. At a time when smartphones and digital systems produce and circulate images instantly, sealing a room and waiting for light restores the duration by which light becomes an image. Homma refers to Nicéphore Niépce, Nobuo Yamanaka, and Jun’ichirō Tanizaki, using the dark chamber as an entry point into photographic history and the modern organization of vision*5.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Tokyo Suburbia, 1998—Thick Pages and an Externally Framed Suburbia

Tokyo Suburbia comprises sixty-three color photographs of residential districts, roads, commercial facilities, children, and young people. Its board-book construction, made from laminated card, gives the volume considerable physical weight, while full-bleed printing brings the reader into direct contact with the page surface. The light palette of the city meets the book’s physical heaviness, introducing bodily resistance into the act of viewing suburbia as an abstract image*4.

In 1999, the Kimura Ihei Award, followed by a 2000 exhibition at Fotomuseum Winterthur, brought Homma’s restrained color photographs wider international recognition*3. Current reassessments consider both the book’s reinforcement of 1990s suburban discourse and the ways its location list, infants, and the gazes of its figures fracture that typology*22. The coexistence of formal clarity and social selectivity remains a central issue in the book’s reception.

Tokyo and My Daughter, 1999–2010—The Family Album and the Displaced Author Credit

Tokyo and My Daughter follows a girl’s growth from 1999 alongside Tokyo streets, houses, airports, and family snapshots. She is the daughter of a friend, and the book includes images made by her parents as well as rephotographed existing photographs*13. Grain, color, and distance remain uneven within the volume, placing images preserved in the home on the same timeline as the artist’s urban photographs. The autobiographical expectation created by the words “Tokyo and My Daughter” conflicts with the actual provenance of the pictures, and that gap structures the book.

The Narcissistic City and Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji

In The Narcissistic City, rooms become large cameras that turn fragments of buildings, water towers, roads, and sky into inverted images*14. Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji refers to Katsushika Hokusai’s series and photographs a mountain endlessly repeated through tourism, World Heritage status, and daily life from camera obscuras in different locations*11. Both series record how an image changes as viewing position, architecture, and exposure time change, instead of presenting a single representative view of a famous site.

From Le Corbusier’s Windows to Portraiture and Moving Images

Looking Through: Le Corbusier Windows follows architecture across Europe and India, examining how windows determine light, view, and the position of the body*17. A joint project by the CCA and the Window Research Institute connects the shared structure of windows and camera obscuras to the histories of modern architecture and photography*19. According to the CCA, the research began with Homma’s 2002 photographs of Le Corbusier’s Petite Maison, continued in Chandigarh, and developed into an examination of the common structure of the window and the camera aperture*9. The subject expanded from recording a building’s exterior to studying how architecture itself organizes sight and view.

Portrait of J gathers portraits made since 2002, presenting public figures, friends, and children without a hierarchy of status*15. In 2022, an i-D project photographed nine young queer people on Tokyo streets and placed their portraits alongside their own words*16. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Videodiary developed near-empty Tokyo, domestic interiors, and family voices across twenty-eight videos*18. Across photobooks, magazines, moving images, and architectural research, Homma chooses image duration, sequence, and circulation according to the subject.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Praised Restraint and Critiques of “Ordinariness”

Homma’s reception formed around the bright color of Tokyo Suburbia, the distance that treats people and architecture with comparable temperature, and his movement between magazines and photobooks. In its 2000 exhibition, MU praised his ability to work inside the media while directing a critical gaze toward them; Fotomuseum Winterthur identified socioeconomic fractures beneath the work’s apparent lightness*1.

Aperture’s review of “New Documentary” noted that its discussion of deskilling—mixing amateur photographs with professional technique—sometimes repeated familiar art-historical arguments, and distinguished works in which the concept operated forcefully from those led by institutional explanation*6. The criticism clarifies that titles, editing, design, and display produce critical force only when they act concretely upon each series’ social setting. Homma’s restrained surfaces gain their strength when they serve a precise inquiry into society and media.

The Pictures Generation and Tillmans—Separating Direct Influence from Contemporary Comparison

In the late 1970s, the Pictures Generation appropriated images from magazines, film, and advertising to criticize an art system centered on original authors and originals*28. The available sources do not establish that Homma directly referred to the group. The useful comparison lies elsewhere: those artists moved mass-circulated images into art, while Homma began within commercial image production and moved his own advertising photographs, family snapshots, and urban pictures among different media.

Working at roughly the same time for publications including i-D, Wolfgang Tillmans treated photographs, photocopies, and reproductions of magazine pages as equivalent in a 1993 installation, shifting the hierarchy between printed matter and original prints*25. The sources likewise do not confirm a direct line of influence between Tillmans and Homma. Tillmans rearranged hierarchies of size, support, and mounting within the gallery; Homma traced how suburbia, family albums, and Japanese magazine culture classify images as advertisement, record, private memory, or artwork.

This distinction avoids presenting Homma as a synthesis of Euro-American currents. Eggleston, Robert Adams, and Araki are predecessors he named. The Pictures Generation and Tillmans offer comparisons for authorship and circulation developed in different regions and institutions. Homma’s specificity lies in placing advertising, magazines, suburbia, family albums, and museums within a single field of inquiry in 1990s Japan.

Making the Boundary Between Magazine Photography and Museum Art a Subject in 1990s Japan

Questions of photographic circulation and authorship predate Homma. Daido Moriyama made the printed surfaces of magazines and photobooks integral to the photograph; Nobuyoshi Araki linked private life and authorial identity across a vast publishing output; and art of the 1980s criticized authorship through the reuse of existing images. Homma’s work cannot be adequately described as a personal synthesis of these histories.

Its specificity lies in the circulation systems of 1990s Japan. In Tokyo Suburbia, a color palette and distance developed through fashion magazines were received as visual evidence for suburban discourse. In Tokyo and My Daughter, photographs preserved within a household appeared under the name of a single photographer. In “New Documentary,” magazine covers, commercial photographs, family pictures, and video entered a museum, and the exhibition made changes in their use and evaluation visible*24.

Homma’s place in photographic history depends on treating commercial assignments, private snapshots, artists’ works, and architectural research as connected stages in the changing meaning and evaluation of images. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s 2023 exhibition reorganized his early suburbia photographs, seascapes, mushrooms, Le Corbusier studies, and camera-obscura works around the acts of seeing photographs and examining the camera apparatus*23. Movement between magazines and museums had clear precedents. Homma’s particular contribution was to circulate advertising, suburban photography, family albums, and architectural research within one body of work and thereby show, in post-1990 Japan, how photographic use and authorship are assigned.

takashi-yasumura.html.lead_html: Takashi Yasumura is known for Domestic Scandals, made with a 4×5 camera in his parents’ home among furniture, artificial flowers, fruit, wallpaper, and tableware, and for 1/1, which isolates the surfaces of regional public buildings and harbors from their surroundings. By making slight adjustments, carrying focus across the frame, and reducing spatial clues, he tests the arrangements, commodities, decoration, and perspective that allow homes and buildings to appear natural.
takashi-yasumura.html.thesis_html: As quick snapshots of everyday life gained prominence in 1990s Japan, Yasumura chose the slow procedure of photographing his parents’ home and regional public facilities with a 4×5 camera. In Domestic Scandals, he moves artificial flowers, fruit, wallpaper, and furniture slightly, confusing the scale of garden, model, and object in works such as Japanese Oranges. In 1/1, walls and floors of public buildings are framed frontally, leaving the building as a whole and the clues to its use outside the image. Because he avoids models and digital composites, the strangeness comes from actual products, interiors, and architecture. His work brought misreadings of perspective, focus, and scale into everyday photography as a problem alongside personal disclosure.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
Studying Photography and Finding a Stimulus in New Cosmos of Photography

Born in Shiga Prefecture in 1972, Yasumura studied photography at Nihon University College of Art and graduated in 1995. New Cosmos of Photography began in 1991, during his second year, and he repeatedly visited its exhibitions at P3 in Yotsuya. He has recalled being strongly affected by seeing award recipients create places for their work through both images and words, as well as by reading statements of intent in magazines*1.

He found it difficult to identify with the prominent photography of “my life, my everyday world” and began looking for something that only photography could do*1. His parents’ home offered a familiar space in which the lens repeatedly altered relations of size, distance, material, and use. His concern turned toward the conditions under which a three-dimensional living space becomes a flat image and everydayness begins to lose its stability.

Everyday Photography in the 1990s and Yasumura’s Different Direction

In 1990s Japan, photographs of friends, romance, the body, and the photographer’s immediate surroundings gained broad attention through compact cameras and magazine culture. New Cosmos of Photography was one of the forums where these varied approaches appeared. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum later included Yasumura with Masafumi Sanai, Takashi Homma, Kyoji Takahashi, Hanayo, and others in an exhibition on photography and society during the Heisei era*22. Yasumura also used the private space of his family home, but focused on the way its apparent everydayness disappeared in a photograph. In his statement for the 1999 award, he wrote that conventions within a family can look strange to an outsider and that photography brings the doubtful nature of the everyday into awareness*21. The series was published as Domestic Scandals*20. The 4×5 camera, tripod, extensive depth of field, and limited rearrangement allowed him to examine visual conditions one at a time.

sections.title: Core Ideas
sections.body_html:
Domestic Scandals—The Family Home as an Already Staged Set

Domestic Scandals was photographed with a 4×5 camera over seven years in his parents’ middle-class home. A Yossi Milo exhibition text describes traditional decoration, plastic and mass-produced goods, and Westernized household objects occupying the same rooms*19. Yasumura selected staplers, cassette players, snacks, slippers, walls, and floors and adjusted their color and form within the frame. The house appears as a setting where postwar Japanese domestic normality is assembled from commodities, habits, and imitative materials. The official work page presents the series as a continuous group of images*16. IBASHO’s publication entry records a book in which the photographs are accompanied by three essays treating the home as a stage of representation*3.

Finding Deliberate Awkwardness Through Minimal Arrangement

In an IMA interview, Yasumura contrasted the apparent naturalness of his early series Namanurui Kaze ga Fuku with the deliberate “awkwardness” he intensified in Domestic Scandals*2. He moves furniture and household objects and adjusts focus and light while leaving most of the room intact. The resulting strangeness remains tied to products chosen by the family, habits of display and cleanliness, and seasonal routines. Visible intervention weakens a simple division between natural life and artificial photography. Existing staging and photographic adjustment can be compared within the same frame.

Holding the Entire Frame in Focus and Destabilizing Depth

The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s Japanese Oranges holds the entire frame in focus, making depth and object scale difficult to determine. Tokyo Museum Collection describes household objects as appearing model-like and domestic space as revealing its fictive quality*4. Ordinary vision changes attention and focus with distance. A large-format camera and small aperture hold foreground and background with comparable intensity, and the camera’s descriptive capacity unsettles the apparent naturalness of space.

Why Use Real Rooms Instead of Models?

Yasumura’s photographs can resemble images of miniatures or elaborate sets, although most use actual rooms and objects. IBASHO Gallery presents Domestic Scandals and Nature Tracing as connected investigations of the artificiality of everyday life and the reproduction of nature*5.

A model would make unstable scale the result of a device designed entirely by the artist. Yasumura retains the actual objects and limits intervention to arrangement, camera position, focus, and light. The disturbance therefore returns to commodities, architecture, and household habits. The viewer is led to reconsider which cues of depth, size, use, and material made the space recognizable as everyday.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Japanese Oranges—The Scale of Fruit, Garden, and Model

In Japanese Oranges, citrus fruit, leaves, branches, and background share the same density, making it difficult to decide immediately whether the scene is a potted plant, a garden tree, or a model*4. The title identifies the subject while the photograph destabilizes its size and setting. The color of the fruit anchors the frame, yet the image presents nature as something cultivated, arranged, and observed within domestic life.

1/1—Public-Building Surfaces and the One-to-One Relation of Object and Image

1/1 was made over roughly eight years beginning in 2008 at regional public facilities and harbors, where Yasumura photographed walls, floors, equipment, and decoration with a 4×5 camera. In an IMA interview, he explained that he reduced the “background” inevitably recorded by the camera and made visual depth shallow through composition*2.

The title refers to a one-to-one relation between object and image and to the camera that mediates between them. MISAKO & ROSEN interprets the slash as the camera and explains how, after being photographed, an object gains a different autonomy as a plane of color or flat surface*6. With less information about a site’s function, public architecture approaches abstraction while retaining scratches and material traces. Antenne Books records the publication as containing 111 photographs made between 2008 and 2015*7.

Nature Tracing—Imitations of Nature Brought into the Home

Nature Tracing addresses artificial flowers, synthetic turf, printed plants, and arranged gardens—objects and actions through which everyday life imitates nature. The official site publishes the photographs and gathers imitated nature in domestic and public space as one series*17. The work observes how nature is reduced in scale, maintained, commodified, and brought indoors. As with the mass-produced objects in Domestic Scandals, naturalness is produced through material, arrangement, and repetition.

The Photobook Domestic Scandals and Comparison Across Pages

According to the official bibliography, Domestic Scandals was published by Osiris in 2005 with thirty-six color photographs and essays by Martin Jaeggi, Akihito Yasumi, and Shinobu Kuraishi*18. 1/1 contains 111 images across 132 pages, a comparison by Minoru Shimizu with Alfred Stieglitz’s Equivalents, and a text by Yasumura*18. Repetition in book form allows mass-produced domestic goods and public-building surfaces to be compared as visual habits within the same society. Format and sequence establish a common viewing distance across distinct spaces.

The Slowness of the 4×5 Camera and Minimal Intervention

The official site and biography show Yasumura’s sustained attention to homes, objects, and landscapes through precise color photography*8. MISAKO & ROSEN documents the continuity of his solo exhibitions and series*13, while IBASHO Gallery brings together images and collection information from Domestic Scandals through Nature Tracing*14. Yossi Milo records that Domestic Scandals was made with a 4×5 camera over seven years*19. The slow apparatus produces long observation before exposure as well as detailed images. Setting up the tripod, viewing the inverted image on the ground glass, and adjusting arrangement and focus temporarily detach the room from the flow of domestic life. Limited intervention in actual objects and camera conditions keeps the work centered on how reality changes as an image.

sections.title: Criticism and Reception
sections.body_html:
New Cosmos of Photography and Doubts About “Everydayness” Itself

New Cosmos of Photography began in 1991. As a university student, Yasumura attended exhibitions at P3 in Yotsuya and observed award recipients creating working contexts through their photographs*1. During the 1990s, the competition drew attention to varied uses of private life, the body, cities, staging, and photobooks. Yasumura also chose his parents’ home, but centered the disappearance of everydayness within photography. Preparing a 4×5 camera, moving furniture and objects, and adjusting focus, color, and distance turned a private setting into a place for testing realist description. PARCO’s 2005 exhibition and the photobook Domestic Scandals presented seven years of repetition as one public series*9. The work shared familiar subject matter with contemporary everyday photography while directing attention toward the perceptual structure that makes the everyday seem natural.

Photographic Distance Learned from Shigeo Gocho’s SELF AND OTHERS

In an IMA conversation, Yasumura described the influence of Shigeo Gocho’s SELF AND OTHERS and emphasized the importance of distance between photographer and subject even in his own photographs of things*2. Gocho approached intimate subjects without enclosing them entirely within the photographer’s emotion. Yasumura applied that distance to the family home, a setting too familiar to see easily, and to the objects within it. Camera distance and preparation make the known observable again.

Comparing Household Goods and Public Architecture with the Same 4×5 Camera

Yasumura photographs plastic, appliances, snacks, artificial flowers, wall materials, and public-facility equipment as elements that make contemporary life. Essays in the official Domestic Scandals publication treat the family home as a stage of representation and examine social changes beneath its quiet surfaces*18. Focus, color, and scale show how objects exist photographically without turning household goods into sentimental possessions or sociological specimens.

In 1/1, the same method turns toward regional public buildings. Domestic arrangements and architectural surfaces differ in character, yet the same 4×5 camera allows mass-produced goods, imitation materials, walls, and floors to be compared. Still life expands from the tabletop to the arrangement of objects that constitute homes and public institutions. shashasha’s artist and publication page situates Domestic Scandals and 1/1 within a continuing photobook practice*10.

The Family Home and Public Facilities as Different Conditions of Reality

Domestic Scandals shows plastic, artificial flowers, appliances, snacks, and simulated wood or stone accumulating the time and consumer choices of Yasumura’s parents’ home. In 1/1, he moves close to walls, floors, and equipment in public facilities, ports, and gymnasiums, leaving signs of function and the building as a whole outside the frame. Art Platform Japan records the two major publications and exhibition history since the late 1990s*11. In the first series, furniture and commodities produce domestic depth; in the second, reduced background turns walls and floors toward fields of color. Yasumura adjusts arrangements at home and removes surrounding information in public buildings while retaining the same 4×5 camera and color realism. The two series show how a sense of reality depends on depth, scale, use, material, and the amount of background. Formal consistency makes it possible to measure these conditions across domestic and public space.

Selection and Responsibility in Teaching and Jury Work

Canon’s archive records Yasumura as a New Cosmos of Photography juror for four consecutive years, from 2018 through 2021*12. In an English-language interview, he reflects on work from his award-winning series to recent projects and discusses how photographing, selecting, and forming a series produce a finished work*15. This continues his long-standing attention to selection after exposure, sequence, and print size. The work is not complete when an interesting object is found; the distance and scale at which its image will appear are also composed.

takeji-iwamiya.html.lead_html: Takeji Iwamiya developed a photographic practice on the border between document and formal inquiry, focusing on Japanese temples, gardens, craft objects, Buddhist sculpture, and vernacular tools. Rather than reproducing tradition as tourism, he reconfigured it through a photographic vocabulary, giving his work a distinct place within postwar Japanese photography.*1*2

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Born in Osaka in 1920, Iwamiya worked in advertising photography while developing long-term personal projects on temples, gardens, craft objects, Buddhist sculpture, and vernacular tools. His best-known publications include Katachi: Japan's Traditional Forms I and II (1962), followed by large-format books on Kyoto and historical gardens. He died in 1989.*1*2

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
What consistently supports Iwamiya's photography is a sustained attention to contour, material, and the rhythm of space. By isolating details such as pillars, eaves, stones, moss, drapery folds, fingers, rims, and wood grain from surrounding visual noise, he presents his subjects not simply as records but as visual questions. His framing often reduces the scene to form and interval, placing photography on the border between document and formal meditation. Although his subjects are largely traditional Japanese cultural objects, his method does not treat them as tourist imagery or educational record. It rearticulates them through a photographic vocabulary of pattern, mass, silhouette, and spacing.*1*3

This method has an explicit basis in Iwamiya's own words. His statement that he wanted to use photography to confirm something like the roots of Japanese culture, and that he felt unable to close his eyes without doing so, frames the project not as nostalgia but as critical necessity.*2 The camera functions here not as a device for preserving "Japanese beauty" but as a tool for rediscovering structure, texture, and rhythm. Photography and tradition do not simply document one another; they meet as a testing ground for a modern visual language.

Iwamiya's importance within postwar Japanese photography lies in this distinct position. Unlike photographers centered on gritty grain, street reportage, or direct social critique, he confronted the problem of visually rewriting Japanese culture through architecture, sculpture, and craft. His work fits neither ethnography nor pure abstraction. Instead it uses traditional subjects to ask what it means to see in the first place. That position has been confirmed by later retrospectives and sustained archival attention.*1*4

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: Iwamiya has been received as an important mediator between postwar photographic modernism and a renewed visual understanding of Japanese tradition. Retrospectives and archival projects by institutions such as FUJIFILM Square and The Third Gallery Aya show that his work is read neither as pure cultural preservation nor as abstract art alone, but as a photographic practice that bridges the two. The double capacity of photography to function as both document and formal inquiry remains central to his historical reception.*1*3

takeyoshi-tanuma.html.lead_html: Takeyoshi Tanuma recorded postwar Japanese civic life and the transformation of Tokyo across more than sixty years, beginning in the immediate aftermath of the war. His civic and humanist attention to people as the measure of history gives him a place distinct from more oppositional currents in postwar Japanese photography.*1*2

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Born in Tokyo in 1929, Tanuma began photographing the city in the immediate aftermath of the war around 1948 and continued for more than sixty years to record urban transformation, children, and later international humanitarian issues. He also served as an official photographer for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics and was later known for projects with UNICEF. Through a long term as president of the Japan Professional Photographers Society, he also played a major institutional role in postwar Japanese photography. He died in 2022.*1*2

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
At the core of Tanuma's photography is a view of human presence as the measure of history. Even while recording Tokyo during high economic growth, he repeatedly returned to children, familiar neighborhood faces, and shared public space. Early images such as the SKD rooftop dancers and the paper-storyteller of Tsukudajima turn the bustle of the postwar city into lived collective memory rather than abstract social record. In these photographs, the "reconstruction of Tokyo" appears not as a statistic or concept but as an accumulation of concrete people, expressions, and spaces.*1*3

His formal characteristics include clear, person-centered framing, direct but never overbearing observation, and a documentary force grounded in emotional clarity. Rather than objectifying situations, Tanuma maintains respect for the subject and a close human gaze. That difference separates him from more oppositional or formally radical photographers of the same period, placing him closer to a civic and humanist concern than to aggressive social critique.*1*2

Historically, Tanuma's early work belongs to the Tokyo of the 1940s through 1960s, when reconstruction was advancing both materially and socially. In a city where ruin remained in memory even as daily life was renewed, his camera recorded the temperature of civic life. Later collaborations with UNICEF and projects on children abroad extended concerns developed at home into a wider humanitarian horizon. His long practice, together with his institutional involvement, also helped raise the public standing of photography in Japan.*1*4

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: Retrospectives at institutions such as the Setagaya Art Museum and the TOP Museum position Tanuma as one of the most important witnesses to postwar Tokyo. Criticism tends to value the continuity of his practice and the breadth of its subjects, from local neighborhoods to the welfare of children across the world. The emotional clarity of the images is read not as sentimentality but as a civic gaze, and that has become central to his historical reception.*1*2

takuma-nakahira.html.lead_html: Takuma Nakahira photographed Tokyo at night, roads, underpasses, plants, waterfronts, and islands, moving from grainy black-and-white images to lucid color. Across PROVOKE, For a Language to Come, Circulation, Overflow, and Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary?, he examined photographic language, the photographer’s body, paper and printing, the systems that organize urban space, and the exhibition wall. Whenever an acquired visual style hardened into an authorial signature or a marketable product, he criticized it and changed how he photographed and presented his work.
takuma-nakahira.html.thesis_html: Nakahira unsettled the idea that a photographer’s consistency should be demonstrated by repeating a single visual style. He refused to treat PROVOKE’s are-bure-boke—grainy, blurry, and out-of-focus imagery—as a final form, moving instead to the same-day installation of Circulation, the enumerative method of Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary?, and the color wall of Overflow. He showed both photography’s potential to escape established language and its tendency to harden into a code, a commodity, or an authorial brand through a sustained cycle of self-critique and methodological change.

sections.title: Before PROVOKE: Why Takuma Nakahira Moved from Editing to Photography
sections.body_html:
Nakahira studied Spanish at Tokyo University of Foreign Studies. After graduating in 1963, he joined the editorial staff of Gendai no me (The Contemporary Eye). There he encountered Shōmei Tōmatsu’s work and helped edit the exhibition One Hundred Years of Photography. He left the magazine in 1965 and began working as a photographer and critic*16. Between 1965 and 1977, he published more than one hundred essays*19.

Nakahira initially hoped to become a poet and joined a leftist study group focused on Latin American revolutions. He became increasingly skeptical of the way political and artistic language subsumed particular places and things under general concepts. He later compared the word “tree” with a single tree photographed at a specific time and place*8. Photography exposed critical abstractions to light, distance, time, and the surfaces of things, while the photographer’s body encountered the speed of the city and the resistance of its subjects. Daniel Abbe analyzes Nakahira during this period as a “body in the world”*23. Photography allowed him to test, through movement and sensation, a reality that concepts alone could not verify.

In 1968, Nakahira, Kōji Taki, Yutaka Takanashi, and Takahiko Okada founded PROVOKE; Daidō Moriyama joined with the second issue. Its subtitle, “Provocative Materials for Thought,” stated an intention to remove photography from its role as illustration and present it as material whose meaning had not yet been settled*20. Tristan Ignas-Menzies reads the magazine as a collective practice of realism formed in response to a society undergoing rapid economic growth that no single viewpoint could encompass*24. Its unit of production was the collision among photography, criticism, poetry, editing, and the printed page.

Coarse grain, camera shake, missed focus, and extreme tonal contrasts delayed the immediate attachment of journalistic explanations to the subject*4. Philip Charrier notes that an indistinct visual language intended to dislodge established codes could itself become a new code through repetition*25. The success of are-bure-boke forced Nakahira into his next act of self-critique.

sections.title: Photography and Language: For a Language to Come and Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary?
sections.body_html:
For a Language to Come: Are-Bure-Boke, Paper, and Print

Published in 1970, For a Language to Come sequences grainy black-and-white photographs of roads at night, underpasses, windows, people, animals, and signs. Designed by Tsunehisa Kimura, the book arranges 192 images across glossy double-page spreads*5. Full bleeds, black margins, repetition, and shifts in scale control the pace of page turning and create collisions between images.

Jelena Stojković argues that deep blacks, blown-out highlights, coarse grain, and flash reflections make the viewer aware of the subject and the printed surface at the same time*17. Gyewon Kim considers urban signs, lettering, and walls alongside the material properties of paper, ink, and the page*26. Just as roads organize human movement, gutters and variations in ink density alter the order of looking. The roughness of the printed book challenged two assumptions: that a photograph transparently explains the city, and that paper transparently carries the photograph.

Landscape Theory: Television News, Roads, and the Administration of the City

The landscape theory, or fūkeiron, that Nakahira shared with Masao Matsuda, Masao Adachi, and others turned away from central protagonists and toward roads, underpasses, construction sites, suburbs, and reclaimed land. Stojković analyzes the Tokyo waterfront as an image of circulation networks carrying commodities, information, and labor*17. Franz Prichard reads it as a record of the spatial imprint of rapid economic growth and the Cold War order*18.

Written in 1972, “The Illusion Called the Documentary” examined the belief that documentary images transmit events intact, against the backdrop of televised coverage of the United Red Army incident and the reversion of Okinawa*7. Yuriko Furuhata argues that news media produced “current events” by repeatedly showing political confrontation, while landscape theory located state administration in roads and urban infrastructure without visible protagonists*28. Nakahira redirected his camera from the protagonists of an event to the screens that circulated it and the infrastructure that governed everyday movement.

Around 1970, the All-Japan Students’ Photo Association traveled to Minamata, Yokkaichi, Ashio, and other sites, incorporating photographs of damage, historical records, and statistics into its books. Kelly Midori McCormick places this activity within the formation of ecocritical photography in Japan*29. The association foregrounded victims and data, while Nakahira turned toward unpeopled roads. Both confronted the transformation of land by industrial and state systems.

Circulation: Paris, 1971—Same-Day Shooting and Installation

At the 1971 Paris Biennale, Nakahira photographed the city each day, developed the film at night, and added new prints to the wall the following day. The production of roughly two hundred images a day, his movement through the city, darkroom labor, the expanding wall, and the movement of viewers formed a continuous work*8. The work in SFMOMA’s collection is part of that unfolding activity*9.

Abbe analyzes the work as a process in which the photographer’s body moved through flows of traffic, commodities, and information, then returned the resulting images to the exhibition site*23. Because the interval between exposure and display was compressed, the work had no fixed final form until the exhibition ended. Nakahira later recalled that this project marked the first time his statements and actions began to coincide*8. Walking, darkroom labor, installation, and audience response all took place within the city’s circuits.

Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary? From Authorial Style to the Differences Among Things

Why an Illustrated Botanical Dictionary? is a collection of essays published in 1973. Nakahira criticized the way are-bure-boke had become a recognizable style of dissent that advertising and publishing could consume. Chikuma Shobō describes the book as charting his move from criticism of his early work toward a photography that would record things as things*10. Charrier examines this shift through postwar photographic realism and mechanical objectivity*11.

The “illustrated botanical dictionary” did not mean photographing plants alone. Nakahira placed plants, roads, buildings, and animals before the camera one by one, without using them as narrative symbols or substitutes for the author’s feelings. By refusing a single central image and granting unlike subjects equal status, he sought to limit the photographer’s power to assign meaning in advance. Prichard analyzes this enumeration as an open procedure in which fragments continue to accumulate*18.

Scholars have also noted the influence of Alain Robbe-Grillet and J. M. G. Le Clézio. Stojković compares Nakahira with the nouveau roman’s effort to detach objects from psychology and narrative and describe their form, position, and repetition*17. Neil Matheson discusses Nakahira’s critique of placing the human subject at the center of the world*3. Abbe draws attention to his contemporaneity with Lee Ufan, Mono-ha, and the phenomenological idea of the “encounter”*23. The method depended on a viewing body and a thing meeting in the same place before the object was absorbed into a familiar name.

The photographer’s body remained present in distance, framing, color, and the moment of exposure. Abbe and Prichard emphasize the reciprocity between the viewer and the viewed*19. Charrier questions whether the declaration that displaced the author actually achieved “true realism”*11. Nakahira turned to the dictionary because the success of his early photographs had created a new category of “Nakahira-like images.” He accepted as a photographic problem the contradiction that body and choice remain even in images attempting to evade classification.

Overflow: Forty-Eight Color Photographs and Contemporary Art

In Overflow (1974), forty-eight color photographs of manholes, subways, buildings, roads, signs, sharks, and other subjects occupied a wall approximately six meters wide. Taka Ishii Gallery relates the installation to the proliferation of photographic media and the sense that images were surging beyond the artist’s control*2. The reconstructed work is documented at approximately 1.6 meters high and six meters wide*12.

All the photographs appear at once on the wall, and their combinations change with the viewer’s position. Prichard argues that the installation transformed a media surplus delivered in one direction into an arrangement that could be read along multiple paths*18. Yasufumi Nakamori identifies Overflow as a turning point in Nakahira’s engagement with photography and 1970s contemporary art*27. A photograph of the Tokyo waterfront also appeared on the cover of the catalog for the 1970 Tokyo Biennale, Between Man and Matter. By incorporating the wall and the viewer’s movement, Nakahira made photography operate within the same field as conceptual art and intermedia.

sections.title: Major Works, Photobooks, and Exhibition Methods
sections.body_html:
La nuit and For a Language to Come

In SFMOMA’s La nuit 1, a dark street and traces of human presence sink into coarse grain and dense black tones*6. The photobook repeats 192 such images and removes information that would return the city to a familiar place. Nakahira’s self-critique began when this indistinctness became a recognizable visual signature.

Circulation: Date, Place, Events, 1971

In Circulation: Date, Place, Events, Nakahira repeated exposure, development, and display throughout the exhibition. By eliminating the delay in which a completed work would normally be presented after the fact, he placed the body walking through the city, the darkroom, the gallery, and the audience within one production process.

Overflow, 1974

Overflow retains the varying sizes and orientations of its forty-eight color photographs, extending advertisements, plants, roads, and industrial equipment across the viewer’s peripheral field. The 2024 retrospective placed this work, Nakahira’s magazine work, the islands, and his post-illness color photographs within a continuous account of his work*1. The sequence of images is produced by the viewer’s movement along the wall.

Okinawa, the Amami Islands, and the Color Photographs After His Illness

Nakahira photographed Okinawa in 1973 and the Amami and Tokara Islands, among other locations, between 1974 and 1977*16. Prichard examines sea routes, military bases, ports, and roads as structures that produced relations between mainland Japan and its peripheries*22. Abbe reads the tilted frames, close distances, and unstable spaces of the Amami photographs as “records of encounter” that depart from a viewpoint seeking orderly possession of its subject*23. The visual footing from which the mainland might organize the islands becomes unstable within the frame.

In 1977, Nakahira collapsed from acute alcohol poisoning and sustained serious impairments to memory and language. After recovering, he walked through Yokohama photographing in color, publishing the results in Aratanaru gyōshi (1983) and Adieu à X (1989), among other books. Recent reassessments have resisted dividing his work before and after the illness into two separate artistic identities*1. An SFMOMA film shows how walking and photographing became part of his daily life after the illness*14.

The later work was not a simple return to the “illustrated botanical dictionary.” SFMOMA describes a growing emphasis on the differences among individual subjects that resist classification and generalization*16. Untitled, from Documentary uses lucid color and frontal composition unlike the early black-and-white work*15. Yet he continued to test difference through each act of walking and photographing, without quickly attaching the subject to an established meaning.

sections.title: Criticism, Reassessment, and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Why Did Takuma Nakahira Criticize His Own Photography?

For many years, Nakahira’s reputation outside Japan rested largely on PROVOKE and are-bure-boke. Abbe and Prichard note that the emphasis on this novelty obscured his more than one hundred critical essays and the methodological changes of the 1970s*19. Nakahira criticized his early style because its success had made it an imitable sensibility, turning a method intended to free images from explanation into another fixed sign.

His writing analyzed where the preceding method had failed to grasp reality; the next photographs, edits, and exhibitions tested that analysis under different terms. Body and editing remained in the dictionary’s enumeration, just as selection remained in the same-day installation. Nakahira did not resolve these contradictions in a single theory. He continued testing them by changing visual style, production time, exhibition space, color, and location.

Nakahira’s place in photographic history rests on his sustained test of the hope that photography, once independent from language, could reach reality directly—and on his recognition that photographs also become fixed as codes, commodities, and an artist’s name. He reworked the photographer’s body, paper and printing, editorial time, the exhibition wall, and the viewer’s movement as terms of production. The blind spots created by one successful method became the starting point of the next work.

International Scholarship: Body, Collective Work, Paper, and Islands

The Yokohama Museum of Art’s 2003 exhibition examined Nakahira’s post-illness work alongside his early photographs*13. The National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo’s 2024 exhibition presented Overflow, his magazine work, the islands, and the post-illness color photographs as a continuous history*1. In 2025, At the Limits of the Gaze, the first English-language selection of his writings, was published*19.

International scholarship has increasingly examined the circumstances from which Nakahira’s methods emerged. Ignas-Menzies addresses collective production*24. Charrier considers structuralism and codes*25. Kim analyzes paper and the materiality of the city*26. Furuhata situates television news in relation to landscape theory*28. McCormick examines contemporary pollution photography*29. Nakamori traces the intersection of photography and contemporary art*27. Abbe extends the discussion to the photographer’s body and the spaces of Amami*23.

In 2026, the Spanish newspaper El País also introduced Nakahira as a theorist concerned with power, language, and the act of seeing*21. Nakahira is now being reconsidered beyond the author of a particular visual style, as a photographer and critic who tested the terms of photography through the body, collective work, printing, urban infrastructure, exhibition, and island spaces.

talbot.html.lead_html: Talbot invented the calotype, establishing the negative-positive principle that made photography reproducible from a single exposure. The Pencil of Nature (1844–46) was the first commercially published photographically illustrated book, demonstrating photography as record, art, and reproductive medium simultaneously.
talbot.html.thesis_html: Talbot invented the calotype, a negative–positive process, and introduced the principle of photographic reproducibility into the history of the medium. Where the daguerreotype was a unique, unrepeatable object, Talbot's process allowed any number of positive prints from a single negative, laying the foundation for the reproductive logic that would later underpin twentieth-century magazines, newspapers, books, and advertising. With “The Pencil of Nature” (1844–46) he realized the first commercially published, photographically illustrated book, showing that photography could function at once as record, art, and reproduction. His strict management of patents ironically slowed the spread of his methods, yet in conceptual and technical reach his contribution extends across twentieth-century photographic culture.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
William Henry Fox Talbot was born in 1800 at Melbury Sampford, Dorset. He studied Latin, Greek, mathematics, and natural science at Cambridge and later produced work across linguistics, botany, and astronomy — a nineteenth-century polymath whose photography was only one strand of a broad scientific practice*1.

The turning point came in October 1833 at Lake Como, on his honeymoon. Trying to sketch with a camera lucida, he was frustrated by what he saw as his own inability to draw. He later wrote that once he looked away from the device, "only a faint and imperfect trace" was left on the paper. That frustration prompted the question of whether the camera's projected image might be fixed chemically, and he began experiments on his return*2.

In the summer of 1835 he placed small cameras around Lacock Abbey, recording the buildings on sensitized paper. His wife called the boxes "mousetrap cameras." The Latticed Window (c.1835), a fragment barely 2.5 × 2.5 cm, is the oldest surviving Talbot image from this period*3.

When news of Daguerre's success arrived in January 1839, Talbot hastened to publicize his own method. The calotype process, patented in 1841 under that name, used paper negatives and allowed multiple positive prints from a single exposure — the first practical negative-positive photography. The Pencil of Nature, published in installments from 1844 to 1846, was the first commercially produced book illustrated with photographs, demonstrating photography as record, art, and reproduced medium across its twenty-four plates*4.

Talbot's strict patent enforcement significantly slowed British photography relative to France. He also devoted much of his later life to cuneiform decipherment. He died in 1877*5.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
The difference between calotype and daguerreotype is not simply a matter of technical quality. The daguerreotype aimed at a faithful, non-reproducible record on a singular object; the calotype combined paper's grainy, soft texture with the capacity to make multiple copies*6. Talbot's process is the origin of the modern photographic concept in which "photographs are reproduced."

The material character of the paper negative — the way the paper's grain merges with the image — was both a visual limitation and the source of the painterly quality that Hill and Adamson discovered. For the first plate of The Pencil of Nature — Lacock Abbey's latticed window — Talbot wrote one of the earliest theoretical and philosophical texts about photography, raising for the first time what a photograph fundamentally is*7.

The negative-positive principle established by Talbot became the foundation for all subsequent photographic reproduction: film photography, halftone printing, photogravure, and eventually digital image capture. In this respect Talbot's contribution is more conceptual and technical than it is aesthetic, and its full significance emerged over the following century*8.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
Talbot's patent policy became one of photography's early ironies: the inventor of a reproducible medium inhibited the medium's reproduction. British commercial photography was measurably slower to develop than its French counterpart through the 1840s*9. After 1852 Talbot relaxed some restrictions and allowed amateur use without fee.

The core of Talbot's legacy is the negative. That concept — one exposure, many prints — underpinned the entire photographic economy of the twentieth century: magazines, newspapers, books, and advertising. The Metropolitan Museum names him as co-inventor of photography alongside Daguerre*10, and the V&A holds one of the world's largest Talbot collections alongside the in situ holdings at Lacock Abbey*11.

Lacock Abbey (Wiltshire) is preserved by the National Trust; the rooms and darkroom where Talbot worked are open to visitors. The Fox Talbot Museum opened in 1975 and holds original prints and experimental notebooks*12. In recent years, Talbot's photogenic drawings of plant specimens have begun to attract art-historical attention in their own right, as objects that sit between scientific record and aesthetic form*13.

the-atlas-group-walid-raad.html.lead_html: The Atlas Group is a long-term project that Walid Raad began presenting in the late 1990s under the name of a fictional research foundation. Raad made and collected photographs, videos, notebooks, newspaper materials, and data tables, classifying them as documents received from invented historians and donors. The real elements include Raad himself, existing press materials, the artworks he produced, exhibitions, lectures, and the website. The foundation’s institutional history, several of its contributors, and parts of the documents’ provenance were invented. Through “Missing Lebanese Wars,” “The Bachar Tapes,” and “My Neck Is Thinner Than a Hair,” the project shows how histories of war are assembled from images, authors’ names, dates, classifications, narrators, and collecting institutions.
the-atlas-group-walid-raad.html.thesis_html: Discussions of war photography often centered on whether individual images or testimonies were true. To address whose documents the memories of civil war become, and how they enter public history, Raad created the fictional research foundation The Atlas Group. By assuming the roles of author, donor, custodian, and lecturer, he shifted the question from the authenticity of a photograph to the archives and institutions that establish a fact.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
How The Atlas Group Works

Walid Raad conceived The Atlas Group and presented it as a research foundation*6. The photographs, videos, notebooks, exhibitions, lectures, and website produced by Raad are real. The foundation’s institutional history, several donors and researchers, and parts of the provenance assigned to its documents were invented. In exhibitions, photographs and notebooks carrying file numbers appear on walls and in cases; in lectures, Raad explains their origins as a representative of the foundation. A single artist performs the roles of author, custodian, classifier, and interpreter, exposing every stage through which an archive is constituted.*1*4

Raad began using The Atlas Group name publicly in the late 1990s, while the project itself assigns the foundation an operating period of 1989 to 2004.*4. Accounts of its founding date and cofounders changed across presentations, and the biographies of its invented researchers and donors were revised. Through exhibitions, a website, lectures, and archival boxes, the imaginary foundation gradually acquired the outward behavior of an actual research institution.*7. Allowing the organization’s own history to change demonstrated how chronologies and institutional narratives support trust in documents.

Why a Fictional Foundation Was Necessary

The Lebanese Civil War, which lasted from 1975 to 1990, involved multiple political factions, religious communities, foreign armies, and militias. Even after the ceasefire, no shared account of its causes and responsibilities took hold easily. Reconstruction prioritized the physical rebuilding of Beirut, while memories of the war remained divided among political groups, families, exiles, and news organizations. Raad has explained that he collected existing documents and photographs while also imagining “the worlds in which those documents existed”*7. This idea led to a foundation that placed real and invented materials within the same system of classification.

Raad sought to address the events of the war together with the procedures through which fragmentary photographs and testimonies become public history. A work presented under an individual artist’s name identifies its maker, but it cannot reproduce all the authority added through donation, classification, preservation, exhibition, and scholarly presentation. A fictional foundation could attribute conflicting accounts to different contributors, place real and invented materials in the same formats, and allow Raad to explain them in the role of a researcher. The foundation allowed Raad to hold conflicting memories of the civil war within one project and to stage the institutional processes through which history acquires credibility.*18*8

sections.title: How Documents Become Facts
sections.body_html:
“Different Kinds of Facts”

Raad has said that his work begins with facts, and that facts possess historical, emotional, and aesthetic dimensions.A MoMA audio guide presents this statement as a key to understanding The Atlas Group’s method *2. Chronologies and statistics can record the date and location of an explosion and the number of deaths. Emotional memory also preserves the sensation of seeing a red car and anticipating a bomb, the excessive intensity of color, or a body repeating the same gesture. Fictional documents preserve verifiable information and emotional traces as distinct layers, widening the forms through which wartime experience can be conveyed.

Giving Documents a Provenance

Seen without their captions, The Atlas Group’s photographs can resemble newspaper clippings, family snapshots, police records, or research notes. Names such as Dr. Fadl Fakhouri and Souheil Bachar, along with notebook numbers, donation dates, and classification codes, give the materials a provenance. KADIST describes Raad’s manipulation of vernacular photographs and archival documents as an examination of the boundaries between document and fiction, history and memory, discourse and experience*5. In a MoMA audio guide, Raad describes combining old family slides with photographs of assassinations gathered from Lebanese photographic archives, treating images he made and images he collected as materials within the same process*3. The invented author functions as a character within the narrative and as a means of exposing the institutional habit of establishing value by asking whose document it is.

Lecture-Performance

Raad paired wall displays with lecture-performances, showing slides and explaining the origins of files in the manner of a researcher or foundation representative. The narration adopts the measured tone of an academic presentation, while contradictions in dates and relationships gradually emerge. Aperture argues that the lecture itself becomes an artistic form that produces the credibility of the documents in real time*13. The audience compares images, captions, and the speaker’s demeanor, while testing its own inclination to trust a professional mode of address. In a conversation with John Menick, Raad discusses in detail how the work asks viewers to assess both the lecturer’s authority and the credibility of the story*17*14.

Experiences That Escape Classification

The Atlas Group follows the process through which materials receive authors’ names, dates, classification numbers, and donation records, are arranged in orderly sequences, and come to be read as historical evidence. Classification turns fragments into searchable history, while organizing sensation and contradiction into a coherent account. By introducing invented contributors and shifting provenances, Raad placed the understanding produced by archival order beside the experiences that order excludes.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Medium
sections.body_html:
Missing Lebanese Wars

“Missing Lebanese Wars” uses notebooks, clippings, photographs, and annotations to construct the invented story of Lebanese historians who attended the racetrack and wagered on the exact moment the winning horse crossed the finish line. Museo Reina Sofía presents the work as a parallel between faith in photography’s “decisive moment” and the historian’s act of determining when an event begins and ends*20. The racetrack finish photograph makes concrete the question of who selects a war’s beginning, turning points, and end, and which records preserve those decisions.

My Neck Is Thinner Than a Hair

This project is framed as an investigation of car bombs used during the Lebanese wars through the relations among wreckage at blast sites, engines, newspaper photographs, photographers, and the publications in which the images appeared. The official archive describes the work as a study of 3,641 car-bomb incidents*10. By tracing engines thrown far from the explosion and the positions from which press cameras photographed them, the work follows the path through which evidence of violence is produced across the site, the newspaper, and the archive.

The Bachar Tapes

In “The Bachar Tapes,” the testimony of the fictional Lebanese hostage Souheil Bachar is inserted into the history of Western hostages held in Lebanon during the 1980s. The National Gallery of Canada describes the work as an inquiry into which experiences enter international news through the translation, editing, and delay of video testimony*11. By adding a witness who did not exist, the work makes visible how established hostage narratives were edited around particular nationalities, languages, and forms of masculinity. SFMOMA’s artist record also identifies the video as a major work in which photography, testimony, and translation intersect*9.

Comparison with the Arab Image Foundation

During the same period in Beirut, the Arab Image Foundation collected and preserved historic and studio photographs, providing a physical repository for vulnerable regional photographic cultures. A conversation in Bidoun places this real archive beside The Atlas Group: the former preserves material objects and researches their provenance, while the latter uses fictional donors and classifications to question the authority of preservation itself*7. Raad affirms the value of preservation while treating the assignment of preserved objects to particular narratives as a separate artistic problem.

sections.title: Criticism, Reception, and Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Fiction and Historical Responsibility

The Atlas Group can be criticized for relativizing real suffering by mixing invented people and events into the history of an actual war. In a conversation with The Brooklyn Rail, Raad states that he made the project’s images and stories and attributed them to fictional figures, while asking that the method not be reduced to a simple test of truth or falsity *15. A risk remains when only audiences familiar with museum conventions can recognize the device: Lebanese history may then be consumed as a conceptual game. The work’s ethical tension lies in keeping this danger visible and extending the question to who has the right to use fiction. An ICA Boston retrospective presented Raad’s movement between fact and invention together with this ethical unease*12.

Post-Documentary

Photographic history already contained debates over documentary evidence and artistic practices that criticized archival classification and institutional authority. Raad connected those debates to memories of the Lebanese Civil War and combined a fictional foundation, changing provenances, and lecture-performances within a single structure*18. A single invented photograph addresses only the image itself. Ownership, storage, narration, and public acceptance require a larger structure. Through the foundation, Raad created authors, donors, classifiers, a collecting institution, and a lecturer, reconstructing the entire process through which facts gain social credibility. Teaching materials from Art Resources Transfer likewise describe his movement among the roles of archivist, historian, teacher, performer, and artist in order to examine the power and limits of documents to communicate history*16. The Atlas Group’s significance within photographic history lies in shifting the question from “Is this photograph authentic?” to “What makes this photograph credible as a historical fact?”*11*19.

Real and Invented Materials

The real elements are Walid Raad himself; the photographs, videos, and notebooks he produced; existing newspaper photographs and broadcast materials; exhibitions; lectures; and the official website. Invented elements include the institutional history of an independent foundation, contributors such as Dr. Fadl Fakhouri and Souheil Bachar, researchers’ biographies, and parts of the documents’ provenance. Individual files combine the two. “My Neck Is Thinner Than a Hair,” for example, uses actual press materials and field research, reediting them as the foundation’s research files. The construction asks viewers to read the content of an image together with the credibility conferred by an author’s name, a date, a classification number, and a museum display.*1

Through his transition from sculpture to photography and works including Raum, Poll, and Control Room, this page examines his working method, the meaning of his images, and his place in photographic history.

thomas-demand.html.lead_html: Thomas Demand (born in Germany in 1964) works with realities that have already been framed through someone else’s viewpoint—news photographs, documentary images, personal snapshots, and architectural models. He reconstructs them at life size in paper and cardboard, then presents them as photographs.*7 Around 1993, photography shifted from a means of documenting his sculptures to the final work itself, and his subjects expanded from places he knew firsthand to history and politics encountered through other people’s images.*5 In building the models, he must infer depth and dimensions absent from the source image, while deciding which figures, texts, and signs of use to retain. Photographing the model again closes that inquiry back into a single viewpoint and returns it to circulation in the same one-image format as news and documentary photography.*30 Through works including 《Raum》, 《Poll》, 《Presidency》, 《Yellowcake》, 《Control Room》, and 《Dailies》, Demand has examined how photographs do more than lodge events in memory: they also participate in the production of political authority and factual accounts.
thomas-demand.html.thesis_html: From the late 1970s through the 1980s, Jeff Wall restaged events he had witnessed using actors.*26 James Casebere photographed tabletop models, giving seemingly plausible spaces an atmosphere of anxiety and surveillance.*25 Demand took specific news and documentary photographs that many viewers had seen in place of the actual site and rebuilt them as life-size objects, using his hands and body to construct spaces he had never experienced from another person’s single viewpoint.*5 By inferring what the source image withheld and turning the model back into a photograph, he extended constructed photography beyond invented scenes to the process by which news and documentary images become stand-ins for events through selection, omission, and repetition.*40
