tokuko-ushioda.html.lead_html: Tokuko Ushioda is a photographer who has used refrigerators, books, and the light and household objects left in the rooms of Gotokuji to photograph the time of those close to her without relying only on facial expression. After studying with Yasuhiro Ishimoto and Kiyoji Otsuji at Kuwasawa, she began with street portraits, but her hesitation toward photographing people led her toward a frontal, sustained recording of objects touched by daily life. In recent years, My Husband has brought renewed attention to her work as a meeting point of family photography, object photography, photobooks, and the history of Japanese women photographers.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Tokuko Ushioda was born in Tokyo. She entered Kuwasawa Design School in 1960 and graduated in 1963 from its Living Design Department, where she majored in photography*1. AWARE's artist biography notes that she studied at Kuwasawa with Yasuhiro Ishimoto and Kiyoji Otsuji, and that she also came into contact with photographers of the same generation such as Shigeo Gocho*2. From 1966 to 1978 she worked as an assistant and lecturer in photography at Kuwasawa Design School and Tokyo Zokei University, and around 1975 she began working as a freelance photographer*3. In 1976 she held her first solo exhibition, Smiling Handcuffs, at Shinjuku Nikon Salon; in 1978 she married the photographer Shinzo Shimao, and their daughter Maho was born the same year*4. At the beginning of 1979, the family moved into a room in the former residence of Ozaki Yukio, which had been relocated to Gotokuji in Tokyo. Life in this old Western-style house later became the domestic setting behind My Husband and ICE BOX*5. From the 1990s onward, Ushioda developed the long-term project BIBLIOTHECA, photographing books, shelves, libraries, publishing houses, and conservation spaces; in 2018 the series received the 37th Domon Ken Award, the Photographic Society of Japan's Photographer Award, and the Higashikawa Domestic Photographer Award*6. In 2022, torch press published My Husband, a photobook made from family photographs taken from the late 1970s to the early 1980s, and the book received a Jurors' Special Mention at the Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards*7.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Kuwasawa and Kiyoji Otsuji: beginning in a place where photographs were read

What distinguishes Ushioda's photography is not the pursuit of dramatic events, but the act of photographing objects in daily life as traces of use, touch, and time. The photographic education she received at Kuwasawa, together with the environment around Kiyoji Otsuji where students and graduates looked at photobooks and discussed photography, formed an important ground for this attitude. Ushioda recalls seeing Robert Frank's The Americans for the first time at Otsuji's house, studying it with students and graduates until they had almost "worn holes" through it, and also buying books by Paul Strand*3. These recollections show that she encountered photography in an environment where a photograph was not only a single image, but also part of a sequence, a printed book, a structure of light and surface, and a way of looking. In relation to the photographic movements of the period, Yutaka Takanashi, one of her seniors at Kuwasawa, became involved with Provoke, while Ushioda later said that she did not feel drawn to that current and watched it from a distance*3. The Yokohama Civic Art Gallery Azamino leaflet also notes that it is difficult to place the early series To the Street squarely within the context of comporaphoto, even though Ushioda was close to CAMERA WORKS and the movement of independent galleries*8. Rather than absorbing the rough grain and strong movement associated with Provoke, or the delicate urban sensibility of comporaphoto, Ushioda moved toward a practice of photographing the familiar objects of her own living environment frontally and over time.

Hesitation before photographing people, and the move toward refrigerators

Photographing people had been part of Ushioda's practice from the period when she first studied photography at Kuwasawa. In the Azamino leaflet, she recalls that in Ishimoto's class students were assigned to go out into the city, approach strangers, obtain their consent, and photograph them; she went repeatedly to Ginza, Ueno, Asakusa, and Shinjuku*8. In the Kuwasawa interview, she explains that her first solo exhibition around 1976, Smiling Handcuffs, was held at Nikon Salon because she had accumulated photographs of people, including images made in Shinjuku, the sideshows of Asakusa, and Ginza*3. The photographs from this period, later known as To the Street, came out of a practice of approaching people on the street and photographing them after gaining permission. Yet this method soon produced a sense of difficulty. In the Azamino leaflet, Ushioda writes that the more she learned how to photograph people, the more she began to wonder whether the camera had become a weapon, something used to hunt its target*8; in an IMA interview, she also says that as she continued photographing people, she felt her own gaze becoming slanted and unkind toward society and others, and that Shimao told her she should value human dignity when photographing people*9; and in a conversation published by the Canadian Centre for Architecture, she recalls that as her technique improved, pointing the camera at another person came to feel like using a weapon, and that she sensed a limit in that way of photographing others*10. The move toward refrigerators began where this hesitation toward portraiture met the concrete conditions of life in the Gotokuji room. In IMA, Ushioda explains that she tried to photograph inside and around the house as lightly as Shimao did, but felt she was merely imitating him; after stepping away from making work for a time, she looked for something she could do inside the house and began photographing the refrigerator with a 6×6 camera*9. A refrigerator is not a face, but it is used by someone, filled with food, opened and closed, and organized according to the rhythms of a household. Her hesitation before turning the camera toward people did not remove people from her work; it redirected her attention toward the objects that retained the evidence of how people lived.

ICE BOX: seeing the household through a domestic appliance

ICE BOX began when Ushioda photographed her own refrigerator and then expanded the project to the refrigerators of relatives, acquaintances, and friends*11. KYOTOGRAPHIE explains that she began by photographing her refrigerator as if recording her own life, then continued the project for roughly twenty years as she widened the circle of households*12. The Azamino retrospective leaflet gives concrete details: life in the former Ozaki Yukio residence at Gotokuji, the Swedish refrigerator bought as surplus from the occupying forces, and the decision to record the objects in the room*8. In the CCA conversation, Ushioda says that Shimao bought a large used refrigerator that had been sold near a U.S. military base, and that its sound and physical presence in the small room made her think about daily life and led her to begin photographing her days*10. In the same conversation, she explains that she photographed refrigerators almost as if collecting insects: she shot them open and closed from the front, without tidying up the area around them, leaving slippers and household goods in the frame when they were there*10. A refrigerator has no face or gesture, but it quietly contains food storage, shopping habits, the organization of a household, seasonal patterns, and the labor inside the home. In ICE BOX, instead of explaining a person's feelings through facial expression, the door, shelves, contents, and nearby objects show differences in how each household lives. Frontal repetition does not turn the refrigerators into anonymous industrial products; it makes the differences between their uses visible within a shared format. Regarding comparisons with Bernd and Hilla Becher, the Azamino leaflet acknowledges a shared concern with simple format and a defined subject, but stresses that Ushioda's work is not typology itself, because stories and social relations open out from the objects she photographs*8. Tokyo Photographic Art Museum's TOP Collection: Serendipity placed Refrigerator in a section titled "Quiet Gazes, Fullness of Time," alongside works by Shigeo Gocho, Kazuo Kitai, and Shinzo Shimao, a context that helps read the series as a quiet observation of the interior of domestic life*13.

BIBLIOTHECA: books as touched and preserved objects

In BIBLIOTHECA, begun in 1995, Ushioda's subject shifts from refrigerators to books. PGI's exhibition text explains that the series photographs books not only as carriers of information, but as things that have passed through many hands and changed over time*14. The Nikon THE GALLERY text states that Ushioda was not drawn primarily to knowing the contents of the books, but to the beauty of bookmaking and to the presence of books as objects*6. Her shooting notes for Shiseido Gallery include first editions, used books, damaged covers, conservation work, gloves, and experiences of photographing in stacks; they make clear that books are not only containers of content, but objects that are handled, damaged, and protected*15. In the Kuwasawa interview, Shimao explains that, from the letters visible in the photographs, he researched authors, publication years, approximate contents, and page counts*3. The Azamino leaflet also quotes Ushioda recalling that Shimao told her even the most ordinary thing has a story, a remark that released her from hesitation about photographing objects*8. Here, "story" does not mean an anecdote added by the photographer. It means a specific time that becomes visible when one follows the author, publication date, publisher, traces of repair, storage space, and history of possession of the book in the photograph. In Misuzu Shobo, for example, Ushioda photographed the wooden former office building used from 1948 to 1996, its stacks, editorial rooms, editorial meetings, and empty rooms before demolition*8. The same leaflet records her statement that Maruyama Masao's Between War and Postwar, which looked as if it had been left behind on an empty shelf, became one of the triggers for photographing books*8. A book appears not only as a medium for reading, but as an object tied to a publishing house, editorial labor, postwar thought, repair, and the movement of collections. In this sense, BIBLIOTHECA is both still-life photography and a photography of spaces where knowledge is kept: libraries, publishers, private collections, conservation sites, and Kiyoji Otsuji's studio. Bibliotheca [#01], held by the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo and recorded through Art Platform Japan as a gelatin silver print made in 2007 and printed in 2018, also shows that the series has entered museum collections as photographic work*16.

My Husband: the same room, another gaze

My Husband consists of photographs of Shinzo Shimao, their daughter Maho, and life in the Western-style house at Gotokuji*5. In the IMA interview, Ushioda explains that these photographs were not originally made for an exhibition or a book; old prints and negatives were rediscovered during a move, leading the work to be reconsidered roughly forty years later*9. The same family life had also been photographed by Shinzo Shimao in works such as Maho-chan. In the CCA conversation, Ushioda says that because her husband had already produced a successful body of work from the same one-room life, she had not thought of presenting her own photographs, but that the images eventually gathered as My Husband were different from Shimao's photographs*10. In the Kuwasawa interview, she describes Shimao's photographs as images that include blur, camera shake, and ambiguous contrast yet gain atmosphere in print, while she herself worked with a tripod and careful focus*3. Even when the same room, the same family, and the same years are photographed, Shimao's pictures carry a printed atmosphere of blur and movement, whereas Ushioda's photographs preserve the arrangement of light, furniture, paper, dishes, the refrigerator, and cloth by the window.

As a photobook, My Husband is composed of two volumes: Book 1, centered on 6×6 photographs, and Book 2, centered on 35mm photographs*17. PGI describes Book 1 as a 122-page hardcover volume, Book 2 as a 76-page softcover volume, with texts by Yuri Mitsuda and Yurie Nagashima, design by Yuri Suyama, and Japanese and English text*18. Aperture praised the loose band that holds the two books together, one cloth-bound volume, the attention to the details of domestic space, duotone printing that reproduces the tonal range of the black-and-white photographs, and the essays by Mitsuda and Nagashima*7. When My Husband is placed within an international photobook context, the central point is not only the quality of its bookmaking. What matters is that photographs made in a room in Tokyo from the late 1970s to the early 1980s by a woman who was at once wife, mother, and photographer—images of her husband, young daughter, refrigerator, kitchen, bedding, scraps of paper, and visitors from the photography world—came to be read, through editing forty years later, as a record of a period, a household, and a photographer's gaze. At the 2022 Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards, 35 books were selected from 1,026 submissions; My Husband was shortlisted in the PhotoBook of the Year category and received a Jurors' Special Mention*19. Aperture's attention to the two-volume structure, the banded binding, the duotone printing, and the essays by Mitsuda and Nagashima indicates that the photographs made inside a household had become not a nostalgic family album, but a photobook through which readers could encounter domestic life, marriage, childrearing, and a woman photographer's viewpoint in late-1970s Japan*7. The three major bodies of work are linked by the way initially familiar subjects—refrigerators, books, and domestic photographs—are later gathered into books and exhibitions, where they can be read as records of the household, publishing culture, and relationships among photographers.

Criticism and Reception

Ushioda's reception expanded significantly from the late 2010s through domestic awards, photobooks, and international exhibitions. The fact that BIBLIOTHECA received the Domon Ken Award, the Photographic Society of Japan's Photographer Award, and the Higashikawa Domestic Photographer Award in 2018 indicates that this long-term project on books came to be recognized not merely as still life or documentary record, but as one of the central works of her career*6. The reception opened by My Husband is not only a rediscovery of family photographs. PGI explains that the work records not only Ushioda's family life and growth as an artist, but also the period in which Japanese photography, including Zeit-Foto Salon, Japan's first commercial photography gallery, was developing*18. The same exhibition text points out that young figures who later helped shape Japanese photography, including Shigeo Gocho, critic Osamu Hiraki, and photo historian Ryuichi Kaneko, appear through Ushioda's gaze*18. FUJIFILM SQUARE's English exhibition page also presents the publication of the photobook in 2022 as the occasion for renewed attention to photographs made roughly forty years earlier, both in Japan and abroad*5.

When Ushioda was making the photographs that would later become My Husband and ICE BOX in the late 1970s, Japanese photography was marked by several overlapping currents: the aftermath of Provoke, comporaphoto, I-photography, commercial galleries, and photobook culture. At the same time, domestic spaces such as the home, childrearing, housework, and marriage—spaces deeply connected to women's lives—were not always treated as central terms in photographic history. Aperture's I'm So Happy You Are Here: Japanese Women Photographers from the 1950s to Now presents the work of women photographers as a counterpoint, complement, and challenge to existing histories of Japanese photography, emphasizing how women looked at their own lives and at Japanese society*20. Japan House São Paulo's Life that unfolds places Ushioda in dialogue with Rinko Kawauchi, who values Ushioda as an artist who continued working as a photographer at a time when women's social advancement was difficult and who faced everyday life with sincerity*21. Fotomuseum Den Haag also presents the exhibition as a corrective to the Western visibility of male Japanese photographers, foregrounding observation of daily life, women's social positions, and experimentation with photographic form*22. In roughly the same period abroad, women photographers were addressing private life and images of women in different ways. Cindy Sherman began Untitled Film Stills in 1977, restaging female images circulated through film and media; MoMA associates her work with both photography and feminist art*23. Nan Goldin, from the late 1970s into the 1980s, shaped images of friends, lovers, children, violence, and loss into a slideshow and photobook, and MoMA describes The Ballad of Sexual Dependency as an intensely personal narrative built from the artist's own experience*24. Ushioda's work does not restage female images as Sherman does, nor does it present an intimate community as a diary in Goldin's manner. Its distinctiveness lies in recording time spent inside the household through refrigerators, furniture, books, and the details of rooms, not as confession but as accumulated observation. For that reason, the international reception of My Husband does not mean simply that a well-made photobook was praised. It means that photographs of a Japanese household and a woman photographer's viewpoint from the late 1970s became, through the form of the photobook, an entry point through which readers elsewhere could approach a history that had often remained less visible. In ICE BOX, the repeated open and closed refrigerators show food, living arrangements, habits of organization, and differences between households. In BIBLIOTHECA, the content of a book is joined by publication dates, authors, repairs, stacks, former publishing-house buildings, and the histories of collections. In My Husband, private family photographs become, through a two-volume book, essays, and an international photobook award, documents of life and of photographic relationships in Japan from the late 1970s to the early 1980s. Ushioda cannot be contained within a single category such as I-photography, object photography, photobook, or archive. Through the sustained photographing of objects inside the home, she gave family, daily life, publishing culture, and the viewpoint of a woman photographer a photographic form that could be examined later.

tomatsu.html.lead_html: Shomei Tomatsu photographed postwar Japan as a continuing presence in matter and bodies, from melted glass and scarred skin in Nagasaki to English signs around American bases and the sea and rituals of Okinawa. In 11:02 Nagasaki and The Pencil of the Sun, symbolic close-ups, chains of fragments, and photobook sequence produced a view of the atomic bomb, occupation, Americanization, and Okinawa that resists consolidation into a single national story.
tomatsu.html.thesis_html: Tomatsu did not organize the postwar as a completed event. He photographed its duration in melted bottles, skin, signs, chewing gum, fences, sea, and ritual. Moving away from distant views that claim to explain society as a whole, he linked fragments of matter and bodies to photograph how occupation, the atomic bomb, Americanization, and Okinawa persisted within everyday life This approach substantially renewed the critical language of postwar Japanese photography.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
From Iwanami Shashin Bunko to VIVO: Changing the Method of Social Photography

Tomatsu worked on Iwanami Shashin Bunko in the 1950s, gaining experience with photo essays designed to explain regions and industries. In 1959 he formed VIVO with Eikoh Hosoe, Kikuji Kawada, Ikko Narahara, and others, shifting from commissioned social documentation toward self-directed subjects and editing*1. He retained an intense concern with reality while questioning the reduction of postwar Japan to one representative image, turning instead toward material fragments and unstable compositions.

From the Fieldwork of Iwanami Shashin Bunko to VIVO: Postwar Daily Life in Fragments

Through Iwanami Shashin Bunko, Tomatsu photographed social and industrial sites and observed how editorial policy and captions converted photographs into public knowledge. In his later independent work, he approached signs around American bases, damaged objects, consumer goods, and fragments of bodies instead of typical characters or representative events. Postwar daily life contained both resistance to occupation and desire for American culture, a contradiction that could not be contained by a simple moral judgment or reconstruction narrative. VIVO provided a place to transfer that contradiction into sequences of fragments and photobook editing.

The Bases Remain After the Occupation: Photographing the Postwar in the Present Tense

Japan regained sovereignty in 1952, but American military bases and cultural influence remained visible across the country. In Yokosuka, Sasebo, Okinawa, and elsewhere, Tomatsu photographed soldiers, bars, signs, women, fences, chewing gum, and Coca-Cola, showing occupation persisting as an everyday visual field. The National Museum of Asian Art introduces Chewing Gum and Chocolate as a series tracing the American military presence and transformations in Japanese society*2.

After Ken Domon and Ihei Kimura: Inheriting and Displacing Realism

Tomatsu inherited from Ken Domon, Ihei Kimura, and postwar realism the ethical demand to go to actual places and photograph society. He also moved away from making a representative person or decisive event stand for the whole and approached signs around bases, a melted bottle, a stopped watch, and scarred skin—fragments whose meanings did not resolve into one statement. Participation in VIVO became one setting for reconsidering social contradiction through symbolic objects and bodies.

A Critique of Realism: From the Representative Image to a Chain of Fragments

Tomatsu retained realism’s ethical commitment to confronting actual conditions while keeping his distance from the assumption that a forceful photograph could transparently represent a social issue. Research at Osaka University argues that his images do not fix postwar Americanization as either celebration or rejection, but register attraction and humiliation coexisting in everyday life*11. Tilted frames, close-up, and symbolic objects prevented contradictory feelings from being resolved into one explanation. The form was built to preserve that contradiction.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
11:02 Nagasaki: Showing the Atomic Bomb Without a Photograph of the Explosion

Tomatsu began photographing Nagasaki more than a decade after the bombing and could not directly record the explosion or the immediate ruins. He turned to museum relics, survivors’ bodies, the rebuilt city, and religious sites, photographing the time the atomic bomb had left in matter and daily life. 《11:02 Nagasaki》 takes the stopped time of a clock as its title, joining a historical instant to the present of the later photograph*3.

Why Tomatsu Kept Returning to Nagasaki: From Past Catastrophe to Living Bodies

Tomatsu arrived in Nagasaki more than ten years after the explosion. His subject was not the flash preserved in historical photographs, but survivors’ lives and transformations in matter. A melted bottle, a stopped watch, and scarred skin are symbols of the atomic bomb and concrete presences that continued into the time of exposure. Japan Society’s retrospective Skin of the Nation treated Nagasaki as a long-term subject rather than a single assignment; Tomatsu returned for more than half a century*5. Duration restored the city from a fixed stage of tragedy to a place shaped by urban life and generational change.

The Melted Bottle: How Much History Can Matter Carry?

In the close photograph of a glass bottle deformed by heat, the object remains an accessioned relic while appearing as a twisted shape suggestive of a body. The National Museum of Asian Art identifies the image as one of the emblematic works of the Nagasaki series*2. By pressing the deformation left by atomic heat toward the surface of the image, Tomatsu converted historical knowledge into a visual encounter with matter.

The Skin of Survivors: The Ethics of Photographic Proximity

The Nagasaki series includes portraits and bodily details of people injured by the atomic bomb. Close-up brings harm back from abstract numbers to individual lives, while also risking the circulation of wounds as forceful symbols. The Smithsonian’s Nagasaki exhibition places relics, the city, and survivors’ lives within the same history rather than reducing the project to one shocking picture*4. Tomatsu’s formal proximity cannot be separated from the duration lived by the people photographed.

Signs and Bodies Around the Bases: Photographing Americanization in Fragments

Around American bases, English signs, uniforms, cars, entertainment venues, and Japanese youth enter the same frames, presenting occupation culture as a mixture that cannot be simplified into imitation or resistance. Tomatsu located Americanization in the everyday details of products, language, clothing, and bodily distance. Japan Society’s Skin of the Nation brought Nagasaki, the bases, and Okinawa together as changes registered on the “skin” of the postwar nation*5.

Okinawa and The Pencil of the Sun: Bases, Ritual, and Sea Within the Time of One Place

From 1969 onward, Tomatsu repeatedly visited Okinawa and the Southwest Islands, photographing American bases, island rituals, the sea, vegetation, and people’s bodies. In The Pencil of the Sun, strong light, local color, and distinct ways of life establish the rhythm of the book alongside political questions viewed from mainland Japan*1. Okinawa confronted him with histories and cultures that did not share the mainland’s chronology and required a transformation of the method developed in Nagasaki.

How Okinawa Changed Tomatsu’s Photography: From Evidence of Occupation to the Time of the Land

In Okinawa, Tomatsu photographed island ritual, sea, plants, older people, youth, and intense sunlight as well as bases and American soldiers. The increased use of color in work previously associated with monochrome can be understood as a refusal to subordinate the materiality and light of the southern islands to a mainland image of the postwar. Okinawa appears as a place from which the contradiction of a sovereign mainland still dependent on military bases could be viewed in reverse. The change in form shows a photographer continually altering his language in response to place.

The Occupation Series: The Exchange of Chewing Gum and Chocolate

The title Chewing Gum and Chocolate recalls children receiving goods from American soldiers after defeat. The series includes huge military machines, leisure, commodities, bodies, and English entering Japanese everyday life. American culture does not appear solely as an external aggressor; it is also desired and imitated, so attraction and resentment coexist in the image. Occupation becomes a lived experience extending from political institutions to taste and gesture.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Symbolic Close-Up: Photographing Society Without Showing the Whole

Tomatsu’s close-ups fill the frame with bottles, clocks, skin, artificial eyes, and signs, reducing surrounding information. The object remains identifiable while scratches, reflections, and distortions on its surface expand social associations. Tate’s holdings show material fragments functioning as a central vocabulary for his account of postwar Japan*6. Through sequences of fragments, history that no single picture could represent accumulates across the work.

Photobook Sequence: How Are Nagasaki, the Bases, and Okinawa Connected?

Tomatsu edited photographs from different years and places into books including 11:02 Nagasaki, Nippon, and The Pencil of the Sun, as well as publishing them in magazines. Repetition and contrast across pages connect the atomic bomb, occupation, consumption, and the southern islands as several temporalities of postwar Japan. SFMOMA’s artist materials and videos trace his continuing revision of subjects through series and photobooks*7.

The Turn to Color: Releasing Okinawan Light from Monochrome

Tomatsu is known for high-contrast black-and-white work, yet he used color extensively in Okinawa. Color does more than reinforce a tropical image; it gives clothing, plants, sea, and artificial objects a density different from monochrome. The difference between compressing Nagasaki relics into dark tonalities and opening Okinawan color shows an artist who changed his vocabulary according to place rather than remaining fixed within one style.

Plastics: Photographing the Surface of High-Growth Japan

Tomatsu also photographed plastic goods, packaging, and artificial color and light, registering new surfaces produced by postwar consumer society. A bottle deformed by atomic heat and mass-produced plastic carry different histories, but his interest in reading an era through material form connects them. Within the linear story from ruins to reconstruction, close views of commodities and waste show how prosperity altered bodily sensation and environment.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photo History
sections.body_html:
Tomatsu and Kikuji Kawada: Encountering Traces on Site or Symbolizing Them in a Book

Kawada’s The Map also addresses walls of the Atomic Bomb Dome, war relics, and signs of occupation, but organizes the entire photobook as a dark symbolic system. Tomatsu preserves encounters with particular people, objects, and places and develops postwar distortion from their specificity. Both emerged around VIVO and postwar memory, yet Tomatsu places greater weight on contact at the site, Kawada on collision across the page. Their difference shows that postwar Japanese photography cannot be reduced to a single “dark” expression.

Updating the Label “Representative of Postwar Japan”

International exhibitions have often introduced Tomatsu as a central representative of postwar Japanese photography. The label helped establish his reputation abroad, but it can merge the distinct histories of Nagasaki, military bases, and Okinawa into one national image. Tomatsu repeatedly moved toward places, things, and bodies that fell outside a unified account of Japan. As collections and retrospectives at MoMA, Tate, SFMOMA, and elsewhere have consolidated his status, the work is increasingly resituated within the specific times of survivors, Okinawa, and communities around bases*8.

The Force and Limits of Symbolic Fragments: Returning to the Histories of Those Represented

Tomatsu’s bottle and clock became international emblems of postwar Japan. Their strength lies in concentrating complicated history within a single object, but wide circulation can push the specific experiences of survivors and communities around military bases into the background. Recent scholarship and exhibitions have distinguished the political situations and dates of work in Nagasaki, Yokosuka, and Okinawa instead of treating them only under the summary phrase “Japan’s postwar”*12. Tomatsu’s criticism remains active when symbolic form is held together with the histories of the people it came to represent.

Looking at Mainland Japan from Okinawa: Reversing Center and Periphery

Tomatsu moved to Okinawa and photographed the islands over long periods, creating distance from a postwar history centered on Tokyo. After the 1972 reversion to Japan, he continued to follow the persistence of bases, Ryukyuan culture, ritual, nature, and tourism. Time spent living in place brought relations and changes of color unavailable to short assignments. Nagasaki and Okinawa have different histories and durations of exposure, and Tomatsu’s emblematic images remain grounded in the concrete time of people living there.

tomishige-rihei.html.lead_html: Tomishige Rihei founded the Tomishige Photography Studio in Kumamoto, leaving portrait photographs of figures including Natsume Soseki and Lafcadio Hearn and documentation of Kumamoto Castle. His studio became a key institution for photographic practice and regional modernity in Meiji-era Japan.
tomishige-rihei.html.thesis_html: Tomishige Rihei founded the Tomishige Photography Studio in Kumamoto and took on the task of institutionalizing photography in a provincial city. Through a practice ranging from portrait photography and the documentation of Kumamoto Castle and the aftermath of the Satsuma Rebellion to portraits of Natsume Soseki and Lafcadio Hearn, he created a base from which local society could render itself visible through photography. The preservation of the studio's building as a Nationally Registered Tangible Cultural Property, and the continued scholarly study of its archival materials, show that his work is valued beyond individual authorship — as primary material for the visual-culture history of regional modernity. Its continuation through the succession to his disciple Tokuji deepens that institutional significance further.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Tomishige Rihei was born in 1837 in Higo Province (present-day Kumamoto Prefecture), and his original family name was Shinokura. He studied photography in the final years of the Edo period and by the 1870s had opened a photography studio in Kumamoto.*1 The surviving collection includes glass plates, portraits, photographic equipment, and related documents, covering both the practical operations of the studio and visual records of regional modernization.*2 He also left documentary photographs of Kumamoto Castle, the old castle town, and the aftermath of the Seinan War, positioning him as a photographer who witnessed the region's modernization and historical turning points.*3 He is also known for having photographed portraits of Natsume Soseki and Lafcadio Hearn, giving his work connections to literary history. He died in 1912. His studio was succeeded by Tokuji, the second-generation head.*4

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Institutional significance of the Tomishige Photography Studio

Tomishige Rihei must be approached not only through analysis of individual works but as the founding figure of the Tomishige Photography Studio — a commercial photography studio and starting point for a regional archive. The survey report of the Nara National Research Institute for Cultural Properties describes the studio's holdings — encompassing glass plates, equipment, and documents — as a comprehensive archive of modern visual culture, showing that they constitute a complex body of material for understanding studio operations, the studio's connections to local society, and the history of photography as a technology.*5 The city of Kumamoto has registered the Tomishige Photography Studio building as a Registered Tangible Cultural Property of Japan, meaning that its physical structure has also been recognized as cultural heritage.*6 A paper published on J-STAGE by the Japanese Society for the Science of Design, under the subtitle "Centering on the Tomishige Rihei Materials," discusses methodology for surveying materials related to commercial photographers, indicating that the studio's holdings constitute a significant case study for research in photographic history.*7

Portrait culture and regional modernization

The exhibition context's phrase "the modern age of portraiture" is suggestive, indicating that the Tomishige Photography Studio's importance lies in its role in the formation of modern portrait culture in a regional city.*8 Portrait photography extended far beyond commemorative photographs; it was bound up with the modern institutions of self-representation — families, local notables, military, administration, schools — and recorded how urban society in Kumamoto made itself visible. The J-STAGE paper "Photographs That Recorded Japan's Modernization" can be read as a study showing that the Tomishige Photography Studio's materials occupy the boundary between private portraiture and public record.*9 The Kumamoto University exhibition "The Tomishige Photography Studio and the Modernization of Kumamoto" demonstrates that this studio was not merely a commercial establishment but a witness to regional modernization, and it continues to be evaluated in the context of university-community collaboration.*10 Symposium materials from Kokugakuin University reference Tomishige's documentary photographs in the context of tracing changes in Kumamoto Castle and the castle town through old photographs, showing their use from an architectural and urban history perspective.*11

Succession

It is important not to close the study of Rihei's work within a single-artist framework but to treat the Tomishige Photography Studio as an institution that was continued and inherited. The survey report recorded in the National Cultural Properties Registry shows that this body of material was not formed in a single generation but through a process of succession and accumulation.*12 Viewed in relation to the succession by Tokuji as the second-generation head, the significance of Rihei's work lies not in specific individual works but in having established the institution of a regional photography studio and passed it on to the next generation.*13 The Japan Photography Preservation Center's report discusses how the materials of commercial photographers including the Tomishige Photography Studio have been preserved as cultural archives, showing continuing evaluation in the context of preservation activity.*14 The old studio building of the Tomishige Photography Studio as recorded by 10+1 Photo Archives shows that the photography studio as a space has been positioned as a regional modern architectural heritage.*15

Critical reception

The evaluation of Tomishige Rihei has advanced more through the investigation and preservation of the Tomishige Photography Studio's materials than through art-historical evaluation of individual works. His significance has been recognized not as an "artist who left masterworks" but as a case showing how photography became institutionalized in regional society and took root as portraiture, documentation, and commercial practice.*5 Within Japanese photographic history, his work functions as material for reconsidering modernization from the vantage point of Kumamoto as a regional base, counterbalancing a photographic history centered on Tokyo and Yokohama. Kumamoto city's cultural property information treats the Tomishige Photography Studio as a surviving regional photography studio and as a body of materials — glass plates, equipment, and documents — constituting a record of modern visual culture.*6 At present, the available materials are concentrated in the contexts of studio history, materials surveys, and exhibition records rather than in a critical history of the artist as such, and deeper research into individual works is anticipated going forward.*16

tomishige-tokuji.html.lead_html: The second-generation head of the Tomishige Photography Studio, Tokuji continued the institutional practice and documentary record-keeping established by Rihei. He is significant less as an individual artistic innovator than as a figure who sustained photography's role in regional Meiji and Taisho Japan.
tomishige-tokuji.html.thesis_html: As the second-generation head of the Tomishige Photography Studio, Tomishige Tokuji sustained the institutional framework and documentary culture that Rihei had built, across the Meiji, Taisho, and early Showa periods. He is positioned in photographic history less as an individual innovator than as the embodiment of studio succession in provincial modernity. The long-term maintenance of Kumamoto's portrait culture, regional documentation, and commercial-photography network through the Rihei-to-Tokuji succession shows that a local studio could take root as an institution rather than depending on a single generation's talent. That the documentary photographs attributed to Tokuji continue to be consulted by researchers shows how the practice of succession itself has generated materials for photographic history.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Tomishige Tokuji was born in 1862, trained in photography under Tomishige Rihei, and succeeded him as the second-generation head of the Tomishige Photography Studio.*1 The "Tomishige Tokuji Curriculum Vitae" referenced in the Japan Society for the Science of Design survey paper records an outline of his career and shows that he inherited photographic techniques as a direct pupil of Rihei.*2 He assumed responsibilities for the studio's work while Rihei was still alive and continued to maintain its name and base after Rihei's death. He kept the studio operating through the Meiji, Taisho, and early Showa periods, occupying a distinctive position in regional photographic history as a "successor." He died in 1938.*3

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Succession and the continuity of the institution

When discussing Tomishige Tokuji as a practitioner, the most defensible positioning based on currently available materials is as the figure who sustained regional modern visual practice as inheritor of the Tomishige Photography Studio, rather than constructing a thick individual artist account. The survey report of the Nara National Research Institute for Cultural Properties and the records in the National Cultural Properties Registry treat the Tomishige Photography Studio not as the talent of a single generation but as a continuing regional photography studio, and within that framework Tokuji, as the second-generation head, was responsible for the continued accumulation of the studio's materials.*4 As the Kumamoto city cultural property information shows, the Tomishige Photography Studio building itself is protected as a Registered Tangible Cultural Property, carrying significance as regional heritage beyond the individual achievements of any single photographer.*5 The J-STAGE study discusses photography as a record of modernization centering on the studio's materials, and the studio's continued activity including the period of Tokuji's tenure is positioned within that framework.*6

Regional role of the photography studio in regional modernity

The exhibition phrase "the modern age of portraiture" serves as a term indicating that the Tomishige Photography Studio was a site that produced the modern self-image of local residents.*7 The long-term maintenance of Kumamoto's portrait culture, regional documentation, and commercial photography network through the succession from Rihei to Tokuji shows that the photography studio functioned as the foundation for the community's self-representation rather than simply as a commercial establishment. The Kumamoto University exhibition "The Tomishige Photography Studio and the Modernization of Kumamoto" positions the studio's activities spanning both Rihei and Tokuji as a history of Kumamoto's modernization, showing the importance of the succession perspective.*8 The Bunshun Online discussion of photographs attributed to Tokuji showing the Nihongi pleasure district is a rare reference point that presents concrete evidence of his documentary work from later in his career.*9 The Kokugakuin University symposium materials reference the Tomishige Photography Studio's records from the perspective of research into old photographs, indicating connections to architectural and urban history.*10 The old studio building recorded by 10+1 Photo Archives conveys the architectural succession of the photography studio as a space.*11

Critical reception

On Tomishige Tokuji, given that individual critical histories and first-person statements are thin in currently available materials, a more honest evaluation comes from not constructing an inflated account. What matters is that his name survives within the preservation and survey of the Tomishige Photography Studio's materials as the second-generation head, and this in itself demonstrates that the photography studio continued not as a single generation's talent but as a trade, a set of techniques, a client network, and a body of accumulated materials.*12 Within photographic history, Tokuji is a figure who speaks to the continuity of photographic institutions in regional modernity rather than as "an individual innovator." The long-term maintenance of Kumamoto's portrait culture, regional documentation, and commercial photography network through the succession from Rihei to Tokuji provides an important case study for thinking about the regional photographic history of modern Japan.*13

torbjrn-rdland.html.lead_html: Torbjørn Rødland photographs bodies, lotion, fruit, hair, shoes, sculptures, and landscapes with the polished light of advertising and fashion photography, tactile surfaces, and gestures that resist explanation. Although carefully staged, the works preserve physical contingency from analog photography and resistance from their subjects, allowing beauty and discomfort, truth and fiction, devotion and vulgarity to operate at once. Through Fifth Honeymoon and The Touch That Made You, he turns photography from a sign that can be decoded quickly into an image whose meanings become less stable the longer it is viewed.
torbjrn-rdland.html.thesis_html: After Cindy Sherman and Jeff Wall, staged photography became an established critical form for showing how photographs are constructed through cultural codes and production. Rødland questioned a situation in which viewing could end once that construction had been recognized, leaving the viewer safely distanced from desire or disgust. He brought the lighting of advertising and fashion photography, gestures from religious painting, Romantic landscape, and kitsch symbolism into contact with actual skin, liquids, fruit, aging, and the responses of models, producing interpretation and bodily reaction at the same time. Instead of weakening commercial seduction by presenting it as a quotation, he made the viewer’s attraction part of the critique. He reintroduced weight, sensation, and a near-devotional allure into late-twentieth-century staged photography and defined a line of work in which critique and seduction remain active together.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
From Postmodern Quotation to “Re-Enchantment”

Torbjørn Rødland was born in Stavanger in southwestern Norway and began working in the early 1990s. At the time, postmodern staged photography exerted a major influence on art photography by quoting existing images from advertising, cinema, magazines, and pornography to expose their artificiality and power. Rødland focused on what remained after a viewer had identified the source or construction. Even after a landscape is recognized as Romantic or a photograph as advertising, the sheen of skin, sublimity of landscape, and gaze of a figure can still prompt bodily response. To make that response central, he maintained the technical polish of commercial imagery and introduced unease from within its seduction. Serpentine Galleries describes his work as a practice that introduces unpredictable outcomes into carefully staged analog photographs and invites sustained viewing*1.

In the early series In a Norwegian Landscape, Rødland photographed Nordic mountains, forests, and solitary figures that recall Caspar David Friedrich. Working after postmodern critique, he examined moments when a kitsch version of natural sublimity still retains emotional or near-religious force. The quotations from Romantic landscape contain both a critical dismantling of the style and a state in which viewers remain attracted to the image while understanding its conventions. A retrospective essay in The New Yorker connects this early work to a post-postmodern desire for “re-enchantment”*2. Astrup Fearnley Museum identifies the work as an early series begun in 1993 and places it as a search for photographs that would not be exhausted by irony, despite his awareness of the Pictures Generation*13.

From Norway to Los Angeles — Working inside Commercial Image Culture

Rødland later made Los Angeles one of his bases, working in an environment close to the visual languages of fashion, advertising, celebrity, and cinema. David Kordansky Gallery presents his work across photography, video, and publishing as a sustained pressure placed on ordinary objects and bodies through symbolic and psychological associations*3. The light of Los Angeles and the techniques of commercial photography form a production environment that actively shapes the desires of both subject and viewer.

His photographs make deliberate use of advertising’s smooth surfaces. Skin, fruit, plastic, liquid, and fabric appear with seductive detail. Strange contacts, excessive viscosity, awkward expressions, and combinations without a clear purpose interrupt the usual movement toward communicating a product’s use or a model’s appeal. Fondation Louis Vuitton holds Rødland’s work as photography in which everyday motifs shift into unsettling psychological and symbolic relations*4. Commercial seduction draws the viewer close before an uncanny contact suspends the expected movement toward purchase or identification.

sections.title: The Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Holding Staged Photography and Photographic Truth Together

Rødland treats staging as the condition under which contact with reality begins. Staged photography in the 1980s foregrounded sets, costume, and performance in order to challenge the assumption that a photograph offers a natural window onto reality. Rødland inherits this achievement while returning attention to the fact that light touches skin and objects, models react, and liquids and materials change during the shoot. His statement at Bonniers Konsthall—“Even if photography often begins as observation, my dream is a more deepened engagement”—signals an attempt to add physical contact among photographer, subject, and image to the analysis of signs*5.

He chose this method to retain the weight, moisture, age, and resistance of bodies and objects beyond cultural decoding. Costumes, lighting, and composition may be prepared, but actual bodies, liquids, and film change unpredictably. Instead of fully controlling the scene, Rødland brings a concept into contact with physical material and photographs the resulting friction. An interview in Even Magazine presents his position as one that holds constructed scenes together with photography’s indexical relation to the world and gives priority to physical proximity before it is verbalized*6.

The “Wet Process” of Analog Photography and the Tactility of the Surface

Rødland has continued to work primarily with color negative film and darkroom or lab processes after digital imagery became commonplace. In an Artnet interview, he speaks of his attraction to the “wetness of the process” in analog photography and emphasizes the chemical and bodily nature of production*7. Analog photography here is a physical production through film, chemistry, and print. Film color, grain, exposure, and the surface of the print return the photograph from transparent information to a material event.

Scenes in which lotion covers skin, hair touches food, fruit juice adheres to fingers, or ceramic approaches flesh turn looking into an imagined sense of touch. Their discomfort comes from both an uncanny scenario and the sense that the surfaces are too close. Moderna Museet connects Rødland’s motifs to Romantic painting as well as kitsch and popular photography*8. Technical finish brings matter excessively near and intensifies the viewer’s bodily response.

Bringing Desire, Disgust, and Devotion into the Same Contact

Rødland’s photographs include young models, naked bodies, food, devotional gestures, older people, children, animals, and ornaments.His focus falls less on unusual combinations of objects than on the moment when a familiar gesture is tipped toward another meaning by a single thing.In Folded Hands (2012), a muscular man bows his head in a posture associated with prayer, while underwear is wrapped around his wrists. Devotion, restraint, and a sexualized gaze overlap in the position of the hands, allowing several allegories to compete*9.

In The Measure (2010–13), a blond boy sits quietly inside a dog cage. His compliant posture, the cage’s purpose, and lighting polished like an advertisement invite protection and confinement, innocence and a fetishizing gaze at once*9. In another photograph, a child brings a mouth toward an apple embedded with coins and dripping with honey. Biblical temptation, commodity decoration, sweetness, and wounded flesh collect at a single point of contact*2. Rødland retains advertising polish so that the viewer genuinely feels attraction and then recognizes that attraction and anxiety arise from the same act of looking.

His “deepened engagement” concerns the persistence of the viewer’s response more than an approach toward the artist’s intended answer. After the construction of the photograph has been understood, the sheen of skin, wetness of food, age of a figure, and shape of a hand remain, and the balance among desire, disgust, tenderness, and control changes with the viewer’s experience. Staging is selected as a condition for bringing real bodies and objects into contact with several conflicting cultural memories, not for fixing a single meaning.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Fifth Honeymoon — Colliding Meanings across a Series

Fifth Honeymoon is a major project that combines portraits, body fragments, fruit, landscapes, still lifes, and uncanny contacts across a photobook and exhibitions. Images placed beside one another form a chain in which meanings contaminate each other instead of a continuous narrative. The romantic title suggests intimacy or a new beginning, while the “fifth” repetition introduces unease into a model of happiness performed again and again. In an interview with Living Content, Rødland discusses the editing of the photobook, repeated motifs, and a structure that keeps meaning moving in several directions*10. Bergen Kunsthall’s publication notice records that the project was produced collaboratively by institutions in Bergen, Stockholm, and Helsinki and included thirty new photographs and his first video work in eleven years*18.

The series changes classifications such as “strange advertisement” or “uncomfortable portrait” through the pressure of adjacent images. The tenderness of one photograph changes the violence of the next; moisture from food transfers to a picture of skin; the sublimity of landscape drops into an inexpensive interior object. The book joins works through visual and emotional rhyme. Kiasma presented Fifth Honeymoon as an exhibition centered on photography while organized around the video Between Fork and Ladder*19. For Rødland, editing is central to maintaining several possibilities of meaning.

The Touch That Made You — Making Touch the Structure of an Exhibition

The Touch That Made You was held at Serpentine Galleries in 2017 and brought together works from the 1990s onward without arranging them as a chronological survey. The exhibition catalog was published by Serpentine Galleries and Koenig Books.Serpentine described it as an exhibition of carefully constructed everyday scenes that preserved chance and multiple readings, keeping viewers within the act of looking*1. The “touch” of the title extends from contact pictured in the photographs to the touch of light on a subject and the effect of an image on the viewer’s memory and desire.

The catalog gathers major works into one volume and creates new sequences among bodies, objects, and landscapes*11. In the exhibition, print size and spacing regulate tactile intensity. At close range, details become excessive; from a distance, compositions resembling religious painting or advertising emerge. Rødland’s photographs activate the eye that interprets meaning and the body that reacts to surfaces at the same time.

132 BPM — Extending Photographic Composition into Moving Duration

132 BPM (2005) transfers Rødland’s sense of photographic composition into video. For a 2006 solo exhibition, MoMA PS1 described the work as a moving image that links forests, waterfalls, and coastal vegetation in western Croatia to a steady tempo of 132 beats per minute*12. BPM measures the speed of dance music, but the video restrains rapid editing and sustains a fixed pulse across details of the natural world.Plants, light, and moving water are perceived as musical time.

During filming, Rødland manipulated branches and leaves and sometimes illuminated them with a flashlight, introducing small staged actions into the landscape*12.Like the still photographs, the work prepares a composition while admitting unpredictable movements of wind, water, and plants.Bringing the fixed pulse associated with advertising or music video into contact with Romantic images of nature sets artificial speed against physical duration within a single work.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
A View of Photography beyond “Strange” and “Surreal”

Because of its abnormal props and awkward bodies, Rødland’s work is often summarized as “strange,” “surreal,” or a form of “uncomfortable beauty.” Those labels obscure why the photographs retain a polish borrowed from advertising, fashion, and devotional painting. He treats the surface itself as the site where desire, faith, and memory take shape.An Aperture essay describes his concrete method of leaving contingency within meticulously staged situations and making images that resist classification even outside their original series*14.

Symbols call several cultural memories into play. Fruit can suggest sexuality, decay, abundance, a commodity, and an offering in religious painting at the same time. A model’s hand can hold tenderness and control together. An interview in Autre addresses the way his works produce bodily proximity and psychological distance simultaneously*15. The photograph continues to change according to the viewer’s own history of desire and disgust after any authorial message has been understood.

After Cindy Sherman and Jeff Wall — Returning Matter and Sensation to the Constructed Image

Cindy Sherman performed the types produced by cinema and magazines, while Jeff Wall reconstructed events at the scale of painting and film. By the 1990s, the construction of photography through staging and the codes of advertising or cinema had become shared knowledge within contemporary art. Rødland accepts this premise and shifts attention toward the physical event in which light and matter still meet inside a constructed image. An interview in Sleek presents his view of staged photography, photographic truth, observation, and analog production as parts of one problem*16.

His distinction lies in preserving a double response: viewers recognize a landscape as Romantic and still feel moved by it; they recognize advertising light and remain attracted to skin or fruit. This goes beyond returning Romantic allure or sensuality as a post-critical sentiment. During analog production, models, liquid, film, and light deviate slightly from the artist’s plan, and those deviations create friction with cultural codes. Staged photography thereby becomes a site where signs, matter, and the viewer’s reactions alter one another, beyond a picture whose work ends when the source of a quotation is identified.

Place in Photographic History — Turning Commercial Seduction into the Viewer’s Own Critique

It is more accurate to say that Rødland reintroduced another criterion into the critique of construction established at the end of the twentieth century than to claim that he moved staged photography forward along a single line. He preserved advertising appeal and made attraction, disgust, and devotional feeling operate within the work. His statement at Bonniers Konsthall about moving from observation toward “a more deepened engagement” signals a shift from viewing that explains an image toward viewing that accepts responsibility for one’s own reaction*5.

The contact of analog light and matter, the model’s response, the print surface, adjacency within a photobook, and distance in an exhibition were joined as a single method. The Touch That Made You, presented at Serpentine Galleries and Fondazione Prada, brought photographs and videos from the 1990s onward together outside a fixed chronology, allowing images from different periods to alter one another’s intensity of seduction and unease*17. Rødland’s place in photographic history lies in challenging the assumption that staged photography requires coolness or an explicit quotation in order to be critical. He established a form capable of examining the viewer’s desire while retaining commercial seduction, Romanticism, and near-religious feeling.

tracey-moffatt.html.lead_html: In Something More, Scarred for Life, and Up in the Sky, Tracey Moffatt brought B movies, melodrama, magazine photo stories, and colonial imagery into staged photography. The series omit beginnings and endings; captions and scenes do not resolve into a single fact. Across photography and film, she showed how histories of race, gender, and violence are remembered through existing images as well as through lived reality.
tracey-moffatt.html.thesis_html: Photojournalism conveys the facts of discrimination and violence, while autobiographical photography can present lived experience directly. Yet viewers interpret those images through narrative roles learned from cinema, magazines, and colonial imagery. Moffatt used actors, costumes, cinematic lighting, and magazine-style captions, leaving gaps between scenes in a sequence. She made the viewer’s act of supplying familiar narratives of escape, rescue, crime, and tragedy part of the work, extending staged photography from constructed self-images to a critique of the mass culture that forms colonial memory.

sections.title: Historical Background
sections.body_html:
Australia in the 1980s—Who Could Represent Race and Gender, and How?

Moffatt grew up in Brisbane and studied film at the Queensland College of Art. She has worked concurrently in photography, short film, feature film, and video montage. Night Cries: A Rural Tragedy, made in 1989, screened in the official selection at the Cannes Film Festival.*15From the late 1980s through the 1990s, feminism, postcolonial criticism, and debates over Indigenous imagery raised urgent questions about who photographed whom and which institutions circulated those images. The NGA notes that photography and performance became important means of examining gender in Australian art of the period.*14The 1986 NADOC exhibition was among the first contemporary photography exhibitions devoted entirely to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander photographers, and Moffatt played a leading role in its organization.*19As the 1988 Bicentenary, debates over the definition of urban Aboriginal identity, and protests over deaths in custody converged, photography was shifting from an ethnographic instrument that classified Indigenous people to a medium through which Indigenous artists staged and circulated their own images.

Why Staged Photography?—Reality Itself Is Understood Through Existing Images

Photojournalism conveys facts about discrimination, violence, and policy; autobiographical photography presents the maker’s experience directly. Viewers, however, understand those facts through roles and storylines learned from film, magazines, family photographs, and colonial imagery. Showing the photographed event alone leaves the image types that precondition its reception outside the frame. In a BOMB conversation with Coco Fusco, Moffatt describes building meaning from cinematic scenes and multiple references without presenting autobiographical facts as direct confession.*12An NGA essay calls her staged images “believable fictions” and explains how glamour and clothing intervened in the politics of racial imagery.*19The use of actors, costumes, cinematic lighting, and magazine-style captions recreates the familiar templates through which viewers interpret reality.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
Something More—Creating Cinematic Gaps Across Nine Photographs

Something More, made in 1989, comprises six color and three black-and-white photographs.*3A single emblematic photograph can fix the protagonist within familiar roles: Indigenous woman, provincial outsider, victim, or rebel. Moffatt separated nine scenes that suggest aspiration, sexual exploitation, violence, and death, leaving the beginning and ending open. MCA Australia explains that the nine images form an ambiguous narrative about hope being thwarted.*3Colors and poses reminiscent of B movies, road movies, and pulp fiction prompt viewers to supply narratives of escape, social ascent, crime, and tragedy. The Art Gallery of New South Wales notes that each photograph implies an unwritten story and unsettles narrative convention.*4Through the series, the stories viewers bring and the roles they assign the protagonist become part of the work.

Scarred for Life—How Magazine Photo Stories Shape Memory

Scarred for Life restages childhood incidents recounted by friends, combining images resembling Life magazine photo essays with short captions.*7Monash University explains that scenes dated from 1956 to 1977 were reconstructed through period photographic techniques and magazine-like layouts, inserting familiar faces into a monocultural media space.*7The text does not fully explain the image; it opens further questions. The Art Gallery of New South Wales likewise notes that the captions resist closure and locate enduring trauma in the distance between word and image.*8

Up in the Sky—Refusing a Direct Reenactment of the Stolen Generations

Up in the Sky, made in 1997, is a twenty-five-image series photographed in a desolate town. A mixed-race infant, nuns, families, and the suggestion of violence appear in fragments.*13The Art Gallery of New South Wales records Pasolini’s Accattone as a visual reference.*5The series places conflicting narratives of pursuit, protection, abduction, and rescue alongside the history of Indigenous children being removed from their families.QAGOMA’s collection record identifies Up in the Sky as a portfolio of twenty-five photolithographs.*6Because the work consists of twenty-five separate printed sheets, its sequence can be rearranged like fragments of a newspaper or film.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Film Stills, Hand-coloring, and Series—Separating the Work of Memory by Medium

Moffatt’s photographs have the force of individual large-scale works, but within a series, color and black-and-white, close views and distances, acting and empty landscapes alternate, asking viewers to supply missing scenes. The photographic sequence makes viewers use storylines learned from films and magazines as they imagine what came before and after the depicted events. AGSA holds multiple series—from Something More through Scarred for Life, Up in the Sky, Laudanum, and Invocations—confirming the sequence as a central form in her work.*9Her video montages work differently, extracting embraces, insults, destruction, and other motifs from many films and turning individual plots into emotional repetition. The photographic series and the edited video distinguish between memories formed through missing scenes and those formed through recurring formulas.

Laudanum and Invocations—Translating Colonial Desire into the Gothic

Laudanum stages a nineteenth-century interior, relations between mistress and servant, drugs, and sexual domination in sepia-toned photographs. Invocations uses hand-colored photographs and images reminiscent of early cinematic effects; Matthew Marks Gallery introduced the work through its mixture of allegory, dream, and fear.*18The body becomes the site where colonial power takes the form of fear and desire.

Montages—Extracting Emotional Scripts from Fragments of Existing Films

With Gary Hillberg, Moffatt made video montages including Love, Lip, and Doomed, extracting romance, dialogue spoken by Black women, and scenes of destruction from a vast range of films. The Whitney Museum presented these montages, alongside her photographs, as a central part of her critique of repeated cultural types.*10Once the individual film narratives are removed, embraces, insults, and explosions appear as an emotional grammar learned through the culture industry.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Addressing Origin, Class, and Cinematic Fantasy at Once

Moffatt has been introduced internationally as an artist of Aboriginal heritage, while remaining wary of interpretations that reduce her work to an ethnic profile. The National Portrait Gallery records her role as a cofounder of the Boomalli Aboriginal Artists Co-operative, a co-organizer of NADOC ’86, and the first Aboriginal artist to present a solo exhibition at the Venice Biennale in 2017.*16Her works bring race, class, desire, and cinematic fantasy into the same scenes without fixing their characters as autobiographical stand-ins for the artist. Roslyn Oxley9’s artist materials likewise trace her engagement with race, gender, sexuality, and identity across photography, film, and video.*17She acknowledges her background while resisting interpretations governed by a single biographical profile.

A Distinct Position Across Postmodern Photography and Film

Working alongside the staged photography of Cindy Sherman and Jeff Wall, Moffatt also challenged the premise that photographs directly record reality. Her sequences, however, tie Australia’s colonial history, Indigenous imagery, melodrama, and magazine culture closely together. In a conversation with Barbara London, she recalls Up in the Sky as a cinematic construction made from twenty-five photographs, clarifying its difference within the international field of staged photography.*13MCA Australia’s collection of her photographs and films as one body of work also supports reading the still and moving images as equally central to her art.*2

Producing Attraction and Fear Together—How the Critique Reaches Viewers

Saturated color, star-like poses, and cinematic lighting retain the appeal of the mass culture under scrutiny. In a Guardian interview, Moffatt said she becomes interested when an image grows a little frightening.*11Removing attraction and leaving only a correct message would not explain why stereotypes recur. Her photographs make viewers experience both their own attraction and the violence carried by that desire.

Making Staged Photography a Meeting Point for Colonial Memory and Mass Culture

The staged photography of Cindy Sherman and others had shown that photographic personae are constructed roles. Moffatt directed this method toward the cinematic and magazine formulas through which Australian Indigenous imagery, class, care, and colonial memory had been understood. MoMA and MCA Australia collect her photographs, films, and montages as one body of work.*1Photographic sequences ask viewers to supply missing scenes; video montages extract embraces, insults, and destruction repeated across many films. Together, these forms show colonial memory being made through mass-cultural repetition and viewers’ associations. AGSA presents Body Remembers as a ten-part series shown in Venice, indicating that the sequence remained central to Moffatt’s treatment of historical and bodily memory.*20

The Role of Fiction Against Institutional Demands for Authenticity

Indigenous artists and women artists are often expected to speak directly and authentically for a community’s experience. Moffatt uses costumes, actors, cinematic lighting, and existing genres to create scenes in which multiple eras and memories overlap. The National Film and Sound Archive recognizes her Aboriginal and Irish Australian background while presenting her as an artist who challenges representations of race, gender, and history through film, photography, and video.*15Fiction makes viewers aware that they understand lived experience through cinematic and magazine conventions. Omitted endings expose the familiar plots viewers bring to the work and challenge institutions that confine authenticity to a single mode of telling.

og.description: An examination of Valérie Belin’s photography through the precision of straight photography, bodies and artificial objects, post-photography, and the continuity between analog and digital image-making.

twitter.title: Valérie Belin | Mannequins, Bodies, and Photographic Surfaces | Photo Coordinates
twitter.description: An examination of Valérie Belin’s photography through the precision of straight photography, bodies and artificial objects, post-photography, and the continuity between analog and digital image-making.

valerie-belin.html.lead_html: Valérie Belin has photographed glass, silverware, meat, engines, bodybuilders, mannequins, models, and flowers through frontal viewpoints, even lighting, and large-format prints. In her early photographs of silver objects, precise description captured the objects’ outlines while distorted reflections of the surrounding room came to dominate the frame. When mannequins and people were photographed under the same conditions, the visual cues separating skin, makeup, and resin also became unstable. From these experiences, Belin examined how photography records an object accurately while remaking its appearance. Since the 2000s, color, layered exposures, and digital compositing have extended a process that began with lighting and arrangement at the time of exposure into postproduction.This development can be read as a continuous shift from the precise direct photography associated with straight photography to the constructed image-making of post-photography.
valerie-belin.html.thesis_html: The precision of straight photography had served the description of subjects, while typological frontality had enabled comparison among them. Belin photographed silverware, bodies, and mannequins under the same conditions, showing that descriptive precision itself can make an appearance seem artificial. She later moved into digital layering, linking direct photography and compositing as continuous stages in the production of appearance. She made the continuity between straight photography and post-photography materially visible.
