eiko-yamazawa.html.meta_description: Eiko Yamazawa was a Japanese abstract photographer known for What I Am Doing. Through Consuelo Kanaga, American modernist photography, and the photobook Far and Near, this page traces why she moved away from realism and examines her ideas, methods, and later reassessment.
eiko-yamazawa.html.lead_html: Eiko Yamazawa was a Japanese abstract photographer best known for What I Am Doing. She learned photography in Consuelo Kanaga’s studio in the 1920s and, after decades of professional studio work and the photobook Far and Near, moved toward abstract photography built from objects, color, and light arranged before the camera. Drawing on her own words and works, this page traces why she left realism behind and tried to photograph a reality she herself felt.
eiko-yamazawa.html.thesis_html: Eiko Yamazawa expanded photography beyond recording the external world by arranging objects, color, and light before the camera and rephotographing photographic materials and her own earlier works. In What I Am Doing, the materials and procedures of making photographs became subjects in themselves, making her an early practitioner of self-referential abstraction in Japanese photography.
eiko-yamazawa.html.keywords_html: Keywords What I Am Doing Constructed Photography Abstract Photography Color Photography Commercial Photography Modernist Photography

sections.title: Becoming a Photographer
sections.body_html: Yamazawa first intended to become a painter. As a child she was familiar with sun printing and box cameras, and after graduating from the Women’s School of Fine Arts she continued to study oil painting and photography while helping to make group photographs at the Osaka YWCA*1. Around the time of her graduation, she attended meetings connected with Hiratsuka Raichō’s movement and, through Haruko Asai at the Osaka YWCA, encountered activities concerned with the independence of working women*11. In 1926 she went to San Francisco to study painting. After her father died that year, a camera shop introduced her to Consuelo Kanaga*11. She learned practical camera and darkroom work in Kanaga’s studio and later worked in Nicholas Muray’s studio in New York. Through these experiences, Yamazawa chose photography as her profession*11. She returned to Japan in 1929 and opened her own studio in Osaka in 1931*1. After the war, she continued working at a PX in Kyoto and in the photography studio of Osaka Mitsukoshi, started the Yamazawa Photography Study Group in 1950, and reopened a commercial studio in 1952*1. Invited by Kanaga, she returned to the United States in 1955, spent about six months in New York, and also visited Imogen Cunningham*1. She increased her personal work while continuing commercial assignments and closed the studio in 1960*13. Her 1962 photobook Far and Near is now understood as part of her movement toward later abstract work*4.

sections.title: Abstract Photography and What I Am Doing
sections.body_html:
Eiko Yamazawa and American Modernist Photography: Form, Light, and the Studio

In the United States, Yamazawa worked in Kanaga’s studio and in Muray’s fashion-photography studio, where she encountered modernist photography of the period*11. To examine this formative environment, the 2019 retrospective placed her work alongside modernist photographs by Stieglitz, Strand, Adams, Weston, and Cunningham, as well as fashion and advertising photographs by Beaton, Rawlings, and Outerbridge*2. Kanaga, with whom Yamazawa studied directly, addressed both modernist form and social subjects and in 1932 took part in the first Group f/64 exhibition with Weston, Cunningham, Adams, and others*12. Weston and Cunningham photographed plants, bodies, and everyday objects through contour, surface, light, and form*10. In later years Yamazawa photographed vessels, fruit, stones, bricks, and photographic equipment, moving objects, adding color and reflections, and eventually using her own earlier photographs as material*3. Her later works continued to emphasize clear form and texture, with arrangement and lighting decided before exposure. The gap between her 1920s experiences and her mature work was long, however. From the 1950s onward, she moved toward abstraction through her own doubts about realism and a sustained process of experimentation*11.

Why Did Eiko Yamazawa Turn to Abstract Photography?

Her move toward abstraction unfolded gradually during the 1950s. Yamazawa began using photography as a means of abstract expression in 1952–53 and intensified her personal work after returning to the United States in 1955*11. Around that time, she wrote about asking what she truly wanted to photograph and the need to look deeply into herself*16. Looking back later, she said that she had long been concerned with more than the pursuit of facts: she wanted to think about the relationship between human beings and photography, and had wondered whether she “could make art with a camera”*16. Yamazawa had studied Japanese-style painting (nihonga), continued to study oil painting and photography after graduation, published Eiko Gashū in 1921, and later exhibited paper collages*1. Her move into photography was therefore not a simple abandonment of painting; her interest in using the medium for purposes beyond recording remained. Faced with a camera that recorded everything before it, she sought photographs in which only what was true for her would remain*16. In 1960, she described realist expression as something she had left behind and called the state in which abstract methods moved her mind a “vivid reality”*16. In 1982, she again wrote that she wanted to bring her understanding of human beings, gained through everyday life, into expression, and described her work as an experiment in photographic expression*16. In What I Am Doing, she continued that move away from realism through arrangement, reflection, color, and the rephotographing of her own images*3.

The Photobook Far and Near: From Realism to Abstraction

Far and Near contains experiments from the 1950s and 1960s that precede the later What I Am Doing. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum retrospective traced Yamazawa’s formal experiments from the 1950s and presented Far and Near as a stage leading toward the work of the 1970s and 1980s*3. In Still Life from Far and Near (1961), vessels and fruit are placed close together, making form and arrangement the center of the image*2. Art Commons at the National Art Center, Tokyo likewise described the retrospective as tracing her formal experimentation through prewar portraits, early abstractions from the 1960s, and works from the 1970s and 1980s*5.

How What I Am Doing Was Made: Arrangement, Light, Reflection, and Color

In What I Am Doing, Yamazawa determined the position, angle, and lighting of objects before making the exposure. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum notes that the series includes photographs of photographic equipment and earlier works, and that she kept experimenting by changing arrangement, angle, and light*3. The Third Gallery Aya’s English biography describes her 1980s work as close to what would now be called “constructed photography”*8. The image depended on where an object was placed, which surface faced the light, and what was layered, concealed, or made translucent. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum describes her vivid late color photographs as rare in Japan at the time*2. Transparent Blue, made in 1986, is a dye-transfer print*6. In Transparent Blue, translucent and opaque fields overlap, making color itself a structural element of the image.

The Meaning of What I Am Doing: Rephotographing Her Own Work

In What I Am Doing, photographic equipment and Yamazawa’s own earlier photographs became material for new images*3. What I Am Doing No.8 (1980; printed 1986) was included in the 2019 retrospective*2. The image shows a rolled page from one of her own 1976 photobooks; the photograph on that page had itself depicted photographic tools such as colored filters and a light box*13. Photographic equipment becomes a photograph; the photograph becomes a page in a photobook; that page is photographed again and becomes another photograph. No.8 folds the sequence of photographing, publication in a photobook, and rephotographing into the work itself.

What Remained of Commercial and Portrait Photography in Her Later Work?

Yamazawa spent many years photographing people and products. Such work required backgrounds, poses, object placement, and lighting to be set before exposure. Arrangement and lighting also determine much of What I Am Doing. Aperture’s research emphasizes the period when Yamazawa learned studio management and portraiture under Kanaga and Muray and used portrait photography as a site of experimentation*9. Yamazawa herself believed that a good portrait should capture something of the sitter’s inner life*16. Although her later subjects shifted from people to objects, she continued to move beyond simply recording what stood before the camera and to make photographs from what she herself perceived. Professional studio work and What I Am Doing both relied on arranging and lighting before exposure. In the later works, those tools no longer served to present a person or product; they were used to shape relationships among form, light, and color.

sections.title: Historical Position and Reassessment
sections.body_html:
Why Did Eiko Yamazawa Seem So Different from Mainstream Japanese Photography?

Yamazawa opened her own studio in Osaka in 1931*1. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum notes that she worked on a different plane from the mainstream of Japanese photography and that her vivid late color photographs had few parallels in Japan at the time*2. From her prewar portraits through Far and Near and What I Am Doing, she changed subjects from people to objects and photographic materials while continuing to experiment with form, arrangement, light, and color*3. At the center of this work was the question of how a photograph could organize form, color, and light.

Why Was Eiko Yamazawa Reassessed? Exhibitions and International Reception

Yamazawa’s work had been shown internationally since the late 1980s. It appeared in Japanese Women Photographers at Lehigh University Art Gallery in 1987 and An Incomplete History: Women Photographers from Japan 1864–1997 at Visual Studies Workshop in 1998*1. She also appeared in the 1987 documentary High Heels and Ground Glass*1. The 2019 retrospective brought together her prewar portraits, early abstractions from the 1960s, and What I Am Doing in a single exhibition*2. It also placed her work alongside the American modernist, fashion, and advertising photography she had encountered, avoiding an account of her development confined to Japanese photographic history*2. In 2021, portrait photographs from the 1940s were presented within an international history of women photographers in The New Woman Behind the Camera*7. That same year, Peter Schjeldahl in The New Yorker described the portraits made with Yasue Yamamoto in terms of a collaboration between performance and photography*14. Far and Near was also included in What They Saw, a history of photobooks by women, and a spread from the book was reproduced in a FOMU review*15. In 2024, Aperture examined Yamazawa’s studio experience under Kanaga and Muray in detail*9. In 2025, the Shiga Museum of Art exhibition BUTSUDORI: The Photographic Expression of “Objects” placed Objects in a section devoted to form, presenting Yamazawa alongside Minoru Sakata, Kōshirō Onchi, Takeji Iwamiya, and others as an early figure in abstract expression in Japanese photography*17. The same year, To Sway and Surround: Japanese Female Abstraction in Taipei placed her work alongside Atsuko Tanaka, Kazuyo Kinoshita, and others in a history of abstraction by women in Japan*18. Recent exhibitions have thus approached her work through several histories at once: her position as an early professional woman photographer, portraiture, the photobook, photographs of objects, abstract photography, and Japanese abstraction.

What Did Eiko Yamazawa Change in Photography?

Yamazawa’s significance in photographic history lies in her early experiments with abstract photography in Japan and in bringing the materials and procedures of making photographs into the work itself. In What I Am Doing, objects, color, light, photographic equipment, and her own earlier photographs all became material. The work includes arrangement and lighting before exposure as well as the rephotographing of finished images. It is now being reconsidered as an early example of self-referential photography in which the image is constructed before exposure and past work becomes material for new photographs*11. Yamazawa wrote that abstract methods moved her mind and gave her a sense of “vivid reality”*16.

mari-katayama.html.title: Mari Katayama | Self-Portraiture, Prosthetic Legs, and GIFT | Photo Coordinates
mari-katayama.html.meta_description: An introduction to Mari Katayama’s self-portraits through prosthetic legs, gender, disability, pictorial composition, mirror images, and the photobooks GIFT and Synthesis, with comparisons to Cindy Sherman and Yasumasa Morimura, the High Heel Project, and her place in photographic history.
mari-katayama.html.lead_html: Mari Katayama creates prosthetic legs and hand-sewn doubles, then carefully stages them with her own body for the camera. This essay traces how she brings prostheses, clothing, dolls, and mirror images together within a pictorially constructed frame. Her compositions present a body that ready-made clothes and shoes do not accommodate as a body shaped by femininity, disability, everyday life, and relations with others.
mari-katayama.html.thesis_html: Katayama brought prosthetic legs, medical supports, clothing tailored to her body, and hand-sewn doubles into staged self-portraiture. She presents the body of a disabled woman through dress, desire, daily life, and relationships with others, rather than confining it to medical or triumph-over-adversity narratives. By making the clothes and shoes that fit her body—and even the rooms in which she photographs—she developed a form of self-portraiture that does not leave the appearance of her body to other people or to standardized products.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
Sewing and the Beginnings of Self-Portraiture

Mari Katayama’s work began with sewing before it began with photography. Born in Saitama Prefecture in 1987 and raised in Gunma Prefecture, she wore leg braces and specialized shoes as a child, which made ready-made clothing difficult to wear without alteration. Her mother and grandmother sewed clothes to fit her body, and Katayama recalls handling needle and thread before she learned to use a pencil*1. The habit of making what her body needed when no suitable product existed became the basis for carrying sewing from everyday necessity into artmaking.

Katayama underwent a double leg amputation at age nine because of congenital tibial hemimelia and has since lived with prosthetic legs. In high school, she made hand-sewn legs imagined from the limbs she had lost, decorated her prostheses, photographed herself wearing them, and shared the images online. Looking back, she has said that from the beginning she treated her own body, like fabric and prosthetic limbs, as one of the materials with which she made her work*2.

After graduating from Gunma Prefectural Women’s University in 2010 and completing the Intermedia Art program at the Graduate School of Fine Arts, Tokyo University of the Arts, in 2012, Katayama developed a body of work spanning photography, sculpture, sewing, and performance. Her participation in Aichi Triennale 2013, Roppongi Crossing 2016, and the 58th Venice Biennale in 2019 marked the movement of a method that began as personal self-imaging into both contemporary art and photography*3*4.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Why Katayama Makes and Photographs the Work Herself

As a teenager, Katayama modeled for other photographers alongside objects she had made. Although she supplied both her body and the objects, the finished photograph became the photographer’s work. She has described the discomfort this caused and how it led her to decorate the room herself, repeatedly check the viewfinder, and take the photograph on her own*5. In an interview with the V&A, she likewise explained that taking responsibility for both sides of the relationship—the person photographing and the person photographed—was one reason she began making self-portraits*6.

Her process begins with sketches. She sews fabric legs and dolls, prepares clothing, furniture, mirrors, and lighting, and finally places her body within the arrangement to test the composition. Katayama has said that a single setup can take about a week and that she moves repeatedly between the camera and her position in the frame to adjust the image*7. Photography is therefore not a record of sculpture already completed. It is the final stage in bringing sewing, sculpture, the room, and the pose into a single image.

Katayama has said that paintings she saw with her grandfather as a child strongly shaped her present method of holding composition, narrative, and thought within one image without explaining them in words*6. Her photographs can suggest a story before and after the depicted moment, as a film still might, while also presenting body, object, color, and reflection simultaneously within a pictorially organized frame.

Pictorial Composition: Femininity, Prostheses, and Mirror Images

In Cindy Sherman’s Untitled Film Stills, costume, makeup, gesture, and location produce women who seem to belong to imagined films*8. Yasumasa Morimura enters the poses and compositions of canonical paintings and film stars, reperforming familiar figures through a different body*9. Jeff Wall uses actors, lighting, and sets to construct events before the camera that appear to have occurred in the world*10. Katayama also constructs the image in advance. Her central concern, however, is how the living body, prosthetic legs, clothing, dolls, and mirror images relate to one another and come to be seen as a body.

For Katayama, clothes and shoes were first an everyday question of whether anything commercially available would fit her body, before they became costumes selected to perform a feminine image. Because ready-made clothing and footwear did not imagine her body as their wearer, producing a feminine appearance required making clothing, prostheses, and shoes to fit that body*11*1. Her compositions do more than quote existing images of femininity; they bring into the frame the garments and devices that make those images possible.

In you’re mine, a life-size doll cast from Katayama’s body, a self-portrait of her reclining on a bed, and her present reflection in a full-length mirror occupied the same installation. In the photograph, she wears heavy makeup and lingerie and adopts a pose reminiscent of Titian’s Venus, while what appears to be a stocking is a medical compression bandage. Ana Moyer argues that the conjunction of an art-historical female figure, adornment, and medical equipment makes visible both a norm of femininity and a disabled body often placed outside that norm*11. Katayama does not position disability as the opposite of femininity. Dress, treatment, and desire occupy the same body and the same image.

In mirror, a tabletop mirror occupies the center of the composition. Inside it appears an upper-body portrait in which the prosthetic legs are largely absent; outside it, the prostheses and the objects in the room remain visible. Lou-Naëma Fischer-Barnicol reads the mirror as a device that repeats the photographic frame within the image, showing how different portraits of the same body can be produced through different acts of cropping*12. Seen only within the mirror, Katayama approaches the conventions of an ordinary female portrait. Seen with the surrounding room, the body includes prosthetic limbs and its lived environment. The composition reveals how the appearance of a “normal” female body depends on what the image includes and excludes.

bystander #016 overlays the reclining figure of a seaside Venus, Naoshima onna bunraku—a form of puppetry in which a legless figure expresses emotion through the hands—and tentacle-like arms printed with photographs of other people’s hands. Kubiński argues that the overlap of figure, puppet, manipulating hands, and tentacles destabilizes distinctions between viewer and viewed, and between a human body and a fabricated one*13. The idealized female figure, prosthetic limbs, and many-armed double coexist within one composition, allowing different bodily images and materials to operate at once.

tree of life: Mirrors and Reflections

For the recent series tree of life, Katayama built a purpose-made set of mirrored tiles in her studio, where reflections blur the boundaries between floor, walls, and ceiling. She placed her largest hand-sewn sculpture to date, costumes and wall elements reworked from earlier projects, and her own body within the set, then made the image in a single exposure on film*6. The mirrors do not simply multiply the body as decoration. They create a space in which distinctions between self and other, object and reflection, floor and ceiling become unstable.

The Brooklyn Rail describes the works gathered in Synthesis as maximalist compositions in which color, pattern, reflection, shine, bodies, and objects fill the frame*14. American Suburb X likewise notes the growing density of Katayama’s recent images, arguing that they ask viewers to move beyond concentrating on the prosthetic legs alone and to see body, object, studio, and performance as a whole*15.

Sixtysix Magazine describes Katayama’s home and studio in Gunma as a lived yet deliberately arranged space in which household goods, records, fabric, shells, beads, and hand-sewn doubles occupy the same rooms*5. In a 2026 interview with Vogue Japan, Katayama explained that her roles as artist, mother, and wife, together with collaborations with the prosthetics manufacturer Nabtesco and the shoe brand Sergio Rossi, had led her to consider the body through its relations with technology and other people*16. Vogue Japan reads the mirrored space and long exposure of tree of life as part of a shift from the direct encounter with bodily replicas in her early work toward recent attempts to explore distance from and coexistence with objects*16.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
The High Heel Project: Femininity and Choice

The 2011 works Children’s Feet and I’m wearing little high heels, I have child’s feet connect Katayama’s early self-portraits with the High Heel Project. She has explained that I’m wearing little high heels imagines a child longing to become an adult, while Children’s Feet imagines a child backstage at a circus*17. The prostheses and shoes function as devices that support walking and as objects associated with maturity and dress*18.

The immediate catalyst for the project was an incident while Katayama was working at a nightclub, when someone told her that a woman who did not wear high heels was not a woman. Angered by the remark, she consulted a prosthetist and began developing high heels that could be worn with prosthetic legs*17. The experience exposed the kinds of bodies assumed by commercially available footwear and prostheses. Katayama produced high heels in which she could actually walk, addressing dress and mobility through the same act of making.

Katayama has said that she wants high heels to become one ordinary option among many, rather than a sign reserved for a limited range of bodies*19. The project therefore extends beyond decorating a prosthetic limb. It links prostheses, shoes, clothing, walking, the stage, and song, creating within daily life an option that standardized products had not provided.

Access to fashion does not resolve every problem. Laini Burton and Jana Melkumova-Reynolds argue that expressive prostheses can move disabled bodies out of a medical frame while also incorporating them into consumer culture. They distinguish Katayama’s sewn limbs and dolls, which reproduce her own body without correcting it toward symmetry or wholeness, from the normative bodies assumed by fashion models and mannequins*26. The High Heel Project thus holds together two possibilities: access to forms of dress from which disabled bodies have been excluded, and the risk that disability will be repackaged as a new marketable image.

Major Works: you’re mine, bystander, and On the Way Home

The 2014 series you’re mine marked a turning point from early works in which Katayama placed herself in the image to display hand-sewn objects toward a concern with the body as it is seen within society. Through photographs, dolls, and mirrors, she asked “which one is me?” and reconsidered whether the object or the artist should occupy the principal role*20.

For the 2016 series bystander, Katayama drew on the hands of the kuroko puppeteers who support figures in Naoshima onna bunraku. She photographed other people’s hands, printed them onto fabric, and sewed them into many-armed objects*21. This was the first series in which other people’s bodies entered her work. Katayama has said that the process made her experience both the difficulty and the force of “living together”*21.

On the Way Home was photographed in 2016 while Katayama was pregnant, in a river near where she grew up. She has said that thinking about her daughter’s life expanded her sense of time beyond the roughly one hundred years of an individual life toward past and future, making history feel like a personal matter*21. For an exhibition the following year, she also described how reduced mobility and changes in body shape during pregnancy and childbirth heightened her awareness of her body and became material for self-portraiture*17.

GIFT and Synthesis: Editing and Recent Work

Published in 2019, GIFT was Katayama’s first photobook and brought together several series made between 2007 and 2018. Her hand is embossed on the clothbound cover. An eye chart and fragments of the body appear near the beginning, followed by prosthetic limbs, hand-sewn objects, and self-portraits*22. Conscientious Photography Magazine argues that this sequence causes the visually commanding portraits to be reread through the making of the objects and the bodily experience introduced earlier in the book*23.

At the 58th Venice Biennale that same year, Katayama presented work combining photographs and hand-sewn sculptures*4. Both GIFT and the Venice installation were cited when she received the 45th Kimura Ihei Photography Award*24. The inclusion of both the photobook and exhibition indicates that her work was assessed through page sequence and spatial installation as well as through individual photographs.

Published in 2025, Synthesis gathers nine series made from 2019 to 2025, linking Katayama’s body after becoming a mother, her return to life in Gunma, the studio, caryatid, and tree of life*14. Her early interiors centered on the relationship between the artist and her doubles. The recent work brings the home, land, surrounding environment, and earlier works into the frame. American Suburb X describes this development as a totality of making and performance that cannot be reduced to prosthetic limbs alone*15.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Gender and Disability Through Composition

Katayama’s work is often introduced through her prosthetic legs and congenital physical condition. In an interview with LensCulture, she resisted limiting the work to disability rights or body positivity, describing it as an inquiry into conditions shared by human beings*7. Katayama does not deny disability as a subject; she rejects readings that compress the work into an uplifting story of courage, a “new” beauty, or body positivity. Her concerns appear through concrete questions: whether the clothes she wants to wear fit her body, whether she can choose the shoes she wants, whether prosthetic legs can be dressed, and how the body can move within a room or on a stage. Sewing and composition arise from the same experience—making clothes for a body that standardized products do not accommodate, then making the space in which that body will be photographed.

High heels, medical compression bandages, decorated prostheses, and hand-sewn doubles do more than signify disability. They support the body, dress it, enable movement, and connect with femininity and desire in the photographs. Katayama has said that she does not regard a prosthetic limb as external to the body simply because it is artificial, and that neither an operated body nor a landscape altered by human hands can be cleanly divided into natural and artificial categories*25. The visual continuity between the living body and fabricated objects gives form to this understanding.

A 2026 ArtReview essay warns that when prosthesis is used as a metaphor for technological fusion, loss, or trauma, the everyday realities of disabled life can disappear. It argues that Katayama keeps prostheses specific: supports for the body, surfaces she decorates, and objects worn in daily life*27. Her photographs leave seams and joins visible. Prostheses remain things that are worn, maintained, and used, rather than generic signs of “human and machine.”

Katayama treats being a woman as one element available to her work and has said that communicating “female strength” is not its sole purpose*25. Ana Moyer reads the placement of makeup, lingerie, high heels, and medical compression bandages within the same image as a composition that addresses conventions of femininity together with the disabled body*11. Gender and disability do not appear as separate subjects in Katayama’s compositions. They emerge within the same encounters among body, clothing, medical devices, desire, and the gaze.

Mari Katayama in the History of Staged Photography

Simon Baker has situated Katayama’s work in relation to Cindy Sherman, Jeff Wall, and Matthew Barney*2. She draws on established methods: performing with her own body, constructing scenes before the camera, and moving among photography, sculpture, and performance. Her work can also be compared with Yasumasa Morimura’s use of the body to construct images that refer to existing paintings and films*9.

Katayama’s place in photographic history does not rest on inventing staged photography or pictorial composition. It rests on what she brings into those forms. Where earlier staged photographs constructed roles or events, Katayama places clothing made to fit her body, prosthetic legs, medical equipment, hand-sewn doubles, and mirror images within the same frame. These objects do not serve as background information about the figure. They support and dress the body in daily life and sometimes appear as bodies in their own right. Katayama has made self-portraiture a means of showing how a disabled woman’s body appears within particular clothes, devices, spaces, and ways of looking.

Katayama’s work is held by the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum, Mori Art Museum, and Tate, among other institutions, and she participated in the 58th Venice Biennale in 2019*3*4. The selection of both GIFT and her Venice presentation for the 45th Kimura Ihei Photography Award also indicates recognition of her complete method: making objects, arranging them, and presenting them across pages and exhibition space, as well as producing the final photograph*24.

aya-fujioka.html.title: Aya Fujioka | Here Goes River, Snapshot Photography, and Hiroshima Today | Photo Coordinates
aya-fujioka.html.meta_description: Aya Fujioka’s Here Goes River, I Don’t Sleep, and Life Studies are examined through travel, family, New York, Hiroshima, snapshot photography, and photobook sequencing.
aya-fujioka.html.lead_html: Aya Fujioka photographs gestures and disquieting details of everyday life on her travels, in her hometown of Kure, in New York, and in Hiroshima. Through delayed selection and photobook sequencing, she turns meanings she could not grasp at the moment of exposure into finished works. Through I Don’t Sleep, Here Goes River, and Life Studies, this page considers what photographs preserve beyond the photographer’s intention, and how personal experience intersects with the memories of families and cities.
aya-fujioka.html.thesis_html: Fujioka does not separate private photographs of family from the chance encounters of street photography. In Here Goes River, she did not begin with Hiroshima’s established symbols. She recognized recurring bicycles, floodwaters, children, and the Atomic Bomb Dome among thousands of instinctive photographs made while walking through the city. By keeping her own life in Hiroshima—near her hometown—within the work, and by resisting an overly explanatory sequence, she made the city’s history visible together with the photographer’s own position within it.

sections.title: Travel, Kure, New York, and Hiroshima
sections.body_html: Aya Fujioka was born in Kure, Hiroshima Prefecture, and graduated from the Department of Photography at Nihon University College of Art in 1994*1. She has recalled that she did not enroll with a clearly defined ambition to become a photographer; she began taking pictures because she found herself in a photography program*2. Her life in Taiwan and travels through Europe and Brazil began before she had a plan for making a body of work. Photographs accumulated during those journeys were later selected in Japan and published in 2004 as Comment te dire adieu*7. In 2005, she joined a roughly 300-kilometer peace march across Belgium calling for the abolition of nuclear weapons, recording the ten-day experience in photographs and words*23. For her next book, I Don’t Sleep, she traveled between Tokyo and Kure, photographing her family home, relatives, and her mother’s body and working hands*5. In 2007, she moved to New York through the Japanese Agency for Cultural Affairs’ overseas study program for emerging artists, photographing both the city and domestic interiors for about five years*11. After returning to Japan in 2012, she began living in Hiroshima in 2013 and developed Here Goes River while walking along the city’s waterways. The Hiroshima Prefectural Art Museum describes how Fujioka photographed a city where daily life overlaps with past events, treating rivers whose direction changes with the tides as a figure for memory*8. She now works between Kyoto and Hiroshima*1. Across travel, return, and relocation, she repeatedly revisits photographs after time has passed, using them to understand experiences that were not apparent when the pictures were made.

sections.title: The Core of Her Work
sections.body_html:
Snapshot Photography — Preserving What Escapes Explanation

Street snapshots are the starting point of Fujioka’s method. She has said that as a student she repeatedly studied Henri Cartier-Bresson’s photobooks, admired his ability to seize an instant, and has continued to photograph in the street ever since*4. Her present approach does not allow the decision made at exposure to determine the photograph’s final meaning. In Hiroshima, she made an enormous number of pictures because beginning with a theory or intention made it harder to photograph; she later found that the images showed her things she had looked at but failed to notice*2. When reviewing old negatives, she also discovered that she had repeatedly photographed children and flowers, prompting her to consider her own unconscious choices and the reasons she takes photographs*13. Fujioka’s snapshots preserve people and objects that slipped outside her conscious understanding. Later selection brings those overlooked elements to the center of the work.

I Don’t Sleep — Her Mother’s Hands and the Unknown Within the Familiar

I Don’t Sleep was made from photographs of Fujioka’s family and hometown, taken while she lived in Tokyo and returned regularly to Kure. SIGMA SEIN notes that the series was photographed during visits between 2000 and 2006, and that her mother appears through her back and oblique profile, working hands, and gestures more often than through a frontal portrait*5. Fujioka has said that exhibiting the work at the Nikon Salon allowed her to see the flow of the photographs more objectively, while the photobook required repeated decisions about what to include and omit*3. In its large format, sequences of hands, hair, clothing, flowers, domestic objects, and fragments of the body hold together intimacy with family and the sudden realization that those closest to her remain unknowable. The book leaves intimacy, aging, and estrangement from her hometown unresolved instead of explaining identities and relationships like a family album. The English-language annual report Photographic Expression in Japan, published in the year of the book’s release, likewise identified the raw and strange qualities of family bodies and behavior as a defining feature, indicating an early reception that exceeded the category of intimate record*18.

Walking in Belgium — Ten Days Inside a Peace March

The 2005 series Walking in Belgium records, in photographs and words, a peace march calling for the abolition of nuclear weapons that Fujioka joined almost by chance. Over ten days and roughly 300 kilometers, she later recalled becoming so absorbed in the march and its encounters that her awareness of taking photographs began to recede*23. Fugensha presents the experience as an event that occurred about a decade before Here Goes River, placing both works within a continuing engagement with peace and war. Fujioka entered the movement without first organizing a settled position and without fully understanding what she herself was doing. The photographs and words revisit, twenty years later, what it meant to become caught up in the event rather than state a conclusion from outside it. A direct line of influence on Here Goes River cannot be established, but the series anticipates her later tendency to approach historical subjects through events on the ground and her own responses, without reducing them to symbols.

Here Goes River — Why Photograph Everyday Hiroshima?

In the Hiroshima of Here Goes River, the history of the atomic bombing already existed as a powerful set of received images. Fujioka has said that after beginning life in the city, she came to understand how difficult it was to register history through the dense layers of everyday experience. Her view of contemporary Hiroshima also included the many ceremonies and expressions organized around “peace”*6. Early in the project, the more she considered how “Hiroshima” ought to be photographed, the less able she was to take pictures, burdened by the responsibility of producing an image that would stand for history*3. She instead photographed people playing by the river, young people posing, passing bodies, seasonal light, and incidents in the street. Without deciding in advance which symbols would explain Hiroshima, she followed what caught her attention in daily life. The Atomic Bomb Dome and forms that evoked past events then appeared in parts of the frame she had not treated as central while photographing. History emerged by changing the meaning of present-day images when she returned to them later.

Hiroshima mon amour — “Seeing, Yet Not Seeing”

While developing Here Goes River, Fujioka showed editor Nozomi Himeno and designer Hisaki Matsumoto Alain Resnais’s Hiroshima mon amour, scripted by Marguerite Duras, and told them that it suggested something she wanted to do in a photobook. Relating herself to the opening exchange—“I saw it” / “You saw nothing”—she described thinking about a self who was “seeing, yet not seeing”: she lived in Hiroshima and thought she knew the city, but could not present an image and declare, “This is Hiroshima”*3. In a 2025 interview, she again said that photography becomes interesting outside logic and intention, and that images taught her about things she had looked at without noticing*2. A photograph does not merely confirm prior knowledge; it can reveal, after the fact, that the photographer’s understanding at the time was incomplete. Ambiguous photographs and scenes resistant to explanation helped keep Hiroshima from being confined to a single, legible image.

Seven Rivers and Photobook Sequencing — History Through Repetition

In Here Goes River, the seven rivers crossing Hiroshima’s delta are both locations and a model of time that does not move in one direction. Akaaka describes the book as a current whose snapshots reveal relations between history and the present, society and the individual, while moving backward and forming eddies*7. Fujioka and Himeno initially shaped a sequence with narrative in mind. Matsumoto interrupted that explanatory flow and included blurred or indeterminate photographs that were difficult to judge as conventionally “good snapshots”*3. Bicycles, children, rivers, bodies, and the Atomic Bomb Dome recur on separated pages without being assigned one-to-one meanings. The Ina Nobuo Award jury praised juxtapositions in which contemporary bicycles and floodwaters evoke archival images of the bombing and the rivers of August 6, 1945*6. Past and present are not equated. Repetition across distant pages allows the past to be recalled through contemporary scenes.

From Film to Digital — How to Select from an Overwhelming Number of Images

Here Goes River was also made while Fujioka was moving from film to digital cameras. She has described the change in equipment as a shift that transformed both how she photographed and how she presented images—changing the basic character of her process*3. Once the number of exposures became enormous, the work could no longer be determined by the finish of individual pictures alone. Decisions about what to retain and which ambiguous images to include assumed greater weight. Years of walking through Hiroshima produced photographs containing not just intended subjects but also elements that had entered the edge or background of the frame by chance. During later selection, the distance became clear between the Hiroshima she thought she understood while photographing and the city that emerged from the accumulated images.

Life Studies — New York Found Thirteen Years Later

Life Studies, published in 2025, draws on photographs made during roughly five years in New York beginning in 2007 and selected after a long interval. According to Akaaka, the book contains 168 color and black-and-white images made between streets and rooms, moving from an initial encounter with the city through the wandering of an immigrant and toward increasingly private scenes*11. Fujioka has said that the book took about thirteen years to complete. Although its basic structure emerged early, she repeatedly added and removed images and revised the text until shortly before printing*4. Her observation that photographs once made simply to relieve boredom later became important shows that the judgments formed at exposure did not determine the finished work*4. Children, interiors, shadows, objects, and minor incidents in the street take precedence over emblematic views of New York, and the period of living there unfolds through a sequence that moves from public streets toward private space.

Photography as a Record — Old Photographs and Local Memory in Oda

Fujioka’s current activities include “Oda Minzoku Kotohajime,” a community project developed with residents of Oda in Kawachi, Higashihiroshima. In photography workshops, she encouraged participants to photograph whatever interested them in familiar places—the home or garden—instead of searching far away for exceptional subjects. The project also collected old local photographs. Conversations around a single image drew out different memories from different people, including details of work, customs, and daily life that rarely survive in official local histories*2. Fujioka has said that if photographs and words are not preserved, local events may come to seem as though they never happened*2. The aim is not one image that stands for a grand history, but multiple accounts preserved through photographs before personal memories disappear. The project differs in form from Here Goes River, yet it makes explicit the same refusal to place ordinary life outside history.

Photobooks and Exhibitions — A Fixed Book, a Changing Installation

Fujioka does not repeat the same sequence in a photobook and an exhibition. She explains that installations can be adjusted according to wall height, the scale of the room, the viewing route, and how images appear in the space; this makes the exhibition an experimental form*4. In a photobook, the size of each image and the order of pages are fixed in print, and a single viewer can turn through them repeatedly. The flow developed through the exhibition of I Don’t Sleep became the basis of the book. In Here Goes River, exchanges with the designer broke apart an explanatory narrative. In Life Studies, thirteen years of selection reached a fixed form. Walls and the viewer’s movement alter relationships between photographs in an exhibition; format and page order determine the pace of looking in a book. Fujioka treats them as distinct constructions, not as two presentations of an identical sequence.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Comment te dire adieu — A Work Made from an Unplanned Journey

Comment te dire adieu gathers early photographs made while moving through Taiwan, Europe, Brazil, and other places. It received the Visual Arts Photo Award Grand Prix in 2004*1. The journey began before a photographic plan had formed, leaving many images of people, children, bodies, signs, and opaque encounters found by chance in the street instead of explanations of landmarks or local culture*2. Selection after her return foregrounded the people and scenes to which she had responded abroad rather than the itinerary itself. The method—giving greater weight to what is discovered later in a photograph than to the purpose present at exposure—continues from this early work through Life Studies.

I Don’t Sleep — Private Photographs Without Explaining the Family

Published by Akaaka in 2009, I Don’t Sleep places photographs of Fujioka’s family and family home in Kure within a large-format book. Editor Nozomi Himeno has recalled that although such private snapshots were often viewed through the discourse of onnanoko shashin (“girl photography”), Fujioka’s photographs contained both a perspective that surveyed individual scenes and the pressures surrounding women’s lives in regional Japan*3. Pages enlarging the crown of her mother’s head, working hands, her back, and domestic objects do not explain family relations. They hold together a gaze that wants to move closer and another that keeps its distance. Through scale and sequence, the book foregrounds the continuing unknowability of a familiar person more than the disclosure of private life.

Here Goes River — Encountering History in Present-Day Hiroshima

Akaaka published Here Goes River in 2017. The work received the 41st Ina Nobuo Award for fiscal year 2016, followed in 2018 by the Tadahiko Hayashi Award and the Kimura Ihei Photography Award*1. The Tokyo Photographic Art Museum holds chromogenic prints from the series made between 2013 and 2017*9. The Tadahiko Hayashi Award account praises Fujioka’s restrained photographs made while walking through the city across all four seasons, in which memories of the past surface within unremarkable scenes of present-day life*10. Repeated contemporary images make history felt inside the everyday without reenacting the bombing. The sequence was recognized as a way of picturing Hiroshima in the present, distinct from earlier “Hiroshima” photography centered on the bombing’s direct traces.

Life Studies — Suspending the Judgment Made at the Time of Exposure

Published in 2025, Life Studies comprises 192 pages, 168 color and black-and-white photographs, and a long text by Fujioka*11. She did not publish the New York photographs immediately. Work in Hiroshima intervened before she selected the earlier images more than a decade later. An eggplant and domestic objects that she had photographed to relieve boredom eventually became important records of her life at the time*4. As with the early journeys, the family in Kure, and the rivers of Hiroshima, the moment of exposure does not coincide with the completion of the work. The mismatch between an image’s initial assessment and its later selection becomes one of the book’s organizing conditions.

sections.title: Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Early Work Beyond “Girl Photography”

Fujioka began working in the 1990s and has recalled being invited to speak as one of the photographers associated with onnanoko shashin, or “girl photography”*4. The experience later led her back to negatives from her student years. In the 2021 exhibition Hana no Yukue and the 2022 project New Stories, she gathered subjects she had repeated unconsciously since that period—children and flowers among them—and reconsidered why she takes photographs*13. She can be compared with contemporary women photographers such as Yurie Nagashima, Rinko Kawauchi, and Asako Narahashi. Fujioka’s work, however, is distinguished by a time scale that repeatedly returns to decades of photographs involving travel, family, regional cities, and the history of Hiroshima. Images from her student years were presented in Hana no Yukue and New Stories through categories different from those of her later works.

Whose Point of View Has Street Photography Used to Picture the City?

Street photography developed as a major form of modern photography by recording chance events and human gestures in public space without staging them. In the 1930s, Henri Cartier-Bresson photographed fleeting arrangements of moving people and urban space, and his work became closely associated with the idea of the “decisive moment”*20. In postwar Japan, photographers who had lived through occupation, rapid urbanization, and political upheaval treated the street as a site of social change. Around PROVOKE in the late 1960s, grain, blur, camera shake, and contingent framing challenged the assumption that photography could describe the world clearly and neutrally*21. The 1968 exhibition A Century of Photography had already raised public questions about photographers’ wartime responsibility and the credibility of documentary images; Takuma Nakahira and Kōji Taki, who participated in editing the exhibition, went on to launch PROVOKE*22. Cartier-Bresson, PROVOKE, and Fujioka cannot be joined as a direct line of influence. They nevertheless provide a useful comparison for tracing how street photography’s concerns expanded from seizing an instant in public space to considering the photographer’s own position and historical relationship to a place.

The “Reflexive Turn” — From Where Does Aya Fujioka Photograph Hiroshima?

Yoshiaki Kai argues that Japanese street photography after 1990 underwent a “reflexive turn,” incorporating the photographer’s own relationship to the place photographed; he cites the Hiroshima works of Aya Fujioka and Keiko Sasaoka as examples*15. “Reflexive” here means that the image addresses not just what a city looks like, but who is photographing it, from what position, and with what relation to the place. Canonical accounts of street photography have often presented anonymous passersby and fleeting incidents as scenes discovered in public space. For Fujioka, who was born in Kure and later returned to live in Hiroshima, the street is not a detached field of observation. Her private photographs of family in Kure and her street photographs of Hiroshima’s rivers and roads do not belong to separate domains. High school students dancing in front of the Atomic Bomb Dome, play along the river, and rooms crowded with household objects register the city’s present alongside the experience of return, family memory, and the distance produced by living amid Hiroshima’s history. Fujioka retains the sensation of the “instant” she admired as a student while selecting, years later, elements she did not consciously notice at exposure. Because selection continues long after the shutter is released, the work’s meaning is not completed in that instant; her relation to the place becomes visible over time*4. In Here Goes River, chance encounters in the street become a form capable of including the photographer’s own belonging and memory.

Things She Carries — Approaching War Through Life in the Present

The 2023 exhibition Things She Carries at SEIZAN Gallery in New York brought together Miné Okubo, Aya Fujioka, and Yukiko Hata. It considered how the Second World War has been represented and how its history remains within the experience of women living in the present*16. The exhibition introduced Here Goes River as a project that began as a personal record through which Fujioka sought to recover a relationship with her hometown, then turned toward photographing the contemporary city instead of a “Hiroshima” fixed as a sign of catastrophe. At an artist talk in New York, it was reported that a photograph of high school students practicing a dance in front of the Atomic Bomb Dome had been criticized on social media for dishonoring the victims’ memory*17. Fujioka explained that without the Dome the image would not carry the same meaning, and that she wanted the symbols contained in the photograph to prompt viewers to think instead of imposing a single lesson. Her report that the same image drew no backlash when shown in Tokyo demonstrates how reception changes with the location of an exhibition. In a different response, the World Socialist Web Site argued that the 2025 London exhibition hiroshima, by treating war through everyday life and personal memory, risked pushing the political and historical causes of the atomic bombing into the background*19. In Here Goes River, everyday life does not replace history. The act of photographing the present brings the work into an active dispute over what Hiroshima should preserve as memory.

Compared with Ken Domon’s Hiroshima — Where Does History Appear in a Photograph?

Ken Domon photographed Hiroshima in 1957 and published the photobook Hiroshima the following year. The Met describes the book—containing survivors, hospitals, an orphanage, people blinded by the bombing, and families rebuilding their lives—as a major work in the history of Japanese photobooks*24. Writing about Here Goes River, ARTnews JAPAN observed that Fujioka evokes the “Hiroshima” latent within quiet daily scenes, including high school students dancing in front of the Dome and elementary school pupils looking in the same direction, through a method different from Domon’s*25. Their difference cannot be reduced to direct versus indirect expression, or to a contest between an older realism and a newer approach. Domon’s photographs include hospital and family life; Fujioka’s contain the Atomic Bomb Dome as an explicit historical sign. The distinction becomes clearer when asking where the history of the bombing appears in the image. Domon centered wounded bodies and ongoing damage, demonstrating that the atomic bombing had not become past. Fujioka photographed Hiroshima more than seventy years later, when people playing by the river, dance practice, school commutes, family life, and historical signs coexist within the same urban time. Here Goes River does not make the damage invisible. It uses distance and recurrence between photographs to register the past in a period when its direct traces have become harder to distinguish from everyday life.

Awards and Reassessment — Questions That Continue Beyond Hiroshima

After Here Goes River received three awards, Fujioka presented New Stories, selected from earlier negatives; Hana no Yukue, based on photographs of flowers made over many years; and Life Studies, drawn from her New York archive. The 2023 Higashikawa Awards New Photographer Award considered several of these recent activities, including New Stories, a group exhibition addressing third-wave feminism, and Hana no Yukue*13. From 2024, I Don’t Sleep appeared in I’m So Happy You Are Here and related exhibitions reassessing Japanese women photographers from the 1950s to the present*3. In 2025, the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum included Fujioka among the contemporary artists in its thirtieth-anniversary exhibition*12. That year, The Guardian introduced Here Goes River as a series in which the weight of the past remains within the everyday life of contemporary Hiroshima*14. Reception now extends beyond Here Goes River to her early family photographs, selections from old negatives, and New York work.

yuki-tawada.html.title: Yuki Tawada | Burned and Scraped Photographs and I am in You | Photo Coordinates
yuki-tawada.html.meta_description: Yuki Tawada scrapes, burns, and layers photographs of cities, crowds, family members, and the sea, turning the photographic surface into a site of memory, healing, and ritual. Through WHITE OUT, Burnt Photographs, and I am in You, this page examines the necessity of her methods and her place in photographic history.
yuki-tawada.html.lead_html: Yuki Tawada’s work begins with photography’s double status: it circulates as an objective record while acting forcefully on memory and the unconscious. She scrapes, burns, and layers prints of cities, crowds, family members, and the sea. Through WHITE OUT, Burnt Photographs, and I am in You, this page traces how she returns the mark of the hand to mass-consumed images and transforms photography from a device of preservation into an object through which forgetting, healing, and ritual can be tested.
yuki-tawada.html.thesis_html: Tawada made the photographic surface a site of production, working from photography’s dual role as evidence of reality and as an emotionally charged surrogate for its subject. Damaging the image becomes a means of rendering the unseen force of crowds, releasing subjects gathered in the city from stasis, and approaching fear of the sea and family memory. To make photographs speak again, she treats the support as active material rather than a neutral carrier.
yuki-tawada.html.keywords_html: Keywords WHITE OUT Burnt Photographs I am in You Photographic Materiality Phototherapy Folk Belief Post-Photography

sections.title: Toward Photography as Object: Education and an Interest in Healing
sections.body_html:
Tawada began to study photography seriously while an exchange student at the University of California, Santa Barbara, during her time at Tohoku University. Drawn to the medium there, she went on to major in photography at Camberwell College of Arts, University of the Arts London, before completing master’s and doctoral programs in Intermedia Art at Tokyo University of the Arts*1. At Camberwell, her attention shifted from composing what the camera recorded to the physical properties of the photograph and the possibility of intervening in its surface*12.

Her turn toward paper and surface cannot be understood as material experiment alone. In a later official statement, Tawada explains that she works with photography because it is publicly treated as an objective medium even as it acts deeply on private emotion and the unconscious*2. The photographic surface became a meeting point between depicted content and the body’s response to the image.

Her master’s thesis at Tokyo University of the Arts, “A Method of Treating Memory through Photography,” considered how photography might participate in psychological healing through phototherapy. According to the examination summary for her doctoral dissertation, “The Contemporary Significance of Magic Realism,” Tawada sought to introduce aura and emotional movement into still photographs and to render unseen forces operating within everyday life through tactile methods informed by sympathetic magic and art therapy*14. Healing here lies less in a finished artwork’s medical efficacy than in reorganizing one’s relation to memory and fear through the act of touching photographs. Tawada’s account of feeling that her own face was being burned when she applied a heated iron to a self-portrait shows how a photograph can be experienced both as a paper object and as a surrogate for its subject*6. This duality led her interventions on the surface beyond formal experimentation and toward acts that engage memory and emotion.

sections.title: Core of Her Work
sections.body_html:
Making Photographs Speak Again in a Culture of Image Consumption

Her official statement frames the work as a search for ways to make photographs consumed amid the overabundance of information in contemporary life speak again, beyond the reproduction of magical or therapeutic effects*2. This concern, articulated later in her career, runs through the scraping, folding, and burning she has pursued since WHITE OUT. Manual intervention does more than add an effect. It records the history of someone touching the photograph, hesitating, choosing, and making an irreversible change.

At a 2025 workshop at Fotografie Forum Frankfurt, Tawada framed the assignment around “experiencing a photograph as an object,” “beginning a story through touch,” and allowing “traces to open memory and reality”*11. By retaining the reality recorded by the camera while adding scratches, folds, and burns to its surface, she gives physical form to memories and emotions that had no visible shape at the moment of exposure. This is how her idea of magic realism becomes a concrete working method.

WHITE OUT: Erasing the Crowd’s Information to Draw an Unseen Force

In the early major series WHITE OUT, Tawada abrades large-format prints of crowds in stadiums and cities with erasers, needles, and sandpaper. A 2007 exhibition text explains that she sought to capture the energy that arises once a crowd passes a certain scale, rather than individual facial expressions, and that erasing the image released a torrent of white light*7.

A crowd photograph can record faces, clothing, seats, and architecture in detail, yet the excitement, anxiety, conformity, and frenzy generated by a group do not appear in the figure of any single person. Instead of adding more information, Tawada removes parts of the recorded bodies and makes the white beneath the ink function as light, smoke, or explosion. The doctoral dissertation’s idea of introducing “movement” into the still photograph to render unseen emotional forces is enacted here through erasure*14. Scraping becomes a reverse form of drawing. By reducing the details through which the crowd is read as a collection of individuals—faces, clothing, and other markers—Tawada adds the group’s previously formless force as a white trace.

Burnt Photographs: Sacrificial Motifs and the “Empty Shell”

With Burnt Photographs, Tawada adds fire to the more controlled process of scraping the surface. She likens the work to drawing out and releasing something like the soul of a subject trapped in the print, and calls a burned photograph an “empty shell” that retains a presence after the substance has departed*6.

The choice of subjects is deliberate. They include taxidermied animals, tropical plants in botanical gardens, dances performed for tourists, religious objects removed from temples and shrines, and people who left their home regions for the city—all displaced from their original land or purpose and turned into objects of display, performance, or observation. Tawada links flowers, animals, Buddhist figures, halos, and dancing bodies to motifs once offered in sacrifice, writing that burning returns the fixed photograph to an organic state*6. Photography can transport a subject into the city and fix it as a specimen; burning opens that fixity back into change.

Erasers and needles allow comparatively fine control over gesture and form. Fire irreversibly alters the paper’s contour, strength, and thickness as well as the image. Tawada’s experience of feeling that her face was actually being burned when she burned a self-portrait reveals the difficulty of fully separating photograph and subject in the psyche*6. The sense that an act performed on an image can reach the thing it depicts parallels the logic of sympathetic magic, in which effects pass between things that resemble or have touched one another*20. Burning carries contradictory sensations of harm, sacrifice, and release. Tawada has described both the pleasure of breaking a taboo and, ultimately, a feeling of being forgiven by the subject*6. Fire’s irreversible transformation gives material form to the psychological identification between photograph and subject by taking it on as damage to the paper.

I am in You and Family Ritual: Approaching Fear and Family Memory

I am in You, Tawada and her mother burned photographs of waves breaking on shore against the background of her intensified fear of the sea after the Great East Japan Earthquake. On a gallery tour, she explained that she repeatedly burned away the water while preserving the sea foam in an attempt to soothe her fear of the sea and the injury it had left*19.

Tawada applies fire to the photograph that recorded the sea itself, keeping the fear tied to its source. By repeatedly touching an image that points to past reality and deciding with her mother what to retain and what to let disappear, fear moves from an emotion enclosed in the mind to a concrete task carried out together. Shadow Dance and Family Ritual also use photographs and archival images from the maternal line. The roles of photographer, owner, subject, and person altering the image overlap, extending private memory into a process handled within the family*4. Healing appears as the creation of an order and duration through which fear and the past can be approached via photographs, rather than as their erasure.

Making Loss Spatial: Why the Prints Are Layered, Lifted, and Suspended

Tawada does not press her burned prints flat against a single wall. She layers them, lifts them on pins, and sometimes suspends them from the ceiling. Seeing as Though Touching at the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum treated photography as matter with a support, surface, and mode of installation, as well as depicted content, and presented I am in You as a central example*5.

A flat photograph hung on a wall encourages the viewer to read the image frontally. Hiroshi Uemura argues that experiencing a photograph as an object requires an installation that prompts changes in viewpoint—walking around the work, peering into it, or looking upward*10. When lifted and layered, the burned holes disclose another water surface or the wall behind; charred edges cast shadows; and the overlap of images changes with the viewer’s position. Loss no longer remains blank space. It transmits light, reveals another image, and becomes a spatial structure that sets the viewer in motion.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
WHITE OUT and Missing Folklore: Crowds and the Urban Unconscious

WHITE OUT strips information from images of crowds and renders the force arising across the group as white form. In the subsequent Missing Folklore, erasure extends to architecture, roads, and night views; contours and signs that identify the city are replaced by white traces*3. The Japan Times described the exhibition as a group of large works in which the surfaces of urban photographs had been scraped, blurred, and scratched*8.

As her subject shifts from people to the city, the underlying problem remains: the visible appearance captured by the camera cannot fully convey the feelings and memories that animate a place. Removing place names, functions, and identifying details shifts the city from a legible location into a psychological field where heat, tension, and forgetting overlap. The white scars keep the city grounded in reality while adding forces that operate within it but do not register directly in a photograph.

From Shadow Dance to Ash and Ceramics: What Remains after the Image

In Shadow Dance, Family Tree, and I am in You, burned family and seascape photographs are reconstructed in layers, so that loss within the image, support, and shadow form a single work. The 2024 book Her smoke rose up forever brings together series on matrilineal memory and collaborations in which the ash of burned photographs becomes glaze on ceramic works by Fuku Fukumoto*15.

In these collaborations, the photograph persists as ash fixed to a ceramic surface after it can no longer be read as an image*16. The progression from print to charred paper, ash, and glaze holds preservation and disappearance together. Image information is lost, while the matter that composed the photograph and the history of its making pass into another support. Tawada’s “empty shell” is a form for sensing presence in matter after the image has departed, rather than destruction that leaves nothing.

Presented at Fotogalerie Wien in 2025, Lachrymatory was described as a work in which participants burned personal photographs they had brought and used the ash in the glaze of tear vessels, transferring private memory into a tangible form while questioning the materiality of images and the fragility of memory*21. In a French article on the Rencontres d’Arles, curator Mariko Takeuchi explained that Tawada also uses the remains of found snapshots made by ordinary consumers, addressing invisible connections between her own family and anonymous families*22. Even after private photographs lose their original owners and contexts, their burned remnants and ash can become material for new relations.

In Scent of the Sky (2025), she also tested a structure in which viewers or owners intervene in the work’s transformation, leaving its final state and moment of completion to the owner*23. Photographic transformation thus extends beyond the passage from paper to ash or ceramic to questions of time and ownership: who touches the work, and when it is considered complete.

Post-Photography: Giving Reproducible Images a Singular History

With Shigeo Goto and others, Tawada organized Photography Mutates: MUTANT(S) on POST/PHOTOGRAPHY, presenting photography as a medium that changes state among print, three-dimensional form, moving image, and digital processing*13. In an essay on the project, Keiju Kita takes Tawada’s statement—“for now, we can still let materials speak”—as a point of departure and analyzes how images originally made for a photobook are reused in THEGIRLWHOWASPLUGGEDIN and repeated as material within the exhibition space*18.

Post-photography here does not mean what comes after photography’s end. It names the way one image acquires a different temporality and mode of touch each time it moves among book, print, cut paper, installation, ash, and ceramic. In 2025 Tawada described photographs, in an era when AI can generate images resembling reality, as “touchable dreams” marked by the hand*12. Scraping, folding, and burning do not signal a return to analog photography. They inscribe infinitely reproducible images with a history of a particular person touching, judging, and making an irreversible alteration.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Healing and Ritual: Changing One’s Relation to Memory

In Tawada’s master’s and doctoral research, healing lies in changing one’s relation to memory and fear by touching photographs, repeating actions, and working with others; it is not a medical effect delivered by the finished work. In I am in You, she and her mother repeatedly burned away the water while preserving the foam, turning fear of the sea into a duration they could work through together. The work leaves fear unresolved and shows the sequence and duration of actions constructed to approach it.

Charred edges, lace-like holes, and overlapping shadows have a strong visual impact. Their beauty and the skill of burning can come forward so quickly that the family history, fear, and urban displacement behind them recede. In a 2018 exhibition review, Kotaro Iizawa observed that although the works’ material presence attracts attention, it is underwritten by conviction and urgency in grasping reality through this method*9. Reading the works therefore requires attention to the form of the damage, the photographed subject, the person making the alteration, the collaborators, and the extent of transformation.

Photographic Materiality and Magic Realism

Photography historian and anthropologist Elizabeth Edwards argues that an exclusive focus on depicted content obscures the photograph’s status as an object that is made, handled, stored, and damaged*17. Art historian Toshiharu Ito likewise notes that photographic supports have repeatedly changed over the medium’s short history and writes that the photographic image has continually searched for a body in which to dwell. He interprets Tawada’s handwork as an attempt to reawaken photography’s magical materiality and aura*2. Seeing as Though Touching at the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum approached photography and moving images as material media that act on the viewer’s senses*5. Tawada’s work can therefore be situated within debates about photographic materiality and post-photography that intensified after the 2000s.

Tawada belongs to a broader field of material approaches to photography. The 2024 international exhibition I’m So Happy You Are Here organized the work of Japanese women photographers around three lines: observation of everyday life, critiques of social roles, and experiments with and expansions of photographic form. Alongside prints, it presented installations, moving images, and photobooks as part of photographic history*24. Tawada’s work appeared within this broader movement beyond the flat print.

The Photographers’ Gallery Bookshop in London likewise describes her scraping and burning as an inquiry that crosses photography, painting, and sculpture and pursues photography as a material medium*25. This is an example of international reception rather than an academic classification, but it shows that Tawada is being introduced as an artist who expands photographic form beyond material experiment alone.

Tawada extends the exposure of the support into questions of photography’s surrogate function and emotional force. Because a photograph is received as objective evidence while also acting as a proxy for its subject, physical interventions in the image become ways of engaging unseen forces, fear, and memory. In her doctoral dissertation, magic realism is defined less as a technique for producing fantasy detached from reality than as a process of psychological healing that gives tactile trace to feelings and auras at work within visible everyday life*14.

The “aura” and magical force invoked in her official statement do not call for a literal revival of older beliefs. They describe a way of returning nonexchangeable histories—scratches, burns, the uncertainty of the hand, and labor shared with family—to images that are endlessly reproduced and consumed, allowing photography’s effect on feeling to be experienced anew. Tawada’s place in photographic history lies in her expansion of the photograph from flat image to three-dimensional object, and in her use of prints that retain traces of reality to give form to what photographic objectivity cannot easily hold. Material transformation, psychological healing, and rituals drawn from folk belief converge in a single working method.

og.title: Yuki Tawada | Burned and Scraped Photographs and I am in You | Photo Coordinates
og.description: Yuki Tawada scrapes, burns, and layers photographs of cities, crowds, family members, and the sea, turning the photographic surface into a site of memory, healing, and ritual. Through WHITE OUT, Burnt Photographs, and I am in You, this page examines the necessity of her methods and her place in photographic history.
